script: Brothers and sisters, good morning. Today we are going to learn a lesson together called “The Selfless Life”, with the subtitle “No Longer I, but Jesus”. Our theme verse is Galatians 2:20: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me.” Brothers and sisters, notice this: Paul is not boasting about how spiritual he is. He is bearing witness to one thing: someone else now sits at the centre of his life. That is “selflessness”.

In AD 1543 the Polish astronomer Copernicus, just before he died, published a book that said just one thing: the earth is not the centre of the universe. Brothers and sisters, have you noticed? Copernicus didn’t destroy the earth; he simply put the earth back where it had always belonged. Inside each of us there is an “earth-centred universe” too, and its language has only three phrases: I want, I feel, I think. Something happens, and our first reaction is, “I feel he shouldn’t treat me like this.” Our whole day goes round in circles inside those three phrases. Selflessness is not losing yourself; selflessness is changing the centre.

Galatians was written around AD 48 to 49, and it is Paul’s earliest letter. At the time some people were telling the Gentile believers: believing in Jesus isn’t enough; you must also be circumcised and keep the law. The context is even more striking. Chapter 2, verses 11 to 14, records that Peter had been eating at the same table as the Gentiles, but as soon as the men from James arrived, he drew back and separated himself. The Bible says he was “fearing those who were of the circumcision”. Brothers and sisters, it wasn’t that Peter couldn’t work out the theology — he was afraid. Afraid of what people would think, afraid of losing face. That is “the self-centred life”: while “I” still sit at the centre, even an apostle will play the hypocrite.

The first shift is a shift in the goal of our lives: no longer living for myself, but letting people see Jesus. Philip said to the Lord, “Lord, show us the Father.” How did the Lord answer? “He who has seen me has seen the Father.” Brothers and sisters, the whole life of the Lord Jesus was a transparent window. What people saw through him was the Father. And what about us? No longer chasing people’s praise, their attention, their liking, but letting people see, through the way we live, the glory, gentleness and reality of Jesus.

The Lord said, “For I have come down from heaven, not to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me.” Brothers and sisters, think about the moon. The moon gives off no light of its own; its surface reflects only twelve per cent of the light that falls on it — about as dark as old asphalt. Yet it can light up the whole night, because it faces the sun, and it never claims that the light is its own. When is the moon at its least bright? When it squeezes into the middle, wanting to stand right at the front — that’s called a solar eclipse. Brothers and sisters, when are we least able to let people see Jesus? Precisely when we push in front of Jesus. True revival is this: when people see you, they see Jesus.

The second shift is a shift in the way we live: no longer relying on myself, but wholly relying on Jesus. The Bible says, “Trust in Yahweh with all your heart, and don’t lean on your own understanding.” The Hebrew picture behind the word “trust” is leaning your whole weight on something, like someone lying full-length on a bed. Not steadying yourself with a hand, but resting your whole weight on it. God did not say, “Have no understanding”; God said, “Don’t lean on your own understanding.” You may use your head, but don’t rest your whole life on your head.

The Lord Jesus said, “The Son can do nothing of himself, but what he sees the Father doing.” If even the Son of God chose not to rely on himself, how much more should we? In 2009 the Max Planck Institute in Germany carried out an experiment: they had people walk through a forest and a desert. As long as they could see the sun or the moon, people could walk more or less in a straight line; but once there was no reference point in the sky, they began walking in circles without realising it — and were completely unaware of it. Brothers and sisters, isn’t that us? That is why 321 says: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the heart and you’ll be glad, rely on the brain and you’ll be troubled.

The third shift is a shift in the centre of gravity of our lives: no longer seeking my own benefit, but pleasing Jesus. Paul says, “Therefore also we make it our aim, whether at home or absent, to be well pleasing to him.” In the original, “we make it our aim” means “to be ambitious”. Brothers and sisters, Paul doesn’t tell us to abolish ambition; he redirects it. A truly selfless person does not ask, “Is this of any benefit to me?” but, “Will this make the Lord’s heart glad?”

Israel has two lakes, both fed by the same river Jordan. The Sea of Galilee has water coming in and going out, so its water is alive and fish abound. The Dead Sea only takes in and never gives out; it has no outlet, its salinity reaches around thirty per cent, and nothing living can survive in it. Brothers and sisters, the same source of water — so why is one a sea of life and the other a sea of death? There is only one difference: one is willing to give out, and the other keeps everything for itself. A life lived only for yourself looks like “storing up”, but really it is “turning to salt”. That is why the Two Core Values of 321 are: let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory.

Brothers and sisters, let’s practise. First, ask yourself every day: this thing I’m doing today — is it so that people will see me, or see Jesus? Second, when facing a choice, learn to lay down your own judgement and first pray: Lord, what do you want me to do? Third, name one thing in which you still cling to “satisfying myself”, and ask the Holy Spirit to help you turn it into “pleasing the Lord”. These three practices go together with the eight stages of changing our mindset: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication. Please remember: a change of mindset doesn’t come from being moved once; it comes from repetition.

One last reminder: selflessness is not disappearing; it is being renewed. When you lay down “me”, Jesus appears; when you stop being in control, God’s power goes to work. Brothers and sisters, the sun accounts for more than ninety-nine per cent of the total mass of the solar system, and the earth is insignificant beside it; yet the earth has not lost its worth because of that. It is precisely because it keeps to its place, going round the sun, that there are seasons, day and night, and life. The earth’s worth does not lie in whether it is the centre, but in whether it is in the right place. Are you in the right place today? Letting Jesus be King is not throwing you out; it is bringing you home.

Let us pray together. Dear Lord Jesus, we confess that the “I” inside us is far too big. Lord, today I am willing to be crucified with you. Please invite me down from the throne at the centre, and take your seat there. Holy Spirit, remind me every day: my goal is to let people see Jesus, my way is to rely wholly on Jesus, and my centre is to please Jesus. May every person I meet see you because they have seen me. In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen. May the Lord bless you and keep you; may the Lord make his face shine on you and be gracious to you; may the Lord lift up his face toward you and give you peace.

Brothers and sisters, good morning. Today we are going to look at a lesson together called “The Selfless Life”, with the subtitle “No Longer I, but Jesus”. Our theme verse is Galatians 2:20: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me.” Brothers and sisters, this verse is often treated as a spiritual slogan, but Paul is not boasting about how spiritual he is. He is bearing witness to something very concrete: someone else now sits at the centre of his life. Today we will look at three shifts: a shift of goal, a shift of means and a shift of centre.

I’d like to begin with a piece of the history of astronomy. In AD 1543 the Polish astronomer Copernicus, lying on his deathbed, received a freshly printed copy of On the Revolutions of the Heavenly Spheres. The book said just one thing: the earth is not the centre of the universe; the earth goes round the sun. At the time that sounded close to absurd, because people looked up at the sky and plainly saw the sun rise in the east and set in the west. Yet once humanity accepted that shift, the whole of astronomy for the first time could calculate accurately, see clearly and go far. Brothers and sisters, notice this: Copernicus did not remove the earth, nor did he destroy it. He simply put the earth back in the place where it had always belonged.

Inside each of us, too, there is a deeply rooted “earth-centred universe”. Its language is easy to recognise, because it has only three phrases: I want, I feel, I think. Something happens, and our first reaction is, “I feel he shouldn’t treat me like this.” A decision has to be made, and our first criterion is, “What do I want?” Our whole day goes round in circles inside those three phrases. Interestingly, in 2001 Marcus Raichle, a neuroscientist at Washington University in the United States, proposed the “default mode network”: when the brain is idle, the most active group of regions is chiefly busy thinking about “self”. Science cannot stand above the Bible, but it confirms from the side what Scripture said long ago. Brothers and sisters, selflessness is not losing yourself; selflessness is changing the centre.

Let’s look at the background. Galatians was written by Paul, and most scholars believe it is his earliest letter, written around AD 48 to 49 to the churches planted on his first missionary journey. At the time a group of Judaizing teachers were saying: believing in Jesus isn’t enough; you must also be circumcised and keep the law. Brothers and sisters, the essence of legalism has never been godliness; it is “the self-centred life”. The context of our theme verse is even more striking: in chapter 2, verses 11 to 14, Peter had been eating at the same table as the Gentiles, but as soon as the men from James arrived, he drew back and separated himself. The Bible says he was “fearing those who were of the circumcision”. It wasn’t that Peter couldn’t work out the theology — he was afraid. Afraid of what people would think, afraid of losing face. While “I” still sit at the centre, even an apostle will play the hypocrite.

The first shift is a shift in the goal of our lives: no longer living for myself, but letting people see Jesus. Once Philip said to the Lord, “Lord, show us the Father.” How did the Lord answer? “Have I been with you such a long time, and do you not know me, Philip? He who has seen me has seen the Father.” Brothers and sisters, every day the Lord Jesus lived on earth, his aim was not to make people know him, but to make them know the Father. His whole existence was like a transparent window. And what about us? Our lives today should bear witness to Christ in the same way: no longer chasing people’s praise, their attention, their liking, but letting people see Jesus through the way we live.

The Lord also said, “For I have come down from heaven, not to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me.” The word “will” in Greek is thelēma, meaning intention, purpose. Brothers and sisters, notice that it is not that the Lord Jesus had no will of his own. In the garden of Gethsemane he said, “Father, if you are willing, remove this cup from me.” He had feelings; he had desires. But straight after that he said, “Nevertheless, not my will, but yours, be done.” That is selflessness — not having no will, but placing your own will beneath the Father’s will. That is why the Lord could say: he who seeks his own glory is not true, but he who seeks the glory of him who sent him is true.

Brothers and sisters, think about the moon. The moon gives off no light of its own. Astronomers have measured it: the moon’s surface reflects only about twelve per cent of the light that falls on it — it is about as dark as old asphalt. And yet this grey, dull ball can light up an entire wilderness at night. Why? Because it faces the sun, and it never claims that the light is its own. What’s more interesting still: when is the moon at its least bright? When it squeezes in between the sun and the earth, wanting to stand right at the front — that’s called a solar eclipse. At that moment it blocks the light, and the sky goes dark. Brothers and sisters, when are we least able to let people see Jesus? Precisely when we push in front of Jesus because we want to be seen.

Why do we long so much to be seen? To a large extent, we have been taken hostage by an illusion. In 2000 Thomas Gilovich and his colleagues at Cornell University in the United States proposed the “spotlight effect”: they asked students to put on an embarrassing T-shirt and walk into a classroom full of people. The students guessed about half the people would notice; in fact only a quarter did. We live as though there were a spotlight above our heads, when in fact that light is switched on only inside our own hearts. That is why 321 says: the focus is Jesus — not ourselves, not other people, not our circumstances. And the Lord put it in perfect balance: “Even so, let your light shine before men; that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father who is in heaven.” The deeds are to be seen, but the glory is to be passed on. John the Baptist put it most beautifully of all: “He must increase, but I must decrease.”

The second shift is a shift in the way we live: no longer relying on myself, but wholly relying on Jesus. The Bible says, “Trust in Yahweh with all your heart, and don’t lean on your own understanding. In all your ways acknowledge him, and he will make your paths straight.” Brothers and sisters, notice: it is trust “with all your heart”, not with half of it. For if our goal is Jesus but the method is still “me”, the road still leads nowhere. Once the goal has changed, the means must change with it.

There are three Hebrew words in this verse worth pausing over. “With all your heart” literally means “with the whole of your heart”. The picture behind “trust” is vivid: it means leaning your whole weight on something, like someone lying full-length on a bed — not steadying yourself with a hand, but resting your whole weight on it. “Understanding” means discernment, comprehension. Brothers and sisters, God did not say, “Have no understanding”; God said, “Don’t lean on your own understanding.” Where is the difference? The difference lies in where you rest your whole weight. You may use your head, but don’t rest your whole life on your head.

The Lord Jesus said, “Most certainly, I tell you, the Son can do nothing of himself, but what he sees the Father doing.” Brothers and sisters, what astonishing words. The one speaking them is the Son of God. If even he, in his days on earth, chose not to act on his own, how much more should we? Joshua chapter 9 records how the Gibeonites put on worn-out clothes and carried mouldy bread to deceive the Israelites. It isn’t that the Israelites didn’t check — they looked at the clothes, touched the bread and listened to the story. The Bible explains why they were taken in with a single sentence: they “didn’t ask counsel from Yahweh’s mouth”. And the result was a mistaken treaty that stayed with Israel for hundreds of years.

In 2009 Jan Souman and his colleagues at the Max Planck Institute in Germany published a study in Current Biology. They had people walk through a forest and the Sahara Desert, recording their routes by GPS. They found that as long as the sun or the moon was in the sky as a point of reference, people could walk more or less in a straight line; but once clouds covered the sun, people began to walk in circles without realising it — and were completely unaware of it. Brothers and sisters, isn’t that us? Without an outside point of reference, a person is bound to walk in circles while believing he is moving forward. That is why Jeremiah says that the one who trusts in Yahweh is like a tree planted by the waters, which does not fear when heat comes, because its roots are not at the surface — they are in the water. 321 says: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the heart and you’ll be glad, rely on the brain and you’ll be troubled.

The third shift is a shift in the centre of gravity of our lives: no longer seeking my own benefit, but pleasing Jesus. Brothers and sisters, selflessness is not only humility in behaviour; it is a transformation of motive. Behaviour can be faked; motive cannot. So long as “satisfying myself” remains our starting point, our lives will still be held captive by Satan, even when what we do is good; but when we turn to seeking “to please the Lord”, we are set free from the dominion of sin. Paul says, “Therefore also we make it our aim, whether at home or absent, to be well pleasing to him.”

There are two Greek words here. “We make it our aim” literally means “to hold honour dear”, “to be ambitious”; in the Greco-Roman world it was a word full of drive. Brothers and sisters, Paul doesn’t tell us to abolish ambition; he redirects it: the one great ambition of my whole life is to please the Lord. The other word is “constrains”, which carries the sense of “gripping tightly, hemming in”, the way riverbanks hold the water in so that it can only rush in one direction. Paul says, “For the love of Christ constrains us… that those who live should no longer live to themselves, but to him who for their sakes died and rose again.” This change of motive does not come from gritting our teeth and holding on; it is love that drives it.

Israel has two famous bodies of water, both fed by the same river Jordan. In the north is the Sea of Galilee: the Jordan flows in from the north and flows out again to the south. Water comes in and goes out, so the water is alive, fish abound, and most of the Lord Jesus’ ministry took place there. In the south is the Dead Sea: the Jordan flows in and never flows out again, because there is no outlet. The water can leave only by evaporation, and the minerals build up year after year, until its salinity reaches around thirty per cent — roughly ten times that of ordinary seawater. The result? No fish can live there, and no water plants can grow. Brothers and sisters, the same source of water, the same sunshine — and only one difference: one is willing to give out, and the other keeps everything for itself. A life lived only for yourself looks like “storing up”, but in reality it is “turning to salt”.

In 2008 Dunn, Aknin and Norton published a study in the journal Science. In the morning they gave participants a sum of money; half were to spend it on themselves and half on someone else. That evening they measured how happy they were, and the group that had spent the money on others was clearly happier. The Bible is the highest standard and psychology can only play a supporting role, but this at least reminds us that human beings were made to flow out. The missionary Jim Elliot wrote in his journal in 1949: “He is no fool who gives what he cannot keep to gain what he cannot lose.” Six years later he was martyred in Ecuador; he was just twenty-eight. Brothers and sisters, this is precisely the Two Core Values of 321: let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory. Paul says we have this treasure in clay vessels; the moment a clay vessel starts drawing attention to how finely made it is, people can no longer see the treasure.

Let’s practise. The first practice: ask yourself every day, this thing I’m doing today — is it so that people will see me, or see Jesus? Today, deliberately choose one thing where you pass the credit on. The second practice: when facing a choice, learn to lay down your own judgement and first pray: Lord, what do you want me to do? This week, for every important decision, pray for three minutes before deciding, without exception; it must come before the decision, not after it. Both of these practices go together with the eight stages of changing our mindset: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication. Brothers and sisters, a change of mindset doesn’t come from being moved once; it comes from repetition.

The third practice: name one thing in which you still cling to “satisfying myself”, and ask the Holy Spirit to help you turn it into “pleasing the Lord”. Please grow quiet and pray: “Search me, God, and know my heart. Try me, and know my thoughts.” Then write it down specifically — perhaps a position you won’t let go of, a relationship you won’t forgive, a sum of money you won’t release your grip on. Writing it down is the beginning of conviction. Then hand it over in concrete terms. If you find you’re still clutching it, hand it over again. The Lord said, “If anyone desires to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross daily, and follow me.” Daily — not once. Finally, when you have experienced release, go and tell someone who is still in bondage; your freedom will become their hope.

Let’s spread out the whole picture of 321. The Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide. The Two Core Values: let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory. The Goal: establish God’s system. The self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall. The serpent said to the woman: you will be like God, knowing good and evil. When Satan fell, he said “I will” five times. So 321 puts it with great precision: pride is leaving our originally intended position and grasping power, wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down power and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God. Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win. Life first, then relationships, then ministry; everyone we relate to is our “2”, and we practise living out the selfless “0”, bearing the ninefold fruit of the Spirit.

Brothers and sisters, one last reminder: selflessness is not disappearing; it is being renewed. When you lay down “me”, Jesus appears; when you stop being in control, God’s power goes to work. Paul speaks of being “transformed by the renewing of your mind”, and in the original that is the very kind of change by which a caterpillar becomes a butterfly — the caterpillar is not destroyed; it is renewed. So selflessness is not passively letting go; it is actively turning round. Think about it: the sun accounts for more than ninety-nine per cent of the total mass of the solar system; yet the earth has not lost its worth because of that. It is precisely because it keeps to its place, going round the sun, that there are seasons, day and night, and life. The earth’s worth does not lie in whether it is the centre, but in whether it is in the right place. Brothers and sisters, are you in the right place today? Letting Jesus be King is not throwing you out; it is bringing you home.

Let us pray together. Dear Lord Jesus, we bow down before you. Lord, we confess that the “I” inside us is far too big; we want to be seen, we want to be affirmed, we want to do things our own way. Please forgive us. Thank you, Lord Jesus. Though you existed in the form of God, you emptied yourself and took the form of a servant; you humbled yourself and became obedient to the point of death. Lord, today I am willing to be crucified with you. Please invite me down from the throne at the centre, and take your seat there. Holy Spirit, remind me every day: my goal is to let people see Jesus, my way is to rely wholly on Jesus, and my centre is to please Jesus. May every person I meet see you because they have seen me. In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen. May the Lord bless you and keep you; may the Lord make his face shine on you and be gracious to you; may the Lord lift up his face toward you and give you peace.

sections.heading: Introduction: Who Is in the Pilot’s Seat of Your Life?
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning. Today we are going to reflect together on a lesson that looks simple yet takes a lifetime to learn — “selflessness”.

Let me begin with a rule from the world of aviation. In the cockpit of a passenger airliner, when control passes between the captain and the first officer, there is a set of call-outs that must never be left vague. The one handing the aircraft over says, “Your aircraft.” The one taking it replies, “My aircraft.” The one handing over confirms once more: “Your aircraft.” Only when those three lines have been spoken do his hands leave the controls. Why go to so much trouble? Because high in the air, the most dangerous situation is not that nobody is flying the plane, but that two people both think they are flying it — or that two people both think the other one is. When authority is unclear, disaster has already begun.

Brothers and sisters, our lives are an aircraft too. The spiritual predicament of many Christians is not that they don’t know Jesus, but that they have never clearly handed over the controls. With our lips we sing, “I will follow you,” but our hands still grip the yoke tightly. In the meeting we say, “Lord, you are King,” but back at the office, back at home, back in front of our bank account, the one reigning as king is still ourselves. And so our lives keep flying in a state of “two people fighting over the controls” — now high, now low, now hot, now cold, and utterly exhausted.

“Selflessness” is not an abstract spiritual idea; it is a way of living that has to be practised every day. It is not merely a wish in our prayers but a choice in our lives — in every thought, decision and action, laying down “my sovereignty” and letting Jesus truly reign. Revival does not begin with outward enthusiasm; it begins with inward surrender. When a person is willing to lay himself down and let the Lord have first place, the kingdom of God comes in his life.

Today’s message comes down to one sentence: hand over the controls and say, “Lord, it’s your aircraft.” You will be saying that sentence for the rest of your life — and every time you hand the controls over, the kingdom of God moves one step further forward.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: Two Passages, One Kingship
sections.html:
This lesson has two theme passages, one from the Gospel of John and one from the Gospel of Matthew; one is a man’s testimony, the other is the Lord’s teaching. Taken together, they give us the whole picture of “selflessness”.

Church history is unanimous that the author of the Gospel of John is John, the disciple whom the Lord loved. He wrote it in Ephesus in Asia Minor around AD 80–90, for a wide readership — Jews as well as Gentiles of the Greek world. John states his purpose in John 20:31: “but these are written, that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that believing you may have life in his name.” The backbone of the whole book is the exalting of Christ’s glory.

The scene in John 3:22–30 is an awkward case of “ministry competition”. Jesus’ disciples were baptising in the Judean countryside, and John the Baptist was also baptising at Aenon near Salim. John’s disciples came running to him with a complaint: “Rabbi, he who was with you beyond the Jordan, to whom you have testified, behold, he baptizes, and everyone is coming to him.” (John 3:26) That sentence is full of alarm — “everyone is coming to him”: our numbers are draining away, our influence is shrinking. It’s an anxiety every leader, every parent and every co-worker understands.

At exactly that moment John the Baptist spoke the words that have shaken every generation since. And before he said them, he laid down three sentences as groundwork. First: “A man can receive nothing unless it has been given him from heaven.” (John 3:27) Second: “You yourselves testify that I said, ‘I am not the Christ,’ but, ‘I have been sent before him.’” (John 3:28) Third: “He who has the bride is the bridegroom; but the friend of the bridegroom, who stands and hears him, rejoices greatly because of the bridegroom’s voice. This, my joy, therefore is made full.” (John 3:29) Only then came the summing-up: “He must increase, but I must decrease.” (John 3:30)

The original language deserves attention. “Increase” is the Greek αὐξάνω (auxanō), meaning “to grow, to increase, to become larger”; “decrease” is ἐλαττόω (elattoō), meaning “to lessen, to become smaller, to be lowered”. In the original both verbs are in the present tense, indicating an ongoing process — not a one-off stepping aside, but a lifetime of continually giving way, a daily, continual becoming smaller. More importantly, both verbs carry the force of “must”: this was not a fate John grudgingly accepted, but an order he willingly embraced.

The Gospel of Matthew, by contrast, was written for Jewish readers. Matthew had been a tax collector before he was called to be an apostle. He completed the book between AD 50 and 70, and it quotes the Old Testament again and again to prove that Jesus is the Messiah King the Old Testament promised. The Lord’s Prayer in Matthew 6 sits right at the centre of the Sermon on the Mount, and of its six petitions the first three are all about God — your name, your kingdom, your will — and only the last three are about us — our food, our forgiveness, our temptation. The order itself is a sermon: God first, then me.

“Your Kingdom come” — “kingdom” is the Greek βασιλεία (basileia). The emphasis of the word is not territory but “kingship, rule, reign”. So this line of the Lord’s Prayer means, “May your kingship come and be at work here.” And “will” is θέλημα (thelēma), meaning “desire, intention, what has been decreed”. In other words, the heart of the Lord’s Prayer is a handover of sovereignty: not my name, but your name; not my kingdom, but your kingdom; not my will, but your will.

Brothers and sisters, do you see it? What the prophet in the wilderness lived out over a lifetime is exactly what the Lord Jesus teaches us to pray every day. John says, “I must decrease”; the Lord teaches us to ask, “Your Kingdom come” — two sides of the same thing. Today, let us receive this lesson under three headings.

sections.heading: 1. The Core Definition of “Selflessness”: Laying Down Our Own Sovereignty and Letting Jesus Reign
sections.html:
“Selflessness” is not just an emotional humility; it is a transfer of authority. When we say, “Lord, may your will be done,” it means I no longer insist on my own ideas but am willing to let Jesus be King.

Please notice the distinction: emotional humility is a feeling; a transfer of authority is a decision. A person can be moved to tears in a meeting and feel very small, and then, as soon as the meeting ends, go straight back to his own throne. That is emotion, not selflessness. True selflessness is handing over “the final say” to the Lord in concrete matters.

The Lord Jesus himself is our role model on this road. On that night in Gethsemane he said, “Father, if you are willing, remove this cup from me. Nevertheless, not my will, but yours, be done.” (Luke 22:42) Look at the turning word — “nevertheless”. The Lord did not pretend he wasn’t in anguish; he honestly said, “remove this cup”. But after speaking his own will, he added one word: “nevertheless”. Brothers and sisters, the practice of “selflessness” very often takes place inside that “nevertheless”. You can have your ideas, you can have your struggles, you can pray honestly; but you must learn to add one sentence after every idea: “Nevertheless, not my will, but yours, be done.”

So it was with Paul too. He says, “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me.” (Galatians 2:20) “No longer I, but Christ” — this is not self-annihilation but a change of sovereignty. Paul is still Paul; his abilities, his learning, his passion are all still there. What has changed is who sits on the throne.

The first command the Lord Jesus gave to those who follow him is about exactly this: “If anyone desires to come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me.” (Matthew 16:24) “Deny” is the Greek ἀπαρνέομαι (aparneomai), meaning “to disown completely, to refuse to acknowledge”. Interestingly, the same word appears again a few chapters later, when the Lord says to Peter, “tonight, before the rooster crows, you will deny me three times.” (Matthew 26:34) When Peter “denied” the Lord, this is the word used. So this is what the Lord means: just as you once disowned me, so now you must disown yourself. When “self” pops up and says, “On this one, you should listen to me,” you need to be able to say to it, “I don’t know you.”

The life of “selflessness” can be measured by one question: “Whose hands hold the sovereignty over this matter?”

First, do I let my own reasoning be in charge, or the Lord’s word? Second, do I let my emotions control my decisions, or the Holy Spirit guide my actions? Third, do I rely on my experience to judge, or do I seek the Lord’s heart? The Bible puts it very clearly: “Trust in Yahweh with all your heart, and don’t lean on your own understanding. In all your ways acknowledge him, and he will make your paths straight.” (Proverbs 3:5–6)

There is a misunderstanding to avoid here: true “selflessness” is not losing your mind but bringing your mind into submission to Christ; not abandoning judgement but letting the Holy Spirit direct your judgement. God has never wanted us to become people without brains. What he wants is a renewed mind: “Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what is the good, well-pleasing, and perfect will of God.” (Romans 12:2) To “prove” takes thinking — only that thinking has been renewed and has submitted.

Psychology has a fascinating finding that helps us see through the self-deception of “self”. In 1975 the Harvard psychologist Ellen Langer published her famous study of the “illusion of control” in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology. She had participants take part in a lottery: one group was handed tickets at random, while the other could “pick their own”. The result? Those who had chosen their own tickets wanted a markedly higher price to sell them back — even though both groups had exactly the same chance of winning. As soon as people feel “I chose it myself”, they overestimate how much control they have over the outcome.

Brothers and sisters, we often cling tightly to sovereignty not because we can really control things, but because holding on feels safer. The book of James saw through this long ago: “Come now, you who say, ‘Today or tomorrow let’s go into this city, and spend a year there, trade, and make a profit.’ Whereas you don’t know what your life will be like tomorrow. For what is your life? For you are a vapor that appears for a little time, and then vanishes away. For you ought to say, ‘If the Lord wills, we will both live, and do this or that.’” (James 4:13–15) It turns out that what we’ve been gripping was never the control column at all — only a stick we hold to comfort ourselves.

From the perspective of 321, this is exactly the watershed between “the old self, self-centred, and the new self, selfless”. The self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall; pride is the root of every problem. Satan’s fall began with five “I will”s: “You said in your heart, ‘I will ascend into heaven! I will exalt my throne above the stars of God! I will sit on the mountain of assembly, in the far north! I will ascend above the heights of the clouds! I will make myself like the Most High!’” (Isaiah 14:13–14) Pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God. That is why we say: humility overcomes pride, and selflessness overcomes Satan.

And the “less” in “selflessness” is not zero, not emptiness, not nothing. Selflessness is entering the infinite and living out the infinite; “I” no longer live, but Christ lives in me. Only when a cup has been emptied can it hold something new; only when nothing blocks a pipe can living water flow through it. Selflessness doesn’t shrink you down to zero; it connects you to the Infinite One.

sections.heading: 2. The Role Model of “Selflessness”: The Life Testimony of John the Baptist
sections.html:
The life of John the Baptist is the finest portrait of “selflessness”. When the crowds began to leave him to follow Jesus, he was not jealous, he did not compare, he did not feel a sense of loss; on the contrary, he said joyfully, “He must increase, but I must decrease.” (John 3:30)

To feel the weight of those words, we first need to know just how “popular” John the Baptist was at the time. The Bible records: “Then people from Jerusalem, all of Judea, and all the region around the Jordan went out to him. They were baptized by him in the Jordan, confessing their sins.” (Matthew 3:5–6) Even King Herod feared him; even the priests and Levites came down from Jerusalem specially to ask him, “Who are you?” (John 1:19) He was the most influential spiritual leader in the whole land of Israel at the time. And then, at the very height of his influence, he pointed the crowds with his own hand towards another: “Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!” (John 1:29)

How could he do it? On the strength of the three sentences he had spoken earlier.

The first: “A man can receive nothing unless it has been given him from heaven.” (John 3:27) This is the eye of grace. A person who is convinced that everything he has was received will not cling to it as private property. Paul says, “For who makes you different? And what do you have that you didn’t receive? But if you did receive it, why do you boast as if you had not received it?” (1 Corinthians 4:7) The reason we find it so hard to let go is that we wrongly think it is “mine”.

The second: “I am not the Christ,” but, “I have been sent before him.” (John 3:28) This is the eye of our originally intended position. John knew clearly who he was, and knew clearly who he was not. The greatest confusion in the spiritual life is being unclear about our originally intended position — putting ourselves in God’s place, or putting someone else in God’s place.

The third: “He who has the bride is the bridegroom; but the friend of the bridegroom, who stands and hears him, rejoices greatly because of the bridegroom’s voice. This, my joy, therefore is made full.” (John 3:29) This is the eye of order. In Jewish wedding custom, “the friend of the bridegroom” played an important part in the wedding: he took charge of all the preparations, the arrangements and the escorting of the bride, rushing about for days on end. But on the wedding night, his job was to stand outside the door, hear the joyful voice of the bridegroom within, and then go home content. He never got one thing wrong: the bride was not his. Brothers and sisters, this is something every servant of God must learn: the flock is not mine, the children are not mine, the ministry is not mine, the fruit is not mine — the bride belongs to the bridegroom.

His focus was not on how many people he could attract, but on fulfilling what God had entrusted to him — preparing the way for Jesus. This is what “selflessness” really looks like: first, not measuring worth by results, but counting it an honour to make Jesus complete; second, not seeking to be seen, but seeking for Jesus to be seen; third, not fearing being replaced, because he knew he was only preparing the road for the Lord.

Speaking of “not seeking to be seen”, psychology has a very apt finding. In 2000 Thomas Gilovich of Cornell University and his colleagues described the “spotlight effect” in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology. They had participants put on an embarrassing T-shirt and walk into a room, then asked them to guess how many people had noticed. The participants generally assumed about half would notice; in fact only about a quarter remembered. It turns out that the spotlight we fear all our lives is mostly one we have trained on ourselves.

Brothers and sisters, so much of our anxiety, comparison and rivalry comes from living under a spotlight that doesn’t even exist. And John the Baptist’s freedom lay precisely in this: he had long since turned the spotlight round and trained it on the bridegroom. When you no longer need to be seen, you never again need to fear being replaced.

Management studies have made a similar observation. In Good to Great, published in 2001, Jim Collins studied eleven companies that had leapt from mediocrity to excellence, and found that their chief executives all had what he called “Level 5 Leadership”: a blend of personal humility and professional will. He observed that these leaders “look in the mirror” to take responsibility and “look out of the window” to give credit to others. A leader who truly achieves great things is often the one who least needs to be seen. If that is true even in the world, how much more in the kingdom of God?

The Lord Jesus’ verdict on John the Baptist was: “Most certainly I tell you, among those who are born of women there has not arisen anyone greater than John the Baptizer.” (Matthew 11:11) Brothers and sisters, this is God’s arithmetic: the one most willing to become small is the greatest in God’s eyes.

A life like this is a life that has laid down its sovereignty completely. When John the Baptist chose to “step back behind the scenes”, Jesus’ ministry was lifted high; when he chose “not to fight for a place for himself”, God’s will was brought to completion in him.

C. S. Lewis has a penetrating passage in Mere Christianity which says, in essence, that a proud man is always looking down on people and things; and as long as you are looking down, you can never see the One who is above you. The reason John could see the beauty of Christ was precisely that all his life he was looking up.

In 321 terms, this is “Jesus is the focal point — not ourselves, not other people, not our circumstances”. John’s disciples fixed their focus on someone else — “everyone is coming to him”; John fixed his focus on Jesus — “He must increase.” The same event, a different focus, and a completely different ending: focus on people, and comparison and jealousy are born; focus on the Lord, and joy and contentment are born. This is also the Two Core Values in practice: let Jesus be King; let Jesus receive all the glory.

sections.heading: 3. The Practice of “Selflessness”: Prayer and Action That Transfer Sovereignty
sections.html:
The Lord’s Prayer says: “Let your Kingdom come. Let your will be done on earth as it is in heaven.” (Matthew 6:10) The heart of this prayer is “laying myself down and letting the Lord reign”.

We should take note of the order of the Lord’s Prayer. When the Lord taught his disciples to pray, he said: “Our Father in heaven, may your name be kept holy. Let your Kingdom come. Let your will be done on earth as it is in heaven.” (Matthew 6:9–10) First “your name”, then “your Kingdom”, then “your will” — and only after that does it come to “our daily bread”. Brothers and sisters, if from the very first line our prayer is, “Lord, please give me …”, it shows that we are still sitting on the throne and simply treating God as a supplier. The Lord’s Prayer is a daily coronation: every time we pray it, we place the crown on the Lord’s head again.

The coming of God’s kingdom is not only an end-time hope; it is a discipline of daily living. Every time I choose to obey the Lord rather than myself, God’s kingdom expands a little further in me.

First, when I am willing to forgive someone who has wronged me, Jesus reigns in that relationship. Forgiveness is hard because it means giving up the right to “get justice”. The Lord says, “For if you forgive men their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you.” (Matthew 6:14) When you hand the right to judge back to God, God’s kingdom has come into that relationship.

Second, when I lay down my habit of wanting to control my family, Jesus is King in my home. Much of the pain in many families is not because there is no love, but because the love is mixed with control. Paul says, “subjecting yourselves to one another in the fear of Christ.” (Ephesians 5:21) “Subjecting yourselves to one another” — the moment those words walk through the door, the home gains one King and loses two kings.

Third, when in my service I don’t fight for credit or a name but only want the Lord to be glorified, God’s will is carried out in the church. The Lord says, “It shall not be so among you, but whoever desires to become great among you shall be your servant. Whoever desires to be first among you shall be your bondservant.” (Matthew 20:26–27)

God’s kingdom will not come into a heart that still insists on its own sovereignty; only a “selfless” heart can carry the glory of God’s kingdom.

The Old Testament has a startling contrast. King Nebuchadnezzar, walking on the roof of the royal palace of Babylon, said, “Is not this great Babylon, which I have built for the royal dwelling place, by the might of my power and for the glory of my majesty?” (Daniel 4:30) While the words were still in his mouth, the kingdom departed from him; he was driven away from people, ate grass like an ox, and seven times passed over him. When at last he lifted his eyes to heaven and his reason returned, he spoke entirely different words: “Now I, Nebuchadnezzar, praise and extol and honor the King of heaven; for all his works are truth, and his ways justice; and those who walk in pride he is able to abase.” (Daniel 4:37) Brothers and sisters, the same man, the same mouth — one time it’s “I built”, the other time it’s “his works”. Between “I” and “he” lay seven seasons in the wilderness. May we not need to go through such a wilderness; may we step down from the throne ourselves, today.

Scripture declares this spiritual law again and again: “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.” (James 4:6; 1 Peter 5:5) Peter goes on: “Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in due time.” (1 Peter 5:6) Notice that “humble yourselves” is an active verb — not waiting for circumstances to press you down, but stepping down yourself. This is the direction in which grace flows: grace is like water; it always flows to the lowest place. If you build yourself into a high platform, grace has no choice but to flow around you.

So will laying down our sovereignty make life lose its direction and its fruitfulness? Quite the opposite. There is a wonderful design in nature called “apoptosis” — programmed cell death — a concept formally proposed in 1972 by John Kerr and his colleagues. The cells in the human body, following their instructions, bring themselves to an orderly end at the proper time so that the whole body stays healthy. The webbing between an unborn baby’s fingers can separate into five nimble fingers precisely because those cells “deny themselves” on time. Conversely, when cells refuse to die and insist on expanding without limit, that is called cancer.

Brothers and sisters, how true this picture is: in the body of Christ, whatever insists on expanding itself becomes a source of disease; whatever is willing to deny itself in due time brings health and beauty to the whole. The Lord says, “unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains by itself alone. But if it dies, it bears much fruit.” (John 12:24)

This is exactly what 321 means by “life first, then relationships, then ministry”. Many people have the order reversed: they charge into ministry first, patch up relationships next, and think about life last of all — and so the bigger the ministry gets, the emptier the life and the more broken the relationships. The Lord’s order is this: first let Jesus be King in our life; then there will be forgiveness and submission in our relationships, and power and glory in our ministry. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things. And relationships have an order too: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last of all with things. If this morning you hand your sovereignty over to the Lord, your relationship “with God” is set right — and only then, for the rest of the day, can the other relationships be set right.

sections.heading: Integrating the 321 Vision: Selflessness Is the Ticket into God’s Kingdom
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, when we place today’s message within the framework of 321, it becomes clearer still.

The Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model — in Gethsemane he said, “not my will”, the highest demonstration of selflessness; the Bible is my standard — it isn’t right because I feel it is right; what the Lord’s word says is what counts; the Holy Spirit is my guide — not relying on our own cleverness, but relying on the heart and the Holy Spirit. The Two Core Values: let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory. The Goal: establish God’s system. Brothers and sisters, look: the three key points of this lesson are exactly a concrete unfolding of the Three Foundations, the Two Core Values and the Goal. The core definition of selflessness is letting the Bible be our standard and the Holy Spirit our guide; the role model of selflessness is letting Jesus be our role model; the practice of selflessness is letting Jesus be King and letting Jesus receive the glory, so that God’s kingdom — that is, God’s system — comes on earth.

The fivefold change shows that selflessness is a road with an order to it: change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living; change daily living and you change relationships; change relationships and you change ministry. Today what we ask for first is the first of the five — mindset. When your mindset shifts from “this is my life” to “this is the Lord’s life”, everything begins to be different.

The change of perspective is the other side of selflessness. From man’s perspective to God’s: John’s disciples saw “everyone has left”; John saw “the Lord has been lifted up”. From the earthly to the heavenly: earth’s arithmetic says whoever has the most people wins; heaven’s arithmetic says whoever is willing to become small is great. From the temporary to the eternal: influence will pass, applause will pass, but only the one who does God’s will remains for ever. From the worldly to the godly: the worldly wants to grab hold; the godly is willing to let go. The Bible says, “If then you were raised together with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated on the right hand of God. Set your mind on the things that are above, not on the things that are on the earth.” (Colossians 3:1–2)

The 920 practice puts selflessness to work in our relationships every single day. Everyone we are in a relationship with is our “2”; in front of every “2”, we practise living out “0” — the selfless life — and the result is the fruit of the Spirit in all nine of its expressions: “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control.” (Galatians 5:22–23) Brothers and sisters, notice: not one of these nine graces can grow in the soil of “the self-centred life”. A self-centred person cannot have true patience, because patience is precisely laying down your own rights; a self-centred person cannot have true gentleness, because gentleness is precisely having strength and not using it. Every difficult person you meet today is not an obstacle to you, but a lesson God has given you for practising selflessness.

The 235 relationships, for their part, are the fruit of a selfless life. Only when we are selfless within can we become a “2” with another selfless person — a genuine spiritual companion, transparent with each other and praying for each other; only then can we build the “3” — spiritual parents and spiritual children, willing to pass on all we have and rejoicing when our children surpass us; and only then can we finally become the “5” — a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades, of one heart in advancing the gospel. Brothers and sisters, think about it: whom do spiritual parents most resemble? John the Baptist. Because what spiritual parents do all their lives is point their children to Christ and then step back, gladly, into the background.

And the direction of all this is the Path of Serving: Spirit — the Holy Spirit is my guide; Understanding — the Bible is my standard; Life — Jesus is my role model; Service — let Jesus be King; God — let Jesus receive all the glory. From the inside out, from self to the Lord — this is the whole journey of selflessness.

sections.heading: Putting It into Practice: The Eight Stages from Information to Multiplication
sections.html:
The lesson gives us three exercises, and we will deepen them with “the eight stages of changing our mindset” — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.

Practice One: Pray every morning, “Lord, today the sovereignty is yours, not mine.”

Information: first let the truth in. Today you have already heard two passages — John 3:30 and Matthew 6:10. Copy them onto a piece of paper and stick it by your bed or next to the mirror. Revelation: ask the Holy Spirit to make these words not just knowledge but illumination. You might pray, “Lord, please show me what there was yesterday that I did not hand over to you.” Conviction: you must truly believe that handing it to the Lord is safer and better than keeping it in your own hands. Implementation: starting tomorrow morning, the first words when you open your eyes are that prayer — no more than ten seconds, but said out loud. Evaluation: before bed, spend two minutes looking back: at what moment today did I grab the controls back? Correction: not self-reproach, but handing them back at once — “Lord, I’m sorry, I took charge of this myself again; now I’m giving it back to you.” Repetition: keep practising for forty days in a row, until it becomes a habit. Multiplication: find a brother or sister, pass this practice on to them, and remind each other.

Practice Two: Before making a major decision, stop and ask, “Is this from me, or from the Lord?”

Information: learn the standard for discerning. Whatever does not agree with the Bible is certainly not from the Lord; whatever comes from the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes and the pride of life is certainly not from the Lord: “For all that is in the world, the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life, isn’t the Father’s, but is the world’s.” (1 John 2:16) Revelation: be still in prayer and let the Holy Spirit shine on your motives. David’s prayer is worth learning every day: “Search me, God, and know my heart. Try me, and know my thoughts. See if there is any wicked way in me, and lead me in the everlasting way.” (Psalm 139:23–24) Conviction: believe that “to obey is better than sacrifice” — “Samuel said, ‘Has Yahweh as great delight in burnt offerings and sacrifices, as in obeying Yahweh’s voice? Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice, and to listen than the fat of rams.’” (1 Samuel 15:22) Implementation: set yourself a rule — any decision above a certain sum of money, beyond a certain length of time, or affecting your family must be prayed over for a night before it is made. Evaluation: look back at three major decisions from the past six months. Which of them came from me? How did it turn out? Correction: if a decision came from self and went astray, ask the Lord’s forgiveness, and adjust wherever it can still be adjusted. Repetition: make “ask the Lord first, then decide” a fixed procedure in your family meetings. Multiplication: teach this principle to your children or to the members of your small group.

Practice Three: List three areas (such as time, money, relationships) where you most easily “take charge yourself”, and learn to hand the sovereignty over to Jesus.

A pastor named Robert Boyd Munger wrote a widely circulated little booklet, My Heart — Christ’s Home. He describes a man who invites Jesus to live in the house of his heart and hands it over room by room: the study, the dining room, the living room, the workshop; until one day the Lord notices a smell and, pointing to a small locked cupboard at the end of the hall, asks, “What’s in there?” It held the things he couldn’t bear to give up. Brothers and sisters, every one of us has a small locked cupboard like that in our heart.

Information: list three areas honestly. Don’t write spiritual platitudes; write their real names — my diary, my savings, my relationship with so-and-so. Revelation: ask the Lord to show you what that “locked cupboard” really is. Conviction: believe that the Lord is the most trustworthy manager of all: “Commit your way to Yahweh. Trust also in him, and he will do this.” (Psalm 37:5) Implementation: hand them over one area at a time. You might write a simple “handover document” — date, area, signature — declaring to the Lord that from today the sovereignty over this belongs to him. Evaluation: check once a week whether you have quietly taken anything back in these three areas. Correction: if you have taken it back, hand it over again; don’t let it go more than a week. Repetition: after three months, list three new areas. Multiplication: share in your small group how God has worked since you handed over the sovereignty, so that others gain the faith to hand theirs over too.

A Gentle Reminder

Laying down sovereignty is not losing control; it is handing control to the most trustworthy Lord. When you let Jesus be King, his wisdom and peace will guide you forward.

Brothers and sisters, remember: what you hand over is not handed to fate, not handed to luck, and not handed to people; it is handed to the Lord who laid down his life for you and loves you to the end. There is no captain in the world who knows better than he does how to bring you safely home.

sections.heading: Closing and Call: The Threshold of Revival
sections.html:
“Selflessness” is the threshold of revival. When we are willing to let Jesus reign, individuals, families, churches and indeed the whole kingdom will experience the works of God. Revival does not depend on how hard we try, but on how fully we surrender. Lay yourself down and let the Lord reign — this is the only road to the glory of God’s kingdom.

Brothers and sisters, what is a threshold? A threshold is the line you must step over before you can go in. You can stand outside the door for a long time; you can sing, attend meetings and serve outside the door for many years; but as long as you haven’t stepped over that threshold, you cannot enter the room. “Selflessness” is that threshold.

Augustine says in The City of God that two cities have been formed by two loves: the love of self, even to the contempt of God, formed the earthly city; the love of God, even to the contempt of self, formed the heavenly city. Brothers and sisters, which city are you building today?

Every true revival in history has begun not with a new method but with a broken heart. It is commonly said that as a young man D. L. Moody heard a sentence that stirred him deeply: “The world has yet to see what God will do with a man fully consecrated to him.” Moody said, “I will be that man.” Brothers and sisters, this morning, are you willing to be that person?

Let’s go back to that flight-deck call-out. Today the Lord is asking in your ear, “Is it your aircraft, or mine?” May we all be able to answer clearly and out loud: “Lord, it’s your aircraft.”

Let Jesus be King; let Jesus receive all the glory. May he increase; may I decrease. Amen.

keyVerses: “He must increase, but I must decrease.” (John 3:30)
“Let your Kingdom come. Let your will be done on earth as it is in heaven.” (Matthew 6:10)
declarations: Lord, I am willing to lay down my own sovereignty and no longer make decisions by myself. Reign in every area of my life. May your kingdom come, and may your will be done in me as it is in heaven.
practices: Pray every morning: “Lord, today the sovereignty is yours, not mine.”
Before a major decision, stop and ask: “Is this from me, or from the Lord?”
List three areas (such as time, money, relationships) where you most easily “take charge yourself”, and learn to hand the sovereignty over to Jesus
prayer: Dear Lord Jesus, we thank you. You are the King worthy of all glory, yet for our sake you emptied yourself, took the form of a servant, and became obedient to the point of death, even the death of the cross.

Lord, forgive us. With our lips we call you Lord, yet our hands still grip our own sovereignty tightly; in our meetings we surrender, yet in our daily living we still reign as king. Wash away our pride and our self with your precious blood.

Lord, this morning I hand the controls over to you. My time is yours, my money is yours, my family is yours, my service is yours, my future is yours. May your kingdom come in my thoughts and intentions, and may your will be done in my daily living as it is in heaven.

Holy Spirit, remind me every day: whenever “self” climbs back onto the throne, let me step down at once. Make me like John the Baptist, finding my joy in your increase and my contentment in your name being lifted high.
In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: John 3:27 says, “John answered, ‘A man can receive nothing unless it has been given him from heaven.’” In your life right now, what one thing (a gift, a position, a relationship, an achievement) are you most likely to mistake for “mine”? If you truly believed it had been given from heaven, how would you treat it differently?

Matthew 6:10 says, “Let your Kingdom come. Let your will be done on earth as it is in heaven.” Name one specific area (time, money, family, work, service) whose sovereignty you will hand over to the Lord this week. How do you plan to hand it over? Ask the members of your small group to pray for you, and review it together at your next meeting.

blog.title: Have You Handed Over Your Aircraft?

blocks.x: What One Sentence from John the Baptist Teaches Us about Selflessness

In the cockpit of a passenger airliner, when control passes between the captain and the first officer, there is a set of call-outs that must never be left vague. The one handing over says, “Your aircraft.” The one taking it replies, “My aircraft.” The one handing over confirms once more: “Your aircraft.” Only when those three lines have been spoken do his hands leave the controls.
Why go to so much trouble? Because high in the air, the most dangerous situation is not that nobody is flying the plane, but that two people are fighting over the controls at the same time.
And isn’t our life an aircraft too?
Selflessness Is Not an Emotion — It Is a Matter of Sovereignty

The spiritual predicament of many Christians is not that they don’t know Jesus, but that they have never clearly handed over the controls. With our lips we sing, “I will follow you,” but our hands still grip the yoke tightly. In the meeting we say, “Lord, you are King,” but back at the office, back at home, back in front of our bank account, the one reigning as king is still ourselves.

So “selflessness” is not just an emotional humility; it is a transfer of authority. Emotion is a feeling; authority is a decision. It can be measured by one question: “Whose hands hold the sovereignty over this matter?” Do I let my own reasoning be in charge, or the Lord’s word? Do I let my emotions control my decisions, or the Holy Spirit guide my actions?

Take note: selflessness is not losing your mind but bringing your mind into submission to Christ; not abandoning judgement but letting the Holy Spirit direct your judgement. In Gethsemane the Lord Jesus spoke honestly of his anguish, yet he added a turning point: “Father, if you are willing, remove this cup from me. Nevertheless, not my will, but yours, be done.” (Luke 22:42)
The practice of selflessness very often takes place inside that “nevertheless”.
A Man Unafraid of Being Replaced

John the Baptist is the finest witness on this road. People from Jerusalem and all Judea were going out to him, and even King Herod feared him. Then, at the very height of his influence, his disciples came running to him with a complaint: everyone is going to Jesus.
His answer has shaken every generation since: “He must increase, but I must decrease.” (John 3:30)

How could he do it? Because he had long since made three things clear: everything is given from heaven; I am not the Christ, only the forerunner; I am the friend of the bridegroom. In Jewish wedding custom, the friend of the bridegroom rushed about for days preparing everything, yet on the wedding night he stood outside the door, heard the bridegroom’s joyful voice, and went home content. He never got one thing wrong: the bride was not his.

Psychology has a finding called the “spotlight effect”: in 2000 Thomas Gilovich of Cornell University showed that people generally overestimate how much attention others pay to them. The spotlight we fear all our lives is mostly one we have trained on ourselves. When you no longer need to be seen, you never again need to fear being replaced.
God’s Kingdom Begins When We Step Down from the Throne

The Lord taught us to pray: “Let your Kingdom come. Let your will be done on earth as it is in heaven.” (Matthew 6:10) In the original, the emphasis of “kingdom” is not territory but kingship. The heart of this prayer is laying ourselves down and letting the Lord reign.

The coming of God’s kingdom is not only an end-time hope; it is a discipline of daily living. When I am willing to forgive someone who has wronged me, Jesus reigns in that relationship; when I lay down my habit of wanting to control my family, Jesus is King in my home; when in my service I don’t fight for credit or a name, God’s will is carried out in the church.

You can start three things today: every morning pray out loud, “Lord, today the sovereignty is yours”; before a major decision, stop and ask, “Is this from me, or from the Lord?”; list three areas where you most easily take charge yourself — time, money, relationships — and hand them over one by one.
Laying down sovereignty is not losing control; it is handing control to the most trustworthy Lord. Revival does not depend on how hard we try, but on how fully we surrender.
Today the Lord is asking in your ear: “Is it your aircraft, or mine?”
Reflection Question
This week, which specific area (time, money, family, work, service) are you willing to name before the Lord and say, in your own words, “The sovereignty is yours”?

brief12.title: Cover: Let Go of Sovereignty, Let Jesus Reign
notes: Slide text:
Practising the Selfless Life (Part 1)
Theme Verse
“He must increase, but I must decrease.”
(John 3:30)
Key points:
Open with a warm greeting; explain that today’s message comes down to one sentence: hand over the controls.
Read the theme verse, John 3:30; explain that “increase” and “decrease” are both ongoing verbs in the original.
Preview the three points: the definition of selflessness, the role model of selflessness, the practice of selflessness.
Main idea: revival begins not with outward enthusiasm but with inward surrender.

brief12.title: Introduction: Who Is in the Pilot’s Seat?
notes: Slide text:
Three call-outs for handing over control
“Your aircraft” “My aircraft”
Unclear authority means disaster
Have you handed over the controls?
Key points:
Describe the airliner cockpit call-outs: the one handing over says “Your aircraft”, the one taking over says “My aircraft”, then it is confirmed once more.
Analogy: the most dangerous thing is not that no one is flying, but that two people are fighting over the controls at once.
Application: many Christians say the Lord is King while their hands grip the yoke, so their lives go up and down.
Lead into the lesson’s introduction: selflessness is a way of life to be practised every day, not an abstract spiritual idea.

brief12.title: Theme Verses and Background
notes: Slide text:
Disciples: everyone is going to him
John: he must increase, I must decrease
“Kingdom” in the original: kingship, reign
Lord’s Prayer: God’s name, kingdom, will first
Key points:
Background: John’s Gospel was written in Ephesus around AD 80–90; the disciples’ complaint in John 3:26 is full of alarm.
John’s three groundwork sentences before his answer: the eye of grace, the eye of our originally intended position, the eye of order (John 3:27–29).
Matthew was written for Jewish readers; the Lord’s Prayer sits at the centre of the Sermon on the Mount, and its first three petitions are all about God.
“Kingdom” is βασιλεία — the emphasis is kingship, not territory; “will” is θέλημα.
Conclusion: what John lived out over a lifetime is exactly what the Lord teaches us to pray every day.

brief12.title: 1. Selflessness at Its Core: A Transfer of Sovereignty
notes: Slide text:
Not emotional humility, but a transfer of authority
“Nevertheless, not my will,
but yours, be done.”
Key points:
Distinguish: emotional humility is a feeling; a transfer of authority is a decision.
The “nevertheless” of Gethsemane — the Lord honestly spoke his own will, then added “nevertheless”.
Galatians 2:20: “it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me” — not self-annihilation, but a change of sovereignty.
Light from the original: “deny” (ἀπαρνέομαι) is the same word used of Peter denying the Lord (Matthew 16:24; 26:34).
Application: when “self” pops up to take charge, be able to say to it, “I don’t know you.”

brief12.title: Measuring Selflessness: Who Holds the Sovereignty?
notes: Slide text:
My reasoning, or the Lord’s word?
My emotions, or the Spirit’s guidance?
My experience, or the Lord’s heart?
Not losing your mind, but submitting it to Christ
Key points:
Go through the lesson’s three measuring questions one by one, with an everyday example for each.
Proverbs 3:5–6: “don’t lean on your own understanding… he will make your paths straight.”
Clear up a misunderstanding: selflessness is not losing your mind, but bringing it into submission to Christ (Romans 12:2, “transformed by the renewing of your mind”).
Psychology: Ellen Langer’s (1975) “illusion of control” lottery experiment — people asked a markedly higher price for tickets they had chosen themselves.
James 4:13–15: “you are a vapor” — what we’ve been gripping was never the control column.

brief12.title: 2. The Role Model of Selflessness: John the Baptist
notes: Slide text:
Everything is given from heaven
I am not the Christ, only the forerunner
I am the bridegroom’s friend, full of joy
Key points:
First describe John’s influence at the time: “people from Jerusalem, all of Judea… went out to him” (Matthew 3:5).
The first sentence is the eye of grace; pair it with 1 Corinthians 4:7, “what do you have that you didn’t receive?”
The second is the eye of our originally intended position: knowing clearly who you are, and who you are not.
The third is the eye of order: in Jewish wedding custom the bridegroom’s friend rushed about, yet stood outside the door rejoicing — the bride was not his.
Application: the flock is not mine, the children are not mine, the ministry is not mine.

brief12.title: Three Marks of True Selflessness
notes: Slide text:
Not measuring worth by results
Not seeking to be seen
Not fearing being replaced
The spotlight is mostly self-made
Key points:
Go through the lesson’s three marks one by one, in a tone both gentle and firm.
Psychology: Thomas Gilovich’s (2000, Cornell University) “spotlight effect” — people overestimate how much others notice them.
Management: Jim Collins, Good to Great (2001), Level 5 Leadership — personal humility combined with professional will.
C. S. Lewis, Mere Christianity, in essence: a proud man is always looking down, so he cannot see the One above him.
The Lord’s verdict: “among those who are born of women there has not arisen anyone greater than John the Baptizer” (Matthew 11:11).

brief12.title: 3. Practising Selflessness: The Lord’s Prayer
notes: Slide text:
“Let your Kingdom come. Let your will
be done on earth as it is in heaven.”
(Matthew 6:10)
Every prayer is a daily coronation
Key points:
Read Matthew 6:9–10 and stress the order: your name, your kingdom, your will — only then our daily bread.
If the first line of our prayer is “Please give me…”, we are still on the throne and treating God as a supplier.
The Lord’s Prayer is a daily coronation: each time we pray it, we place the crown on the Lord’s head again.
The coming of God’s kingdom is not only an end-time hope; it is a discipline of daily living.

brief12.title: Where Does God’s Kingdom Come?
notes: Slide text:
Forgiving: Jesus reigns in relationships
Not controlling: Jesus is King at home
Not seeking credit: his will done in church
Grace, like water, flows to the lowest place
Key points:
Unfold the three everyday settings one by one, each with a verse: Matthew 6:14, Ephesians 5:21, Matthew 20:26–27.
Negative example: Nebuchadnezzar, from “Is not this great Babylon, which I have built…” (Daniel 4:30) to “those who walk in pride he is able to abase” (Daniel 4:37).
Spiritual law: “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (James 4:6; 1 Peter 5:5).
Science: apoptosis — cells deny themselves on time and the body stays healthy; cells that refuse to die and expand without limit become cancer.
321 application: life first, then relationships, then ministry; the order of relationships is God, then ourselves, then others, and last of all things.

brief12.title: Practice: Three Exercises
notes: Slide text:
Pray each morning: the sovereignty is yours
Before deciding: from me, or the Lord?
List three areas and hand them over
Eight stages: Information to Multiplication
Key points:
Read out the lesson’s three practices one by one; demonstrate that the first prayer takes only ten seconds, but must be said out loud.
Pair the second with 1 Samuel 15:22, “to obey is better than sacrifice”, and Psalm 139:23–24.
For the third, cite the “small locked cupboard” in Robert Boyd Munger’s My Heart — Christ’s Home.
Deepen them with the eight stages of changing our mindset: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.
Encourage: practise for forty days in a row and find a brother or sister to remind each other — that is “multiplication”.

brief12.title: Closing and Call: The Threshold of Revival
notes: Slide text:
Revival: not trying harder, but surrendering more
Lay yourself down, let the Lord reign
Let Jesus be King and receive all the glory
Lord, it’s your aircraft
Key points:
Explain “threshold”: you can stand outside the door for a long time and serve for many years, but unless you step over it, you cannot go in.
Augustine, The City of God: love of self, even to the contempt of God, formed the earthly city; love of God, even to the contempt of self, formed the heavenly city.
It is commonly said that D. L. Moody heard, “The world has yet to see what God will do with a man fully consecrated to him,” and replied, “I will be that man.”
Call: return to the opening flight call-out and invite the congregation to answer aloud, “Lord, it’s your aircraft.”
Sum up with the Two Core Values: let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory.

brief12.title: Prayer of Response and Blessing
notes: Slide text:
Lord, I hand the controls over to you
May your kingdom come in my heart
May you increase; may I decrease
May the Lord bless and keep you till we see him
Key points:
Lead the congregation in praying line by line, slowly.

Content of the prayer: confession (calling him Lord with our lips while still gripping sovereignty in our hands), entrusting (time, money, family, service, future), asking the Holy Spirit to remind us daily.
Remember the Lord’s example with Philippians 2:7–8, “emptied himself, taking the form of a servant”.
Close with the blessing, and announce that the next lesson will continue the practice of selflessness.

brief21.title: Cover: Let Go of Sovereignty, Let Jesus Reign
notes: Slide text:
Practising the Selfless Life (Part 1)
Theme Verse
“He must increase, but I must decrease.”
(John 3:30)
Key points:
Greet warmly; explain that this is the first lesson in the “selflessness” practice series.
Read John 3:30; point out that “increase” (αὐξάνω) and “decrease” (ἐλαττόω) are both ongoing verbs in the original.
Preview the three points: the core definition of selflessness, the role model of selflessness, the practice of selflessness.
Main idea: revival begins not with outward enthusiasm but with inward surrender.

brief21.title: Introduction 1: Who Is in the Pilot’s Seat?
notes: Slide text:
Three call-outs for handing over control
“Your aircraft” “My aircraft”
Only then do the hands leave the controls
Unclear authority means disaster
Key points:
Describe the cockpit call-outs in detail: the one handing over says “Your aircraft”, the one taking over says “My aircraft”, and the one handing over confirms once more.
Explain why it is so elaborate: high in the air the greatest danger is not that no one is flying, but that authority is unclear.
Ask: have you handed over the controls of your life?
Set up today’s one-sentence message: hand over the controls.

brief21.title: Introduction 2: Two People Fighting for the Controls
notes: Slide text:
Our lips sing, “I will follow you”
Our hands still grip the yoke
Surrender in the meeting, king in daily life
Revival begins with inward surrender
Key points:
Describe the real situation: in the meeting we say, “Lord, you are King”, but back at the office, at home, in front of the bank account, the one reigning is still ourselves.
Analogy: life keeps flying with “two people fighting over the controls” — now high, now low, utterly exhausted.
Bring in the lesson’s introduction: selflessness is not an abstract idea but a way of life practised every day.
Stress: not merely a wish in our prayers, but a choice in our lives.

brief21.title: Theme Verses and Background
notes: Slide text:
Disciples: everyone is going to him
John: he must increase, I must decrease
“Kingdom” in the original: kingship, reign
Lord’s Prayer: God’s name, kingdom, will first
Key points:
John’s Gospel was written in Ephesus around AD 80–90; for its purpose see John 20:31.
The disciples’ complaint in John 3:26 — “everyone is coming to him” — is full of alarm.
Matthew was written for Jewish readers; the Lord’s Prayer sits at the centre of the Sermon on the Mount; of its six petitions, the first three are all about God.
“Kingdom” (βασιλεία) stresses kingship; “will” is θέλημα; the Lord’s Prayer is a handover of sovereignty.
