blog.title: The Seat in the Middle of the Table Was Empty

blocks.x: Why the Meeting Ended, the Plan Passed — and the People Drifted Apart
A planning meeting: three minutes of prayer, eighty-seven minutes of discussion.

One brother says, “I’ve worked in marketing for ten years — this will definitely work.” A sister says, “But that isn’t the tradition of our church.” A deacon clears his throat: “I started this ministry. I know it best.”
When the meeting breaks up, the proposal has passed — but two people go home wounded.
Nobody in that meeting committed an obvious sin. Nobody lied; nobody was greedy for money. Every one of them was speaking “for the good of the church.”
But the seat in the middle of that table was empty. Jesus was not sitting there.

In AD 1543 Copernicus proposed a correction that was not complicated mathematically: the centre is not the earth; it is the sun. Yet it took humanity nearly a hundred and fifty years truly to accept it. Why was it so hard? Because admitting “I am not the centre” has never been a mathematical problem. It is a problem of the heart.
The “self” in the church is just such a belated Copernican revolution.
That Rod Was Never Moses’ from the First Day
At Horeb God asked Moses, “What is that in your hand?” He said, “A rod.”
It was a shepherd’s staff. Eighty years of life — forty in the palace, forty in the wilderness — now all condensed into a piece of wood in his hand.

God told him to throw it down and then pick it up again. When it went down, it was still “Moses’ rod”; when it was picked up again, Scripture changed what it called it: “Moses took God’s rod in his hand.” (Exodus 4:20)
From beginning to end, that rod was in his hand. Only its name had changed.

That is “selflessness.” Selflessness is not burying our gifts or doing nothing from now on; it is the same hands, the same rod, with a different name hanging on it. Your expertise is still there; your experience is still there. But the name tag no longer says “mine.” It says “God’s.”
Joshua learned the same lesson. As he prepared to attack Jericho, he met a man with his sword drawn in his hand and asked: are you for us, or for our enemies?
The answer came: “No; but I have come now as commander of Yahweh’s army.” (Joshua 5:14)
This is the weightiest “No” in the whole Bible, because the question itself was wrong. God is never anyone’s deputy. God does not come to join our team — God comes to take over the whole battlefield.
The real question is not “Is God on my side?” but “Am I on God’s side?”
Four mindsets — and only one without “we”
The Lord Jesus said it with perfect clarity: “On this rock I will build my assembly.” (Matthew 16:18)
Not “You will build my church,” nor “I will build your church,” but “I will build my church.”
Yet in ministry we often fall into four mindsets:
The first: we will build our church — this is Babel, whose aim is to make a name for ourselves.

The second: we will build Jesus’ church — it looks spiritual, but it is really taking the place of God, accomplishing God’s work by human methods. Like Uzzah reaching out to steady the ark: his motive was good, but he forgot that the ark of God has never needed a human hand to hold it up.

The third: Jesus will build our church — this is using God, hoping he will bless my plans. The Israelites carried the ark onto the battlefield, and the ark was captured. God can be trusted, worshipped and obeyed — but God will never be used.
The fourth: Jesus will build Jesus’ church — this alone is the selfless church.
Set the four side by side, and “we” is hidden in each of the first three. Only in the fourth is it completely absent.

Wherever “we” is the subject, “self” is present. The true church is not an institution built by human effort, but the body that Christ himself raises up; our duty is not to “replace” him but to “obey” him.
That is why John the Baptist spoke those words that will last for ever: “He must increase, but I must decrease.” (John 3:30) We are the best man, not the bridegroom. The bride belongs to the Lord.
God does not work together with “self”; he is with those who are “selfless.” When you let go of “I want,” God begins the work of “he wants.”

This week, why not try three small things: pray for one minute before a meeting begins; bring someone alongside you in your service and give them the front of the stage; when opinions reach deadlock, be the first to say, “Let’s pray together.”
The true leader is not the person standing at the front, but the Lord who reigns behind the scenes.
Reflection question: in the area of service you are most invested in right now, who is the subject? Is it “we build ours,” or “Jesus builds his”?

brief12.title: Let Jesus Build His Church
notes: A Selfless View of Leadership and Ministry
“On this rock I will build
my assembly”
(Matthew 16:18)
Key points:
Read the theme verse, Matthew 16:18, stressing that the subject is “I”.
Explain that this is the second lesson in the “selflessness” series, focusing on practical discipline in service and decision-making.
Set the tone in one sentence: if we insist on “I can, I know, I decide”, then even when doing spiritual things we are still operating in “self”.
Preview three questions: Who is leading? Who is building? What is selfless service?

brief12.title: Who Sits in the Middle Seat?
notes: Three minutes of prayer, eighty-seven of discussion
The plan passed; the relationships were hurt
The seat in the middle of the table was empty
Jesus was not sitting there
Key points:
Open with the planning-meeting scene: three people each bring out their own credentials.
Stress that nobody committed an obvious sin; everyone was speaking “for the good of the church”.

Cite Copernicus, On the Revolutions of the Heavenly Spheres (1543): the centre is the sun, not the earth; admitting “I am not the centre” has never been a mathematical problem but a problem of the heart.
The “self” in the church is a belated Copernican revolution.

brief12.title: Theme Verses and Background
notes: Joshua asks: whose side are you on?
The Lord: “No; but I have come now
as commander of Yahweh’s army.”
(Joshua 5:14)
Key points:
Background: after crossing the Jordan came circumcision, then the Passover, then the manna ceased — and only then Jericho. Life first, the battle after.
Hebrew sar-tsevaʾ-YHWH; sar means a commander, one who holds authority.
That “No” is the weightiest in the whole Bible: he does not take sides; he comes to take command.
Caesarea Philippi: pagan altars and “the gates of Hades” right before their eyes — there the Lord said, “I will build my church.”

brief12.title: 1. Who Is Leading? Moses’ Rod
notes: “What is that in your hand?” “A rod.”
Thrown down: “Moses’ rod”
Picked up: “God’s rod”
(Exodus 4:2, 20)
Key points:
Exodus 3:11, Moses’ retreat; God answers only, “Certainly I will be with you.”
It was a shepherd’s staff — eighty years of life condensed into a piece of wood, the only thing he had.
Key detail: the rod stayed in Moses’ hand throughout; what changed was its name and its owner.
Application: selflessness is not throwing our gifts away, but hanging a new name on the same rod.

brief12.title: Not Fighting for the Lead, Only Ensuring God Is in Control
notes: Joshua worships: “What does my lord
say to his servant?” (Joshua 5:14)
Before the battle, take off your sandals
Not who leads, but whether God leads
Key points:
The real question is not “Is God on my side?” but “Am I on God’s side?”
Joshua 6:2 uses the perfect tense: “I have given Jericho into your hand.” The battle not yet fought, the outcome already settled.
Jim Collins, Good to Great (2001), “Level 5 leaders”: personal humility plus professional will; “the window and the mirror”.
Psalm 127:1 and Zechariah 4:6.

brief12.title: 2. Who Is Building? The First Two Mindsets
notes: We build ours: Babel
To make a name for ourselves (Genesis 11:4)
We build Jesus’: taking God’s place
Doing God’s work by human methods
Key points:
Genesis 11:4: one verse full of “us” and “ourselves” — its soul is “let’s make a name for ourselves”.
The second mindset is the hardest to recognise, because it looks so spiritual.
Examples: Abram and Hagar (Genesis 16:2) — the goal right, the method their own; Uzzah reaching for the ark (2 Samuel 6:6–7).
Three symptoms: very busy, very tired, very little prayer.

brief12.title: The Third and Fourth Mindsets
notes: Jesus builds ours: using God
Asking God to bless my plans
Jesus builds his: selflessness
“I will build my church”
Key points:
The structure of the third mindset’s prayer: my plan, my success, and God called in to stamp it.
Example: Israel carried the ark into battle (1 Samuel 4:3), and the ark was captured. God can be trusted, worshipped and obeyed, but never used.
Isaiah 42:8: God will not give his glory to another.
The role model for the fourth is the Lord himself: “The Son can do nothing of himself” (John 5:19) — not passivity, but the highest form of initiative.

brief12.title: Where There Is “We”, There Is “Self”
notes: “We” hides in the first three
Only the fourth is free of it
Our duty is not to replace him
but to obey him
Key points:
Read all four mindsets side by side and let the congregation see which one fits them.
1 Corinthians 3:6–7: neither he who plants is anything, nor he who waters.
This does not belittle us; it sets us free — the growth is not my responsibility, so I need not be anxious about the outcome.
Psalm 115:1 says “not to us” twice, because we so easily forget once.

brief12.title: 3. Selfless Service
notes: Not passively letting go, but actively entrusting
“He must increase, but I must decrease”
(John 3:30)
We are the best man, not the bridegroom
Key points:
Distinguish letting go from entrusting: letting go is walking away; entrusting is staying, but changing seats.
John 3:27, “A man can receive nothing unless it has been given him from heaven” — pulls envy up by the roots.
Original language: “decrease” (elattoō) is passive — “being made less”, not putting oneself down.
Amy Edmondson’s “psychological safety” and Google’s Project Aristotle: selflessness is the most practical soil for unity.

brief12.title: Putting It into Practice
notes: Pray before every meeting and decision
Learn to step back; the glory goes to the Lord
In disagreement, seek the Lord’s heart first
Eight stages: Information to Multiplication
Key points:
The prayer for Practice 1: “Lord, be Lord here. Let your will be done, not ours.”
The self-question for Practice 2: “Does the glory for this go to the Lord, or to me?” Bring someone alongside and give them the front of the stage.
Practice 3: stop for a moment, pray together, hear the other’s concerns; Acts 15:28, “it seemed good to the Holy Spirit, and to us”.
The eight stages: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.

brief12.title: Closing and Call
notes: The heart of selflessness: let God be God
Hand over your rod; give up your seat
Give the glory back to the Lord who is worthy
Let Jesus be King; let Jesus receive the glory
Key points:
Moses, Joshua, Peter and Paul all knew it: the true leader is the Lord who reigns behind the scenes.
Peter at the Beautiful Gate: “why do you fasten your eyes on us?” (Acts 3:12)
Paul: “yet not I, but the grace of God which was with me.” (1 Corinthians 15:10)
Three calls: hand over your rod, give up your seat, give the glory back.

brief12.title: Prayer of Response and Blessing
notes: Lord, I am willing to let go of my sovereignty
You alone are the head of the church
Let your Kingdom come; let your will
be done on earth as it is in heaven
Key points:
Lead the congregation in reading the declaration of faith together.
A gentle reminder: God does not work together with “self”; he is with those who are “selfless”.
Matthew 6:10: the moment the Lord’s Prayer opens its mouth, it invites us down from the throne.
Close with a blessing: may the Lord lead, build and reign himself.

brief21.title: Let Jesus Build His Church
notes: A Selfless View of Leadership and Ministry
“On this rock I will build
my assembly”
(Matthew 16:18)
Key points:
Read the theme verse, Matthew 16:18, and draw the congregation’s attention to the subject: “I”.
Explain that this is the second lesson in the “selflessness” series, on practical discipline in service and decision-making.
Set the tone: if we insist on “I can, I know, I decide”, then even when doing spiritual things we are still operating in “self”.
Preview three questions: Who is leading? Who is building? What is selfless service?

brief21.title: Who Sits in the Middle Seat?
notes: Three minutes of prayer, eighty-seven of discussion
The plan passed; the relationships were hurt
The seat in the middle of the table was empty
Jesus was not sitting there
Key points:
Open with the planning-meeting scene: three people each bring out their own credentials and reasons.
Stress that nobody committed an obvious sin; everyone was speaking “for the good of the church”.
Make the key point: the seat in the middle of that table was empty.
Ask: in our service, who sits at the centre?

brief21.title: A Belated Copernican Revolution
notes: In 1543 Copernicus said:
The centre is not the earth, but the sun
Admitting “I am not the centre”
was never a mathematical problem
Key points:
In 1543 Copernicus published On the Revolutions of the Heavenly Spheres, proposing that the centre is the sun, not the earth.
Mathematically the correction was not complicated, yet it took humanity nearly a hundred and fifty years to accept it.
Admitting “I am not the centre” has never been a mathematical problem; it is a problem of the heart.
The “self” in the church is a belated Copernican revolution.

brief21.title: Theme Verses and Background
notes: Joshua asks: whose side are you on?
The Lord: “No; but I have come now
as commander of Yahweh’s army.”
(Joshua 5:14)
Key points:
Background: after crossing the Jordan came circumcision, then the Passover, then the manna ceased — and only then Jericho. Life first, the battle after.
Hebrew sar-tsevaʾ-YHWH; sar means a commander, one who holds authority.
That “No” is the weightiest in the whole Bible: he does not take sides; he comes to take command.
The second passage is set at Caesarea Philippi, with pagan altars and “the gates of Hades” right before their eyes.
Matthew 16:21 follows immediately: the Lord must be killed — his way of building the church is the cross.

brief21.title: 1. Who Led the Israelites?
notes: Out of Egypt: we say Moses
Into Canaan: we say Joshua
But they themselves would say:
God led Israel!
Key points:
The two greatest spiritual journeys: the exodus from Egypt and the entry into Canaan.
On the exam paper the answers are Moses and Joshua; the men themselves would answer, God.
The point is not “Who is leading?” but “Is God leading?”
Lead into Moses’ call at Horeb (Exodus 3:11–12).

brief21.title: What Is in Your Hand?
notes: “What is that in your hand?” “A rod.”
(Exodus 4:2)
A shepherd’s staff
Eighty years condensed into a piece of wood
Key points:
Moses’ first reaction was to retreat: “Who am I?” God answered only, “Certainly I will be with you.”
It was a shepherd’s staff — eighty years of life condensed into a piece of wood, the only thing he had.
What God wants to use is precisely the most ordinary thing in our hands.
Ask: what is the “rod” in your hand?

brief21.title: From “Moses’ Rod” to “God’s Rod”
notes: Thrown down, it was my rod
Picked up, it was God’s rod
(Exodus 4:20)
The same rod, a new owner
Key points:
God told him to throw it down and then reach out and take it (Exodus 4:3–4) — that throwing down and picking up was a transfer of ownership.
Key detail: the rod stayed in Moses’ hand throughout; what changed was its name and its owner.
Whether stretched over the Nile or over the Red Sea, the rod was never Moses displaying his power, but God acting.
Application: selflessness is not throwing our gifts away, but hanging a new name on the same rod.

brief21.title: That One Word: “No”
notes: He did not say, “I’m here to help you”
He said, “No”
God is no one’s deputy
God comes to take over the battlefield
Key points:
Joshua asks, “Are you for us, or for our enemies?” (Joshua 5:13) — the most natural military question.
The Lord answers “No”, meaning: you’re asking the wrong question.
The real question is not “Is God on my side?” but “Am I on God’s side?”
God does not come to join our team; God comes to take over the whole battlefield.

brief21.title: Before the Battle, Take Off Your Sandals
notes: Joshua worships: “What does my lord
say to his servant?” (Joshua 5:14)
“I have given Jericho
into your hand” (Joshua 6:2)
Key points:
Joshua’s response was not to argue but to fall down and worship: “What does my lord say to his servant?”
The next order is to take off his sandals (Joshua 5:15) — exactly what Moses heard at Horeb (Exodus 3:5).
Joshua 6:2 uses the perfect tense: the battle not yet fought, the outcome already settled.
Marching around, blowing trumpets and shouting are not tactics; they are worship.

brief21.title: Not Fighting for the Lead, Only Ensuring God Is in Control
notes: Collins’s “Level 5 leaders”
Personal humility plus professional will
Success: the window; failure: the mirror
Unless Yahweh builds the house (Psalm 127:1)
Key points:
Jim Collins, Good to Great (2001): out of 1,435 companies he found eleven truly great ones.
What they shared were “Level 5 leaders”: extreme personal humility plus intense professional will.
“The window and the mirror”: look out of the window when things go well, in the mirror when they go badly; mediocre leaders do the reverse.
Psalm 127:1 and Zechariah 4:6: not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit.

brief21.title: 2. I Will Build My Church
notes: Not “You will build my church”
Not “I will build your church”
But “I will build my church”
He is the subject, and the object too
Key points:
Subject, object and possessive are all his; the verb oikodomēsō is first person singular, future tense.
ekklēsia is made up of ek (out) and kaleō (to call) — the church is a people called out.
Colossians 1:18: he is the head of the body, the assembly, that in all things he might have the preeminence.
The tragedy of a church is often not that it lacks members, but that it has a few extra heads.

brief21.title: The First: The Babel Church
notes: “Let’s build ourselves a city, and a tower
… let’s make a name for ourselves”
(Genesis 11:4)
One verse, “us” over and over
Key points:
Genesis 11:4: one verse full of “us” and “ourselves” — its soul is “let’s make a name for ourselves”.
The first thing God did was not to tear down the tower but to confuse their language.
A group that will not unite for God’s name will sooner or later split over their own.
Ask yourselves: do our reports measure height, or life?

brief21.title: The Second: Taking the Place of God
notes: The goal is right; the method is our own
Uzzah reaches out to steady the ark
(2 Samuel 6:6–7)
Symptoms: very busy, very tired, little prayer
Key points:
This one is the hardest to recognise, because it looks so spiritual.
Abram and Hagar (Genesis 16:2): the goal was right, the method their own, and the result was strife in the household.
Uzzah reaching for the ark: his motive was good, but the ark of God has never needed a human hand to hold it up.
The deepest root of “taking the place of God” is not ungodliness but unbelief.
Ola Svenson’s 1981 survey: 88% of American drivers rated themselves above the median.

brief21.title: The Third: Using God
notes: My plan, my success
God called in to stamp it
Israel carries the ark into battle
And the ark is captured (1 Samuel 4:3)
Key points:
The structure of this kind of prayer: my plan, my success, and God called in to stamp it.
Defeated in battle, Israel did not repent but carried the ark onto the battlefield (1 Samuel 4:3) — and the ark was captured.
God can be trusted, worshipped and obeyed, but never used.
Isaiah 42:8: I will not give my glory to another, nor my praise to engraved images.

brief21.title: The Fourth: The Selfless Church
notes: “The Son can do nothing of himself”
(John 5:19)
“We” hides in the first three
Only the fourth is free of it
Key points:
The Lord’s own example: “The Son can do nothing of himself” (John 5:19) — not passivity, but the highest form of initiative.
1 Corinthians 3:6–7: neither he who plants is anything, nor he who waters.
This does not belittle us; it sets us free — the growth is not my responsibility, so I need not be anxious about the outcome.
Psalm 115:1 says “not to us” twice, because we so easily forget once.

brief21.title: 3. Selfless Service
notes: Not passively letting go, but actively entrusting
“He must increase, but I must decrease”

We are the best man, not the bridegroom
Key points:
Distinguish letting go from entrusting: letting go is walking away; entrusting is staying, but changing seats.
John 3:27: “A man can receive nothing unless it has been given him from heaven” — pulls envy up by the roots.
“The friend of the bridegroom” was a real office; busy for months, yet on the wedding day he stood to one side.
Original language: “decrease” (elattoō) is passive — “being made less”, not putting oneself down.
Philippians 2:5–8: Christ emptied himself (ekenōsen), poured himself out, and became obedient to the point of death.

brief21.title: Putting It into Practice (1)
notes: Pray before every meeting and decision
Lord, let your will be done

Does the glory go to the Lord, or to me?
Key points:
The prayer for Practice 1: “Lord, be Lord here. Let your will be done, not ours.”
Implementation: before any discussion involving more than two people, pray for one minute before anyone speaks.
The self-question for Practice 2: does the glory for this go to the Lord, or to me?
Implementation: this month, bring someone alongside you in service, give them the front of the stage, and step to the back to hand them the tools.
The example of Gethsemane: first honestly speak your own will, then say “nevertheless” (Matthew 26:39).

The eight stages: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.
The test: if the matter is resolved but the relationship is broken, that is not victory — both sides have lost.

brief21.title: The 3-2-1 Vision in Summary

The Spirit my guide; let Jesus be King

Key points:

Isaiah 14:13–14, one “I will” after another, is the prototype of pride.
Satan has no weapon against the selfless: you cannot bribe someone who doesn’t want glory.
Life first, then relationships, then ministry; the fivefold change: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry.
The 920 practice and the 235 relationships: before every “2”, live out selflessness and bear the ninefold fruit.
