script: Brothers and sisters, good morning.

Today let’s read together some words of the Lord Jesus: “I also tell you that you are Peter, and on this rock I will build my assembly, and the gates of Hades will not prevail against it.” (Matthew 16:18)
Notice the subject of that sentence. Not you, not us — “I”.

In the last lesson we came to understand the teaching of selflessness. Today we take a step further: selflessness is not a theory; it is a discipline. In every act of service and every decision, we must learn to let go of our own sovereignty and let Jesus reign.
Brothers and sisters, let me describe a scene.
A planning meeting: three minutes of prayer, eighty-seven minutes of discussion. When the meeting breaks up, the proposal has passed — but two people go home wounded.
Nobody in that meeting committed an obvious sin. Every one of them was speaking “for the good of the church.” But the seat in the middle of that table was empty — Jesus was not sitting there.

In 1543 Copernicus said: the centre is not the earth; it is the sun. It took humanity a hundred and fifty years to accept it. Why was it so hard? Because admitting “I am not the centre” has never been a mathematical problem. It is a problem of the heart.
Let’s look at the first passage.
Joshua was about to attack Jericho. He saw a man with a sword in his hand and asked: are you for us, or for our enemies?
The Lord’s answer was: “No; but I have come now as commander of Yahweh’s army.” (Joshua 5:14)
Brothers and sisters, this is the weightiest “No” in the whole Bible. What he means is: you’re asking the wrong question. I have not come to take sides; I have come to take command.
The real question is not “Is God on my side?” but “Am I on God’s side?”
The first question: who is leading?
Who led the Israelites out of Egypt? We would say Moses. But Moses himself would say: God did.
God asked him, “What is that in your hand?” He said, “A rod.” It was a shepherd’s staff — eighty years of life condensed into a piece of wood.
God told him to throw it down and pick it up again. When it went down, it was “Moses’ rod”; when it was picked up again, Scripture called it “God’s rod” (Exodus 4:20).
Brothers and sisters, from beginning to end that rod was in his hand. What changed was its name.
Selflessness is not burying our gifts; it is hanging a different name on the same rod.
And Joshua? When he heard those words, he fell on his face to the earth and worshipped, saying, “What does my lord say to his servant?”
In that moment, command of Israel’s army was formally handed over.
And the order in the next verse is even more remarkable: before the battle, take off your sandals.
Brothers and sisters, whoever cannot take off his sandals before God is not fit to put on his boots before men.
That is why the Bible says, “Unless Yahweh builds the house, they who build it labor in vain.” (Psalm 127:1)
The point is not “Who is leading?” but “Is God leading?”
The second question: who is building?
The Lord said, “I will build my church.” Not “You will build mine,” nor “I will build yours.”
Yet we often fall into four mindsets.
The first: we build ours. That is Babel. The Bible says, “Come, let’s build ourselves a city, and a tower … and let’s make a name for ourselves.” (Genesis 11:4)

The second: we build Jesus’. It looks very spiritual, but it is really taking the place of God — accomplishing God’s work by human methods. Like Uzzah reaching out to steady the ark: his motive was good, but the ark of God has never needed a human hand to hold it up.
The third: Jesus builds ours. That is using God.
The Israelites were defeated in battle, and instead of repenting they carried the ark onto the battlefield (1 Samuel 4:3). And the result? The ark was captured.
Brothers and sisters, God can be trusted, God can be worshipped, God can be obeyed — but God will never be used.
The fourth: Jesus builds his own. That alone is the selfless church.
How did the Lord himself live? He said, “The Son can do nothing of himself.” (John 5:19) The most powerful one in the whole universe lived a life that relied on himself not at all.
Brothers and sisters, look at these four mindsets: in the first three, “we” is hidden somewhere; only in the fourth is it completely absent.
Wherever “we” is the subject, “self” is present.
Paul says, “I planted. Apollos watered. But God gave the increase.” (1 Corinthians 3:6)
This does not belittle us; it sets us free. The growth is not my responsibility, so I don’t have to be anxious about the outcome.
Our duty is not to replace him, but to obey him.
The third question: what is selfless service?
It is not passively letting go; it is actively entrusting. The one who lets go walks away; the one who entrusts stays — but changes seats.
John the Baptist’s disciples came to him with a complaint: everyone is going to Jesus. John said, “A man can receive nothing unless it has been given him from heaven.”
Then he spoke those words: “He must increase, but I must decrease.” (John 3:30)
Brothers and sisters, we are the best man, not the bridegroom. The bride belongs to the Lord.
When we are willing to step down, Jesus is lifted up.
So how do we practise this? The lesson gives us three things.
First, before every meeting and every decision, pray first: “Lord, be Lord here. Let your will be done, not ours.” Just one minute — but it must not be skipped.
Second, learn to step back in your service and ask yourself: does the glory for this go to the Lord, or to me? This month, bring someone alongside you and give them the front of the stage.
Third, when there is disagreement, first lay down the argument and seek God’s heart together.
From Information, Revelation, Conviction and Implementation to Evaluation, Correction, Repetition and Multiplication — drive it deep, one step at a time.
Brothers and sisters, the heart of selflessness is letting God be God.

Moses knew it, Joshua knew it, and Peter knew it too. When the lame man walked, Peter’s first words were, “why do you fasten your eyes on us?” (Acts 3:12) Paul knew it as well: “yet not I, but the grace of God which was with me.” (1 Corinthians 15:10)
So this morning, three calls:
Hand over your rod. Give up your seat. Give the glory back.
The true leader is not the person standing at the front, but the Lord who reigns behind the scenes.
Let us pray together.
Dear Lord Jesus, the church is yours, not ours; the glory is yours, and not ours either.
We confess that in our hearts we often still sit in the middle seat. Please forgive us.
Speak to us as you spoke to Joshua; let us fall down before you and say, “What does my lord say to his servant?”
May you increase, and may we decrease. Let your Kingdom come; let your will be done on earth as it is in heaven.
In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
Brothers and sisters, good morning.
Today let’s read together some words of the Lord: “I also tell you that you are Peter, and on this rock I will build my assembly, and the gates of Hades will not prevail against it.” (Matthew 16:18)
Notice the subject of that sentence. Not you, not us — “I”.

In the last lesson we came to understand the teaching of selflessness; today we take a step further: selflessness is not merely a theory but an intensely practical discipline — in every act of service and every decision, letting go of our own sovereignty and letting Jesus reign.
If we insist on “I can,” “I know,” “I decide,” then even when we are doing spiritual things, we are still operating in “self.”
Today we ask three questions: Who is leading? Who is building? What is selfless service?
Brothers and sisters, let me describe a scene you may know very well.
A planning meeting. One brother says, “I’ve worked in marketing for ten years.” A sister says, “But that isn’t the tradition of our church.” A deacon says, “I started this ministry.”
An hour and a half goes by: three minutes of prayer, eighty-seven minutes of discussion. The proposal passes — but two people go home wounded.
Nobody in that meeting committed an obvious sin; every one of them was speaking “for the good of the church.”
But the seat in the middle of that table was empty. Jesus was not sitting there.

In AD 1543 Copernicus published On the Revolutions of the Heavenly Spheres. Before that, humanity had believed for fourteen hundred years that the earth was the centre of the universe. His correction was simple — the centre is not the earth; it is the sun. Mathematically it was not complicated, yet it took humanity nearly a hundred and fifty years to accept it.
Why was it so hard? Brothers and sisters, because admitting “I am not the centre” has never been a mathematical problem. It is a problem of the heart.
The “self” in the church is just such a belated Copernican revolution.
Let’s look first at the background.
The book of Joshua records Israel’s entry into Canaan. Notice the order of chapter 5: first circumcision, then the Passover, then the manna stops falling — and only last of all, Jericho.
Brothers and sisters, before the first battle is fought, what God deals with first is not military matters but identity and worship. Life comes first; the battle comes after.
It was then that Joshua met a man with his sword drawn in his hand, and asked: are you for us, or for our enemies?
He said, “No; but I have come now as commander of Yahweh’s army.” (Joshua 5:14)
The Hebrew sar means a commander, one who holds authority. Commentators through the ages have mostly held that this was an Old Testament appearance of Christ, because he accepted Joshua’s worship.
The first question: who is leading?
The exodus from Egypt and the entry into Canaan were the two greatest spiritual journeys in history.
If someone asks who led the Israelites out of Egypt, we answer: Moses. If someone asks who led them into Canaan, we say: Joshua.
On an exam paper, both answers would get the marks. But brothers and sisters, if you asked the men themselves, they would both give the same reply: “God led Israel!”
Let’s look at Moses first.
He was already eighty when he met God at Horeb. His first reaction was not eagerness but retreat: “Who am I, that I should go to Pharaoh?” (Exodus 3:11)
God did not praise his abilities. He said only, “Certainly I will be with you.”
Then God asked, “What is that in your hand?” He said, “A rod.”

Brothers and sisters, it was a shepherd’s staff. Eighty years of life — forty in the palace, forty in the wilderness — now all condensed into a piece of wood. It was the only thing he had, and the most ordinary.
And that rod was exactly what God wanted.
God told him to throw the rod on the ground, and then told him to reach out and take hold of it.

That throwing down and picking up was a transfer of ownership. When it went down, it was still “Moses’ rod”; when it was picked up again, Scripture changed what it called it: “Moses took God’s rod in his hand.” (Exodus 4:20)
From that moment on, every time the rod was raised, it was not Moses displaying his power; it was God acting.
Brothers and sisters, notice a detail we often miss: from beginning to end that rod was in his hand. Only its name had changed.

That is selflessness. Selflessness is not burying our gifts; it is the same rod with a different name hanging on it. Your expertise is still there; your experience is still there. But the name tag no longer says “mine.” It says “God’s.”
Now look at Joshua.
He was about to fight his first hard battle. At a moment like that, any general wants to know one thing above all: who is on my side?
But the Lord’s answer was: “No.”
Brothers and sisters, this is the weightiest “No” in the whole Bible. Because the question itself was wrong.
We often think: I have my plan, and then I pray and ask God to help my plan. But God is never anyone’s deputy. God does not come to join our team; God comes to take over the whole battlefield.
The real question is not “Is God on my side?” but “Am I on God’s side?”
Joshua understood. His response was not to argue but to fall down and worship: “What does my lord say to his servant?”
In that moment, command was formally handed over.
And the military order in the next verse is even more remarkable: before the battle, take off your sandals.

Brothers and sisters, what a strange order! Isn’t the thing a man going into battle needs most his footwear? But God says: before you put on your army boots, let me know that you understand how to take off your sandals.
Forty years earlier, Moses had heard exactly the same words at Horeb.

In chapter 6 God’s plan comes in the perfect tense: “I have given Jericho into your hand.” The battle has not yet been fought, and the outcome is already settled. Marching around the city, blowing the trumpets, shouting — that is not tactics; that is worship.
Brothers and sisters, modern management studies have reached a similar conclusion by another road.

In Good to Great, Jim Collins sifted through 1,435 companies and found eleven that had truly leapt from good to great. He had expected to find star CEOs; instead, these leaders were almost all low-key. He called them “Level 5 leaders”: personal humility combined with professional will. He also observed “the window and the mirror”: when things go well, they look out of the window and give the credit to others; when things go badly, they look in the mirror and take the responsibility on themselves.
If that is true even of a business, how much more of the church of Christ?
“Unless Yahweh builds the house, they who build it labor in vain.” (Psalm 127:1)
The point is not “Who is leading?” but “Is God leading?”
The second question: who is building?

The Lord spoke these words at Caesarea Philippi. That was no ordinary place: pagan altars beside them, Roman power over their heads, and right before their eyes the cave the locals called “the gates of Hades.”
There the Lord said, “On this rock I will build my assembly.”
In the original the verb is first person singular, future tense — the subject is perfectly clear: “I.”
So it is not “You will build my church,” nor “I will build your church,” but “I will build my church.”

The word “church” in the original is made up of “out” and “to call” — the church is a people called out, and the one who calls is not us but the Lord. There is only one head; the tragedy of a church is often not that it lacks members, but that it has a few extra heads.
Yet in ministry we often fall into four wrong mindsets.
The first: “We will build our church.” This is the Babel church.
“Come, let’s build ourselves a city, and a tower whose top reaches to the sky, and let’s make a name for ourselves.” (Genesis 11:4)
Brothers and sisters, count how many times “us” and “ourselves” appear in that one verse. The soul of the whole verse lies in a single phrase: let’s make a name for ourselves.
So the first thing God did was not to tear down the tower but to confuse their language. A group of people who will not unite for God’s name will sooner or later split over their own.
The second: “We will build Jesus’ church.”
This one is hard to recognise, because it looks so very spiritual. But brothers and sisters, it is in fact “taking the place of God” — accomplishing God’s work by human methods.

God promised Abram descendants as many as the stars of heaven, yet Sarai gave her maidservant Hagar to her husband. They did not abandon God’s promise; they simply used their own method to fulfil it — the goal was right, but the method was their own.

David moved the ark on a new cart; the oxen stumbled, Uzzah reached out and took hold of the ark, and he died there beside it. His motive was good, but the ark of God has never needed a human hand to hold it up.
When we reach out to steady God, what we really believe in our hearts is: without me, God can’t hold it together.
This is the deepest root of the disease of “taking the place of God”: not ungodliness, but unbelief.
The third: “Jesus will build our church.” This is “using God.”

We have all heard this kind of prayer: “Lord, please bless our plan, open the way, and make this a success.” The plan is mine, the success is what I want, and God is the one called in to put his stamp on it.

When the Israelites were defeated by the Philistines, the elders did not repent; instead they said, bring the ark here. The ark was treated as a lucky charm, and God as a piece of tactical equipment. And the ark was captured.
Brothers and sisters, God can be trusted, God can be worshipped, God can be obeyed — but God will never be used.
God himself says, “I am Yahweh. That is my name. I will not give my glory to another, nor my praise to engraved images.” (Isaiah 42:8)
The fourth: “Jesus will build Jesus’ church.” This alone is the selfless church.
Someone may ask: won’t that make us too passive? Not at all.
The Lord said, “The Son can do nothing of himself, but what he sees the Father doing.” (John 5:19)

The most powerful one in the whole universe lived a life that relied on himself not at all. Whatever he saw the Father doing, that is what he did. That is not passivity; that is the highest form of initiative.
Paul says, “I planted. Apollos watered. But God gave the increase.” This does not belittle us; it sets us free — the growth is not my responsibility, so I don’t have to be anxious about the outcome.
Set the four mindsets side by side: in the first three, “we” is hidden somewhere; only in the fourth is it completely absent.
Wherever “we” is the subject, there is “self.” Our duty is not to replace him, but to obey him.
The third question: what is selfless service?
It is not passively letting go; it is actively entrusting. The one who lets go walks away; the one who entrusts stays — but changes seats.
John the Baptist’s disciples came to him with a complaint: everyone is going to Jesus.
John first said, “A man can receive nothing unless it has been given him from heaven.” (John 3:27) Brothers and sisters, that one sentence pulls envy up by the roots.

Then he used the picture of a wedding. “The friend of the bridegroom” was responsible for all the preparations and for escorting the bride; he would be busy for months, yet on the wedding day he stood to one side. The bride was not his; she was the bridegroom’s.
So he said, “He must increase, but I must decrease.” (John 3:30)
In the original, “decrease” is in the passive voice — “I am made less.” John did not become small by putting himself down; he simply let Jesus grow.
What he did was simply to follow Christ, who “emptied himself, taking the form of a servant … becoming obedient to the point of death” (Philippians 2:7–8).
So how do we practise this? The lesson gives us three things.

First, before every meeting and every decision, pray first: “Lord, be Lord here. Let your will be done, not ours.” Starting this week, before any discussion involving more than two people, pray for one minute before anyone speaks.

The Lord set the example in Gethsemane: “not what I desire, but what you desire.” Selflessness does not mean you’re not allowed to have ideas; it means that once you have them, you still say “nevertheless.”
Second, learn to step back in your service and ask yourself: does the glory for this go to the Lord, or to me?

This month, take the area of service you handle most easily, bring someone else in to do it with you, and give them the front of the stage. When they do it less well than you would, what is your first thought? That is your real spiritual health report.
Third, when there is disagreement, first lay down the argument and seek God’s heart.
The next time you reach deadlock, take the initiative and say three things: “Let’s stop for a moment.” “Let’s pray together.” “I’d like to hear your concerns.”

When the early church dealt with the dispute over circumcision, their resolution used a remarkable phrase: “it seemed good to the Holy Spirit, and to us.” (Acts 15:28) Not “We have voted; please, Holy Spirit, endorse it.”
Brothers and sisters, these three practices are to be driven deep with the eight stages: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.

Hearing it is Information; being enlightened is Revelation; surrendering in your heart is Conviction; doing it is Implementation; then Evaluation, Correction and Repetition; and finally bringing someone along with you — that is Multiplication.
The test is simple: if the matter is resolved but the relationship is broken, that is not victory — both sides have lost.
Let’s place today’s message within 321.

The Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model — he said, “The Son can do nothing of himself”; the Bible is my standard — God’s first command to Joshua was to meditate on the book of the law day and night; the Holy Spirit is my guide — not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit.

The Two Core Values are the very title of today’s lesson: let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory. The Goal is to establish God’s system — the tower of Babel was a system too; the only difference is whose name is written at the top.
The prototype of pride is recorded in Isaiah 14, one “I will” after another. But humility overcomes pride, and selflessness overcomes Satan — how do you bribe someone who doesn’t want glory?

Life first, then relationships, then ministry; and the fivefold change is mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry. In the 920 practice, the person across the meeting table who disagrees with you is the “2” God has given you today.
Brothers and sisters, the heart of selflessness is letting God be God.
Moses knew it, which is why from the very first day that rod was called “God’s rod.” Joshua knew it, which is why he fell down and worshipped.

Peter knew it too. When the lame man walked, his first words were, “why do you fasten your eyes on us?” (Acts 3:12) Paul knew it as well: “yet not I, but the grace of God which was with me.” (1 Corinthians 15:10)
So this morning, three calls.
First, hand over your rod. When it goes down it is “my rod”; when it is taken up again, it is “God’s rod.”
Second, give up your seat. At the next meeting, let prayer speak before discussion.
Third, give the glory back. When things succeed, you know it wasn’t you; when things fail, you know the Lord hasn’t left.
The true leader is not the person standing at the front, but the Lord who reigns behind the scenes.
Let us pray together.
Dear Lord Jesus, the church is yours, not ours; the will is yours, and the glory is yours too.
We confess that in our hearts we often still sit in the middle seat, wrapping our own wishes in spiritual words. Please forgive us.
Speak to us as you spoke to Joshua; let us fall down before you, take off the sandals from our feet, and say, “What does my lord say to his servant?”
Lord, may you increase, and may we decrease. Lead us yourself, build yourself, reign yourself.
Let your Kingdom come; let your will be done on earth as it is in heaven.
In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
Brothers and sisters, let Jesus be King; let Jesus receive all the glory.

sections.heading: Introduction: The Secret of a Grain of Wheat
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning. Today we begin with a grain of wheat.

A grain of wheat lies in the palm of a farmer’s hand — golden, plump, whole and flawless. It can be stored in a granary for three years, five years, ten years, and it will not spoil. Grains preserved for thousands of years have been found in the pyramids of Egypt, their husks still intact. Yet however long and however well it is kept, it remains just a grain of wheat — a single, solitary grain.

Unless the farmer sows it in the soil. Once it falls into the ground, the seed coat swells with water and bursts, the endosperm inside is broken down and used up, and that once-perfect form disappears completely. From a human point of view, that is called “ruined.” But a few days later, a tender shoot pushes up through the split seed coat and out of the soil; a few months later, a stalk of wheat sways in the wind, bearing dozens of times as many grains.

The Lord Jesus used this very picture to speak of himself — and of us: “Most certainly I tell you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains by itself alone. But if it dies, it bears much fruit.” (John 12:24)

Brothers and sisters, there is an order here that we often get backwards. We tend to think we must first reach the state of “selflessness” before we can talk about “denying of self”; that we must first reach a spiritual height before we can let go of ourselves. And so “selflessness” becomes a distant mountain that belongs only to Moses, to Paul, to the saints in the biographies — and has nothing to do with me, someone who frets every day over the daily grind, the children’s homework and my performance review at work.

But the order in Scripture is exactly the opposite. It is not that we first have “selflessness” and then “deny ourselves”; it is that as we “deny ourselves” every day, “selflessness” naturally flows out. The wheat does not first grow into an ear and then fall into the ground; it falls into the ground, and only then grows into an ear.

The introduction to this lesson puts it beautifully: “selflessness” is not an unattainable ideal, nor a state that only saints can reach; it is a pattern of life that every Christian can live out. It does not depend on human effort but on the grace of Jesus. Jesus’ death broke the dominion of sin, and his resurrection gives us new life, so that we are able to choose: “it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” When we choose every day to “deny ourselves,” the life of “selflessness” will naturally flow out and become the reality of our daily living.

I want to ask you three questions, brothers and sisters. Keep them in your heart as you listen to the whole lesson:

First, have you ever gritted your teeth and “tried hard to be selfless,” only to end up more tired, more defeated, and more aware of yourself?

Second, do you think “denying of self” means losing out, being taken advantage of, trampling yourself underfoot?

Third, do you feel that “self” is too strong — so strong that you’ve given up the fight and just want to keep the peace?

If even one of these three questions has struck home, then today’s lesson is one God has prepared for you. Because today we are going to see together: selflessness is not achieved by effort but received by grace; denying of self is the only road to selflessness; and the strength to keep on denying ourselves lies not in our willpower but in the grace of Jesus.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: Three Scenes Beneath the Cross
sections.html:
To truly understand “denying of self” and “selflessness,” we must first go back to three scenes in Scripture. These three scenes correspond exactly to the three key points of this lesson.

The first scene: the mountain road at Caesarea Philippi (Matthew 16)

The Gospel of Matthew was written by the apostle Matthew for Jews, and is generally thought to have been written between AD 50 and 70. It quotes the Old Testament again and again, to prove to Matthew’s fellow Jews that Jesus of Nazareth is the Messiah promised in the Old Testament, the Son of David, the King of kings.

Matthew 16 is the turning point of the whole book. The place is Caesarea Philippi — a frontier town north of Galilee, built by Herod Philip. The town had a shrine to the Greek god Pan, the cliff face was carved full of niches for idols, and there was a white marble temple dedicated to the Roman emperor. In other words, it was a place “crowded with gods, where the emperor called himself god.” It was in just such a place that Jesus asked his disciples, “But who do you say that I am?” And Peter answered, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.” (Matthew 16:15–16)

Immediately after this confession, Jesus did two things. First, for the first time he spoke plainly of how he “must go to Jerusalem and suffer many things from the elders, chief priests, and scribes, and be killed, and the third day be raised up” (see Matthew 16:21). Second, when Peter took hold of him and remonstrated, “Far be it from you, Lord!” Jesus rebuked him: “Get behind me, Satan! You are a stumbling block to me, for you are not setting your mind on the things of God, but on the things of men.” (Matthew 16:23)

Notice how closely one follows the other: Peter has only just been praised, and in the blink of an eye he is rebuked. Why? Because he put the things of men above the things of God. And the Lord Jesus’ very next words are our theme verse today: “If anyone desires to come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me.” (Matthew 16:24)

So the original setting of “denying of self” was not a monastery or a fasting chamber, but a fork in the road: “Will I set my mind on the things of God, or on the things of men?” To deny ourselves is, at that fork in the road, to yield “my thinking” to “God’s thinking.”

The second scene: the controversy in the churches of Galatia (Galatians 2)

Galatians was written by the apostle Paul and is generally thought to be one of his earliest letters, written around AD 48–55, to the Gentile churches in the region of Galatia in Asia Minor. A group of Judaizers had slipped into the church, insisting that Gentile believers had to be circumcised and keep the law in order to be saved. Paul fought to the end for the gospel truth of “justification by faith.”

Galatians 2:20 is the deepest sentence in that whole controversy. Paul did not write it at a retreat; he wrote it amid the gunsmoke of a battle for the truth: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.”

“I have been crucified with Christ” — in Greek this verb is in the perfect tense (συνεσταύρωμαι), meaning a fact that has been completed and whose effect continues to this day. Not “I am trying hard to nail myself up there,” but “I have already been nailed there; it is an accomplished fact.” This is exactly the foundation of the first key point of this lesson.

The third scene: the arena of Corinth and the inner battlefield of Romans

First Corinthians was written around AD 55, Paul’s letter to a church rich in gifts but riddled with problems. Near the city of Corinth, the Isthmian Games were held every two years, second only to the Olympic Games. Paul uses running and boxing as illustrations: “but I beat my body and bring it into submission, lest by any means, after I have preached to others, I myself should be rejected.” (1 Corinthians 9:27)

Romans was written around AD 57 and is the most theologically complete of Paul’s letters. Chapter 7 describes a most real inner war: “For desire is present with me, but I don’t find it doing that which is good.” (Romans 7:18) All the way to that cry of anguish: “What a wretched man I am! Who will deliver me out of the body of this death?” (Romans 7:24)

Brothers and sisters, keep these three scenes in mind: the fork on the mountain road, the declaration amid the gunsmoke, and the battlefields of the arena and the heart. Today’s three key points unfold from these three scenes.

sections.heading: 1. Selflessness Is Not Achieved by Effort but Received by Grace
sections.html:
We often think of “selflessness” as a spiritual discipline that can only be achieved through perseverance and struggle — as if the spiritual life were a steep slope, and whoever has the strongest willpower climbs the highest. But Scripture tells us plainly:

“Therefore if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old things have passed away. Behold, all things have become new.” (2 Corinthians 5:17)

Notice that Paul did not say, “If anyone tries hard enough, he gradually becomes a new creation.” He said, “If anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation.” This is an identity already established, not a reward still to be won.

Key word: new creation

“New creation” in Greek is καινὴ κτίσις (kainē ktisis). The word for “new” is not νέος (new in time, fresh off the production line) but καινός (new in kind, never seen before). The word for “creation,” κτίσις, is often used in the New Testament for God’s work of creating (for example, “the creation” in Romans 8:19).

In other words, being born again is not a renovation of the old self, a refurbishment of the old self, a self-improvement of the old self; it is an entirely new creation by God. It is not the result of human effort but the work of God’s grace. Just as the light in Genesis 1 did not come from the darkness trying hard to grow brighter; God said, “Let there be light,” and there was light.

The death and resurrection of Jesus: the two cornerstones of selflessness

This lesson points out two things, every word of them the heart of the gospel:

First, Jesus’ death dealt with the root of “self” — sin and the sinful nature. “Knowing this, that our old man was crucified with him, that the body of sin might be done away with, so that we would no longer be in bondage to sin.” (Romans 6:6) The “old man” is the old self — the self-centred “me,” the “me” inherited from Adam, with myself at the centre. It has not been locked up; it has been put to death.

Second, Jesus’ resurrection gives us his life — the selfless life. “Thus consider yourselves also to be dead to sin, but alive to God in Christ Jesus our Lord.” (Romans 6:11) “Consider” — the Greek λογίζεσθε — is an accounting term, meaning “reckon the books this way.” God has already declared it so; all we have to do is reckon accordingly, believe accordingly and live accordingly.

So “selflessness” is not something we produce; it is something Jesus lives out within us. When we are willing to submit to him and let him reign, his life naturally shows itself. Paul gave the most honest testimony to this: “But by the grace of God I am what I am. His grace which was given to me was not futile, but I worked more than all of them; yet not I, but the grace of God which was with me.” (1 Corinthians 15:10)

Listen to the structure of that sentence: “I worked more than all of them” — he gave everything he had; “yet not I, but the grace of God which was with me” — but he was not the source of the strength. He gave everything, but not by relying on himself. That is the difference — as wide as heaven and earth — between effort within grace and effort relying on the flesh.

Psychology confirms it: willpower runs out, grace does not

In a study published in 1998 in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, the American psychologist Roy F. Baumeister and his colleagues proposed the concept of “ego depletion”: self-control is like a muscle, a limited resource; a person who has suppressed a desire in one task is more likely to lose control in the next. In their experiment, participants who were told to resist chocolate chip cookies and eat only radishes then gave up sooner than the control group when working on an unsolvable puzzle.

It should be said that researchers have since debated the size of this effect quite a lot, and replication results have been mixed. But there is one experience every one of us can confirm: in the morning you resolve to be patient today, and you hold on until three in the afternoon — then one remark, and it all falls apart. The harder you push “self” down, the louder “self” gets.

Why? Because suppression just locks “self” in the basement. It hasn’t died; it is only waiting. But the gospel says that “self” has not been locked up — it has already been crucified with Christ. We are not guarding a living prisoner; we are acknowledging a fact of death. The difference between the two is the difference between religion and the gospel — and the difference between weariness and rest.

Moses and Joshua: two witnesses to selflessness

This lesson mentions Moses and Joshua, both of them witnesses to “selflessness.”

For his first forty years, Moses was a prince in the Egyptian palace. He “was instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians. He was mighty in his words and works.” (Acts 7:22) At forty he killed an Egyptian in a fit of temper, thinking he could deliver his people — and ended up fleeing into the wilderness for forty years. When God called him at eighty, his first words were: “Who am I, that I should go to Pharaoh, and that I should bring the children of Israel out of Egypt?” (Exodus 3:11)

Brothers and sisters, Moses at forty said, “I can.” Moses at eighty said, “Who am I?” God took forty years to grind a self-centred prince down into a selfless servant. In the end, Scripture’s verdict on him was: “Now the man Moses was very humble, more than all the men who were on the surface of the earth.” (Numbers 12:3) And his deepest prayer was: “If your presence doesn’t go with me, don’t carry us up from here.” (Exodus 33:15) — without God’s presence, he would rather not go at all. That is selflessness.

Joshua was the same. He was a seasoned military leader, yet the victory at Jericho came not from battering rams but from marching around the city and shouting. Before entering Canaan, he met a man with a drawn sword in his hand and asked, “Are you for us, or for our enemies?” The man replied, “No; but I have come now as commander of Yahweh’s army.” And Joshua fell on his face to the earth and worshipped (see Joshua 5:13–14).

Listen carefully to that answer. Joshua was asking, “Which side are you on?” and the answer was, “I am not on your side; I am the commander.” The real question was never “Is God on my side?” but “Am I on God’s side?” Joshua understood, and so he fell down and worshipped. In that moment the commander became a servant. That is selflessness.

sections.heading: Applying the 321 Vision
sections.html:
The first of the Three Foundations says: Jesus is my role model. The source of selflessness is not our resolve but Jesus himself. He, “existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Philippians 2:6–7). “Emptied himself” is ἐκένωσεν in the original, meaning “to pour oneself out.” He emptied himself first, so that we would have something to receive.

321 says: the old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. The self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall, and pride is the root of the problem. And selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the infinite and living out the infinite — “I” no longer live, but Christ lives in me. Brothers and sisters, hold on to this: selflessness is not reducing yourself to zero; it is letting the infinite Lord come and dwell in the vessel that has been emptied to zero. An empty cup is not a loss; only an empty cup can be filled with living water.

So the conclusion of the first key point is clear: stop asking, “How can I become selfless?” and start asking, “Am I willing to let Jesus be King?” The first question puts the focus on ourselves, and the more we ask it, the more tired we get; the second puts the focus on Jesus, and the more we ask it, the stronger we become. Jesus is the focal point — not ourselves, not others, not our circumstances. That is what 321 reminds us again and again.

sections.heading: 2. Denying of Self Is the Only Road to Selflessness
sections.html:
Jesus said, “If anyone desires to come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me.” (Matthew 16:24)

Brothers and sisters, notice a reminder in this lesson: this is not a suggestion; it is a condition. The Lord did not say, “If anyone desires to come after me, it would be best for him to deny himself.” He said, “let him deny himself.” When Luke records the same saying, the Chinese Union Version — like most English versions — has one word more: “let him deny himself, take up his cross daily, and follow me” (Luke 9:23). Daily — that one word turns the cross from a ceremony into an everyday thing.

Key word: deny oneself

“Deny himself” in Greek is ἀπαρνησάσθω ἑαυτόν, from the verb ἀπαρνέομαι, meaning “to deny, to disown, to draw a clear line against.” The same word appears once more in Matthew, and it cuts to the heart: when Jesus said to Peter, “you will deny me three times” (Matthew 26:34), this was the very word he used.

Brothers and sisters, what a sobering contrast. When Peter denied the Lord, he treated the Lord as a stranger; when the Lord asks us to deny ourselves, he is asking us to treat “self” as a stranger. Every day, you and I choose between the two: either “self” is denied, or the Lord is denied. There is no third way.

So “denying of self” is not “giving up certain things”; it is “disowning a certain person” — the self that keeps wanting to sit on the throne. People can offer up a great many things and still not deny themselves; because if what we give up is not the throne, whatever else we give up is mere decoration.

Denying of self makes room for Jesus

This lesson puts it precisely: “denying of self” is the starting point for entering into “selflessness.” When we are willing to give up our own opinions, feelings, face and rights, we make room for Jesus, so that he can live out his life within us.

Imagine a tiny house, so crammed with furniture that you have to turn sideways just to walk through. Now an honoured guest is coming to live there. What do you do? You don’t build an extension; you first move the old furniture out. Denying of self is moving out the furniture; selflessness is when the guest has moved in and the whole house is filled with his presence.

You don’t first need to learn “how to make the house feel like the guest is there”; you only need to make room, and his presence follows naturally. In the same way, we don’t first need to learn “how to be selfless”; we only need to make room today and let Jesus be King.

Denying of self is not painful asceticism but a willing choice

This is a precious line in the lesson, and it is the very mindset many of us most need renewed.

Denying of self is not gritting your teeth, not punishing yourself, not putting on a long face so that everyone knows how hard done by you are. If we give something up while keeping a ledger, that isn’t denying of self — that’s investing. True denying of self is willing, and it carries joy, because we know what we are giving up, and we know what we are gaining.

The American missionary Jim Elliot wrote a line in his journal on 28 October 1949 that is still quoted today: “He is no fool who gives what he cannot keep to gain that which he cannot lose.” Six years later, while taking the gospel to the Waodani (then called the Auca) in Ecuador, he was speared to death at just twenty-eight. He gave up the years he could not keep and gained the glory he could not lose.

The German theologian Dietrich Bonhoeffer wrote in The Cost of Discipleship in 1937: “When Christ calls a man, he bids him come and die.” That is not tragedy; it is glory. Because the one who calls us to die died first himself — and has already risen.

Where denying of self happens: the moment the thought arises

This lesson points to a very practical place to practise: every time we become aware that “self” is in charge — wanting to control, wanting to argue, wanting to prove ourselves, wanting to protect ourselves — that is the moment to practise “denying of self.”

Brothers and sisters, write these four verbs on your heart: wanting to control, wanting to argue, wanting to prove, wanting to protect ourselves. These four verbs are the four faces of “self.”

Wanting to control is “I want to be in charge”; wanting to argue is “I want to win”; wanting to prove is “I want to be seen”; wanting to protect myself is “I don’t trust God to protect me.” These four faces show up every day in our homes, our offices and our group chats.

A sister once told me that the fiercest row she ever had with her husband started over whether the spoons in the kitchen drawer should lie sideways or lengthways. Afterwards even she thought it was absurd. But she said something very perceptive: “Actually, we weren’t fighting about the spoons. We were fighting about who gets the final say.” Brothers and sisters, eight or nine out of ten conflicts in our lives aren’t about the spoons. They’re about who gets the final say.

321 puts it penetratingly: pride is leaving our originally intended position and seizing rights, wanting to take the place of God; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God. Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility inspires humility, and both sides win. In that moment, if one person is willing to deny themselves first, the fire goes out; if both people insist on winning, both will lose.

The Lord himself walked this road

Denying of self is not a road God asks us to walk but will not walk himself. That night in the garden of Gethsemane: “My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass away from me; nevertheless, not what I desire, but what you desire.” (Matthew 26:39)

Notice that the Lord Jesus did not pretend it wasn’t bitter. He said, “let this cup pass away from me” — real humanity, real struggle. But straight away he said, “nevertheless, not what I desire, but what you desire.” Denying of self is not having no feelings; denying of self is having feelings and obeying anyway.

Brothers and sisters, if today you find denying yourself hard, a struggle, your heart weeping inside, I want to tell you: this doesn’t mean you’re unspiritual. It means you are walking the road the Lord walked. The one whose sweat fell to the ground like great drops of blood understands your struggle at this moment completely.

Psychology confirms it: only willing choices go the distance

Self-Determination Theory, put forward by the American psychologists Edward L. Deci and Richard M. Ryan (first proposed in 1985 and set out systematically in the journal American Psychologist in 2000), shows that when a behaviour comes from autonomy rather than outside pressure, people’s persistence, quality of performance and well-being are all significantly higher. Compliance under compulsion tends to be short-lived; only voluntary commitment lasts.

This fits Scripture exactly. When Paul urged believers to give, he said: “Let each man give according as he has determined in his heart, not grudgingly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver.” (2 Corinthians 9:7) God has never wanted a cross carried under duress. What he wants is a willing heart.

Another study is helpful too. Phillippa Lally’s team at University College London, in a study published in 2010 in the European Journal of Social Psychology, found that it takes an average of sixty-six days for a new habit to become automatic, with individual differences ranging from eighteen to two hundred and fifty-four days. Brothers and sisters, listen to that number — sixty-six days on average. Deny yourself for three days and it is a struggle; deny yourself for sixty-six days and it starts to become like breathing. That is exactly what this lesson says: denying of self is not a one-off but a daily practice; not an emotional impulse but an ongoing decision.

sections.heading: Applying the 321 Vision
sections.html:
The fivefold change of 321 is: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry. Change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living. The first step in denying ourselves is always the renewal of our mindset: from “I want to win” to “I want to let Jesus win”; from the human perspective to God’s perspective, from the earthly to the heavenly, from the temporary to the eternal, from the worldly to the godly.

And the 920 practice is the most concrete arena for denying of self. Everyone we are in relationship with is our “2”; as we practise living out a selfless (0) life before each “2,” the nine graces of the fruit of the Spirit — love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness and self-control (Galatians 5:22–23) — grow naturally.

Brothers and sisters, fruit is never squeezed out by force. Have you ever seen an apple tree grit its teeth to produce apples? Never. Fruit is the natural overflow of life. The Lord Jesus said, “I am the vine. You are the branches. He who remains in me and I in him bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing.” (John 15:5) Denying of self is the branch no longer setting up on its own; selflessness is the sap flowing through freely.

sections.heading: 3. Keep On Denying Self by Grace, and Overcome the Power of Self
sections.html:
We all know that “self” is hard to deal with. That isn’t the complaint of a spiritual failure; it is the apostle Paul’s own confession:

“What a wretched man I am! Who will deliver me out of the body of this death?” (Romans 7:24)

Brothers and sisters, take great comfort today: the Paul who wrote a chapter as glorious as Romans 8 also wrote a cry as anguished as Romans 7. The spiritual giants are not people without struggles; they are people who know where to cry out.

Thank the Lord, the answer comes straight away: “I thank God through Jesus Christ, our Lord!” (Romans 7:25)

Notice the direction of this way out. Paul did not say, “Thank God, I finally figured it out,” nor, “Thank God, my willpower is strong enough.” He said, “through Jesus Christ, our Lord.” The secret of overcoming “self” lies not in suppressing ourselves but in relying on the grace of Jesus.

From chapter 7 to chapter 8: the law and the Spirit

The main character of Romans 7 is “I.” Someone has counted that in this short passage the word “I” appears dozens of times, yet the Holy Spirit is almost nowhere to be seen. But the moment we reach chapter 8, the Holy Spirit becomes the main character: “For the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus made me free from the law of sin and of death.” (Romans 8:2)

There is an important spiritual principle here: one law can only be overcome by a higher law. Gravity makes a sheet of paper fall to the ground, but when it is shaped into the wing of an aeroplane, a higher law — aerodynamics — makes it fly. Gravity has not been abolished; it has simply been surpassed.

The law of “self” works the same way. The more you press it down with “Don’t! Don’t!”, the harder it springs back. But when “the law of the Spirit of life” is at work, you find that you naturally no longer want to fight for the last word. That is why Paul says, “walk by the Spirit, and you won’t fulfill the lust of the flesh.” (Galatians 5:16) — not “try hard not to fulfil it,” but “walk by the Spirit, and you won’t.”

Key word: beat my body

Paul says, “but I beat my body and bring it into submission, lest by any means, after I have preached to others, I myself should be rejected.” (1 Corinthians 9:27)

The Greek for “beat” is ὑπωπιάζω, literally “to strike under the eye” — a term from the boxing ring, meaning to hit an opponent until his eye socket is black and blue. Paul uses the picture his Corinthian readers knew best: the boxing ring of the Isthmian Games.

But brothers and sisters, don’t misunderstand: this is not self-punishment by willpower. The same Paul, in the same letter, says: “yet not I, but the grace of God which was with me.” (1 Corinthians 15:10) The reason he could step into the ring every day was that he knew deeply a fact already accomplished: “Those who belong to Christ have crucified the flesh with its passions and lusts.” (Galatians 5:24)

Put these two verses side by side: Galatians 5:24 says the old self “has been” crucified; 1 Corinthians 9:27 says Paul beats his body “every day.” “Has been” is the fact of our position; “every day” is the practice of our experience. The position is given by grace; the experience is drawn on by faith. Without “has been,” “every day” is mere asceticism; without “every day,” “has been” is mere knowledge.

This lesson puts it well: the old self has already been crucified with Christ, and therefore he chose every day to “deny himself” and let the Holy Spirit be in control. Listen carefully to that “therefore” — not denying ourselves “in order to be crucified,” but denying ourselves “because we have already been crucified.” The first is the logic of religion; the second is the logic of the gospel.

Denying of self is not losing your personality

This point is very important, and this lesson stresses it: “denying of self” does not make us lose our personality; it renews our life so that we become more and more like Christ.

Look at the people in Scripture. After the Lord renewed Peter, he was still the same blunt, impulsive Peter — only that drive no longer charged after his own face; it charged onto the platform at Pentecost. After the Lord renewed Paul, he was still the same Paul, rigorous in logic and strong in will — only that strength no longer persecuted the church; it suffered for the church. John in his youth was a “Son of Thunder,” wanting to call fire down from heaven to burn up a Samaritan village (see Mark 3:17; Luke 9:54); in old age he became “the apostle of love.” God did not take his fire away; God rekindled his fire on the altar.

Brothers and sisters, denying of self does not turn you into someone else; it turns you back into the person God always meant to make. C. S. Lewis says in Mere Christianity: “Give up yourself, and you will find your real self.” What is given up is the “me” twisted by sin; what is found is the “me” created in the image of God.

Science confirms it: repeated choices reshape the brain

In The Organization of Behavior (1949), the Canadian psychologist Donald O. Hebb put forward a famous principle, often summed up since as “neurons that fire together wire together.” What modern neuroscience calls “neuroplasticity” builds on exactly this: the brain’s neural connections are strengthened by repeated use and weakened by long disuse.

That gives us great encouragement. The first time you choose not to answer back, it will feel very strange, like cutting a new path through dense forest. By the tenth time, the path already shows a trace. By the hundredth time, the path has become a highway — and it is the old path that is overgrown with weeds.

Of course, brothers and sisters, we must be clear: neuroplasticity only describes how the body God made works; it can never replace the work of the Holy Spirit. Habits can change behaviour; only the Holy Spirit can change a life. But this shows one thing — the brain God made was designed from the start for “repeated obedience.” “Repetition” among the eight stages is not a cliché; it is a law of God’s creation.

The less we fight for ourselves, the more the Lord fights for us

This lesson’s “Gentle Reminder” is the pearl of the whole lesson: “denying of self” is not passive retreat but actively letting Jesus reign. The less we fight for ourselves, the more the Lord fights for us; the less we try to prove ourselves, the more the Lord displays his glory.

This is the consistent principle of Scripture. When Moses faced the attack of Korah’s faction, Scripture says he “fell on his face” (see Numbers 16:4); he did not defend himself, and God defended him. When David was hunted by Saul, twice he had the chance to strike, and both times he said, “Yahweh forbid that I should stretch out my hand against Yahweh’s anointed” (1 Samuel 26:11) — and God himself opened the way for him. Before the council, the Lord Jesus “stayed quiet, and answered nothing” (Mark 14:61) — and on the third day God himself raised him from the dead.

The South African pastor Andrew Murray wrote in his book Humility in 1895 that humility is the soil in which every virtue takes root. Brothers and sisters, without the soil of humility, all our gifts, talents and service are just cut flowers in a vase — lovely to look at, but without roots, they won’t last three days.

sections.heading: Applying the 321 Vision
sections.html:
The 321 Path of Serving is: Spirit (the Holy Spirit is my guide), Understanding (the Bible is my standard), Life (Jesus is my role model), Service (let Jesus be King), God (let Jesus receive all the glory). The starting point of this path is exactly the answer of the third key point — not relying on our own brains or our own strength, but on the Holy Spirit.

321 reminds us: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the heart and you rejoice, rely on the brain and you worry. Because “out of it is the wellspring of life” (Proverbs 4:23). When we use our brains to calculate, “Will I lose out if I give this up?” we start to worry; when we use our hearts to trust, “The Lord will surely vindicate me,” we find joy.

And the 235 relationships are the most practical protection for keeping on denying ourselves. One person denying themselves alone can easily give way; but when two selfless people become each other’s “2,” spiritual companions who remind each other and pray for each other, they walk steadily. Going further, building “3,” spiritual parents and spiritual children, passes the life of denying of self on; and finally, becoming a “5,” a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades, we establish God’s system together.

Brothers and sisters, remember 321’s order: life first, then relationships, then ministry. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things. The priority of relationships is: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last with things. If we get the order upside down — charging into ministry first and talking about life later — we will feed the very “self” that ought to be denied with the achievements of our ministry. That is the most dangerous failure of all, and the hardest to detect.

sections.heading: 4. Integrating the 321 Vision: From Denying of Self to Establishing God’s System
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, when we place today’s three key points into the whole picture of 321, we see a clear road.

The Three Foundations: denying of self is not a lonely fight

Jesus is my role model. He does not ask us to walk a road he has not walked. The road of Philippians 2 is this: he emptied himself, was made in the likeness of men, humbled himself, became obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross — and then God raised him to the highest place. First down, then up; first give up, then gain — that is an order in the universe that cannot be changed.

The Bible is my standard. How do we know what should be given up and what should not? Not by feelings, not by the look on someone else’s face, not by a passing impulse, but by Scripture. Some things should be given up — my opinions, my face, my rights; some things must never be given up — the truth, holiness, the responsibilities God has entrusted to us. Denying of self never means failing to tell right from wrong, still less tolerating sin. The standard for discernment is the Bible alone.

The Holy Spirit is my guide. Without the Holy Spirit, denying of self becomes a moral performance; with the Holy Spirit, it becomes the overflow of life. In that very moment the Holy Spirit will gently remind you, “Don’t say that.” The one who obeys in that moment gains freedom.

The Two Core Values and the Goal

Let Jesus be King — this is the very centre of this lesson. The third practice in this lesson asks exactly the right question: “Am I in charge here, or is Jesus?” Brothers and sisters, this question can be used to test every decision we make in a day.

Let Jesus receive all the glory — the less we try to prove ourselves, the more the Lord displays his glory. Glory is like water: it only flows downhill. Wherever there is a hollow of humility, it fills up with glory.

Establish God’s system — this is the Goal. We deny ourselves not in order to be lonely good people, but so that God can build his house, his kingdom, his army among a people who are selfless. A stone that insists on keeping its sharp edges cannot be laid into a wall with other stones. A system is built from stones that are willing to be dressed and shaped.

The old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless

321 says again and again: the self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall, and pride is the root of the problem. The serpent’s temptation in Eden was “you will be like God, knowing good and evil” (Genesis 3:5); the fall of the morning star was “I will make myself like the Most High!” (Isaiah 14:14). From heaven to Eden, sin’s recipe comes down to one word: self.

Therefore humility overcomes pride, and selflessness overcomes Satan. This is not a slogan; it is the tactic of spiritual warfare. Satan’s favourite lines of attack are your self-esteem, your sense of grievance, your “What am I, then?” When someone has already denied themselves, Satan can find no foothold — just as the Lord Jesus said: “for the prince of the world comes, and he has nothing in me.” (John 14:30)

Brothers and sisters, think about that. Satan had “nothing” in the Lord — not a single handle he could grab and pull on. The more we deny ourselves, the fewer handles the enemy has to grab. That is the most effective spiritual protection there is.

And selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the infinite and living out the infinite. What you give up is a small “me”; what you gain is the infinite Lord. That is not a loss; it is the best bargain in human history.

The fivefold change and the shift of perspective

The fivefold change of 321 is: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry. In today’s lesson, the most important is the first — mindset.

Exchange the old mindsets: from “selflessness is a state for saints” to “selflessness is the pattern of life for every Christian”; from “denying of self means losing out” to “denying of self means gaining freedom”; from “I must overcome self by willpower” to “I must let Jesus reign by grace.”

When the mindset changes, the life changes; when the life changes, daily living changes; when daily living changes, relationships change; when relationships change, ministry changes. This is the order 321 has witnessed over twenty years, and the road countless brothers and sisters have walked themselves.

At the same time, our perspective must shift in four ways: from the human perspective to God’s — no longer asking “What do others think of me?” but only “How does God see this?”; from the earthly to the heavenly — “Set your mind on the things that are above, not on the things that are on the earth” (Colossians 3:2); from the temporary to the eternal — will today’s quarrel still matter in ten years? In a hundred? From the worldly to the godly — not using the world’s methods to fight for the world’s things.

920 and 235

The 920 practice: everyone we are in relationship with is our “2.” Your spouse is your 2, your children are your 2, and that colleague who opposes you at every meeting is your 2 as well. As we practise living out a selfless (0) life before each “2,” the nine graces of the fruit of the Spirit grow.

Notice the order: it is not that we first have the fruit and then become selfless; we first become selfless, and then the fruit comes. Zero is the soil of the fruit.

The 235 relationships: become a “2,” a spiritual companion, with someone who is selfless, and walk the road of denying of self together; build “3,” spiritual parents and spiritual children, and pass this life on; become a “5,” a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades, and fight for the Lord together. Brothers and sisters, walk the road of denying of self alone and it gets cold; walk it with others and it grows warm.

sections.heading: 5. Practice for Daily Living
sections.html:
This lesson gives us three very concrete practices. We will deepen them one by one following 321’s eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.

Practice 1: Pray every day, “Lord, help me choose to deny myself today, and let your will be done in me”

Information: First put the truth into your head. Today you have learned: denying of self is not a condition but a response to grace; selflessness is not cultivated by us but lived out by Jesus.

Revelation: Ask the Holy Spirit to turn this teaching into your own seeing. You could pray like this: “Lord, let me see with my own eyes that I have been crucified with Christ.” Teaching is given by others; seeing is given by the Holy Spirit.

Conviction: Move from “I know” to “I believe, and I am willing.” Conviction is the moment you hand over sovereignty.

Implementation: Put this prayer at the very start of your day. Try praying it as soon as you open your eyes, before your feet touch the floor. Because whoever takes possession of the beginning of your day shapes the rest of it.

Evaluation: In the evening, spend three minutes looking back: at what moment today did I snatch the throne back? Not to condemn yourself, but to see the truth.

Correction: Don’t say vaguely, “I’ll do better tomorrow.” Say specifically, “Tomorrow morning, when I take the children to school, I won’t use that tone of voice again.”

Repetition: Remember that number? Sixty-six days on average. Set yourself a practice period of at least sixty-six days.

Multiplication: Find a spiritual companion and do this sixty-six-day practice together, checking in on each other and reminding each other. “Two are better than one, because they have a good reward for their labor.” (Ecclesiastes 4:9)

Practice 2: When opinions differ, learn to listen quietly for the Lord’s voice, and don’t rush to argue

Information: Scripture says, “let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger” (James 1:19). Those few seconds between “swift to hear” and “slow to speak” are the battlefield of denying of self.

Revelation: Ask the Lord to show you what you are really trying to protect in the moment you rush to argue. Usually it isn’t the truth; it’s your pride.

Conviction: Believe this — not arguing does not mean admitting defeat; the vindication God gives you is more complete than any you could win for yourself.

Implementation: Make a rule — when you feel the heat rising inside, first count to three silently and pray silently, “Lord, you are King.” Three seconds is often the distance between heaven and hell.

Evaluation: This week, how many times did I manage to stay quiet? How many times did I lose ground? On the occasions I lost ground, what was the common trigger?

Correction: Identify your trigger — being misunderstood? Being interrupted? Being compared? For that particular trigger, write down in advance a sentence you will say, such as: “I need to think about what you’ve said. Let’s talk again in a little while.”

Repetition: Start practising in your safest relationships, then gradually extend it to the most difficult ones.

Multiplication: When your family ask you, “Why have you changed lately?” — that is the door to the gospel opening. Don’t miss it.

Practice 3: When facing a challenge, first ask, “Am I in charge here, or is Jesus?” and choose to obey the Lord

Information: Recognise the four faces of “self” — wanting to control, wanting to argue, wanting to prove, wanting to protect ourselves.

Revelation: Ask the Lord to place this question in your heart in every moment. It is a prayer the Holy Spirit is only too glad to answer.

Conviction: Truly believe that Jesus being King is better than me being in charge. Because he loves the people I love more than I do, and he knows better than I do what is best for me.

Implementation: Write this question on a small card and stick it where you’ll see it most — beside your computer screen, next to the steering wheel, on the kitchen cupboard door.

Evaluation: Each week, pick one specific incident and write three lines: Was I in charge then? What did it cost me? If I had let Jesus be in charge, how would it have ended?

Correction: Hand over your most stubborn area. Everyone has a drawer marked “Don’t touch” — it might be money, it might be your children’s future, it might be a particular wounded relationship. Open that drawer today.

Repetition: Once a day, one thing at a time. Don’t try to hand over everything at once — you won’t manage it.

Multiplication: Share your failures and your victories in your small group. Your failures will give others courage; your victories will give others hope.

sections.heading: 6. Closing and Call
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, the closing words of this lesson are beautiful: “selflessness” is not a faraway dream but a daily choice; “denying of self” is not a painful bondage but the starting point of freedom. When we keep on “denying ourselves” and let Jesus reign, his life will naturally flow out, and the world will surely see Christ because of us.

Let us gather up today’s three key points once more:

First, selflessness is not achieved by effort but received by grace. You don’t have to keep struggling up the mountain, because the cross has already accomplished it.

Second, denying of self is the only road to selflessness. There is no shortcut, but there is grace; you don’t have to be perfect, only take today’s step.

Third, keep on denying self by grace, and overcome the power of self. Not by suppression, but by walking by the Spirit; not by self-punishment, but by letting the King take his throne.

Let’s go back to that grain of wheat from early this morning. Brothers and sisters, when that grain fell into the ground, there was no thunder in the sky, and the earth did not shake. No one took a photo; no one applauded. The soil simply covered it quietly. Denying of self is often just like that — it happens where no one sees: in a retort left unspoken, in a door not slammed, in a little extra done in silence.

But God sees. And a few months later, at harvest time, everyone sees.

So this morning I want to give you a threefold call.

The first call: let Jesus be King. Not your consultant, not your emergency fire brigade — your King. King means that what he says goes.

The second call: starting today, don’t try to get there all at once; just take one step a day. There is one thing today that you already know the Lord wants you to let go of. That one. Don’t put it off until tomorrow.

The third call: let Jesus receive all the glory. When one day people ask you “Why?” because of your gentleness, your patience, your refusal to fight, please don’t leave them with “I’m just good-natured by birth.” Please say, “It isn’t me. It is Christ who lives in me.”

“For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain.” (Philippians 1:21) Brothers and sisters, may these words be the epitaph of every one of us — and, even more, our daily living today.

keyVerses: “Then Jesus said to his disciples, ‘If anyone desires to come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me.’” (Matthew 16:24)

“I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me.” (Galatians 2:20)
declarations: This lesson’s declaration of faith — brothers and sisters, please declare it aloud once every day:

Lord, thank you for your grace, which sets me free from the dominion of “self.” Please help me choose every day to deny myself — not my will, but only yours. May my life become a testimony to your glory, living out the reality of “no longer I, but Christ.”
practices: Pray every day, “Lord, help me choose to deny myself today, and let your will be done in me”
When opinions differ, learn to listen quietly for the Lord’s voice, and don’t rush to argue
When facing a challenge, first ask, “Am I in charge here, or is Jesus?” and choose to obey the Lord
prayer: Dear Lord Jesus,

We come before you this morning confessing how stubborn the “self” within us is. It wants to control, it wants to argue, it wants to prove itself, it wants to protect itself. Many times we have tried in our own strength to overcome it, and time after time we have failed, grown weary and lost heart.

Lord, today you have let us see that our old self has already been crucified with you. This is not a project we must complete; it is a salvation you have already accomplished. Thank you for your death, which broke the dominion of sin; thank you for your resurrection, which gave us new life.

Help us, from today on, to choose every day to deny ourselves. When opinions differ, give us quietness; when we are misunderstood, give us the freedom not to defend ourselves; when we could take control, give us the courage to let go. Holy Spirit, gently remind us in every moment: “Am I in charge here, or is Jesus?”

Lord, be King in our homes, King in our workplaces, King in our church, King in every one of our thoughts. May our lives bear the fruit of the Spirit; may we stand together with our spiritual companions; and may everything we do bring glory to you.
In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: Question 1: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” (Galatians 2:20) Have you ever tried to “reach selflessness by effort”? What did that experience bring you? Now that you have heard today that “selflessness is received by grace, not achieved by effort,” how specifically has your mindset been renewed?

Question 2: “If anyone desires to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross daily, and follow me.” (Luke 9:23, as the Chinese Union Version reads) In your present relationships, which face does “self” wear most often — wanting to control, wanting to argue, wanting to prove, or wanting to protect yourself? Describe one specific situation, and agree with your small group on a sixty-six-day practice of denying of self, praying for one another and reviewing together.

blog.title: The Secret of a Grain of Wheat

blocks.x: Why the harder you try to be selfless, the more tired you get

Have you ever had this experience? In the morning you finish reading a passage of Scripture, your heart is on fire, and you resolve that today you will be patient, humble, not quarrelsome. Then you hold on until three in the afternoon — and one remark, one look, and it all falls apart. That night you lie in bed and ask yourself, “Why am I so hopeless?”
If you have, I have good news for you: the problem is not that you aren’t trying hard enough. The problem is that you are trying in the wrong direction.
Selflessness is not achieved by self-cultivation

Many people think of “selflessness” as a spiritual state that belongs only to Moses, to Paul, or to those unreachable saints in the biographies. So we grit our teeth and climb, and the higher we climb the more breathless we get, and the more breathless we get the more unworthy we feel.
But Scripture says something entirely different:
“Therefore if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old things have passed away. Behold, all things have become new.” (2 Corinthians 5:17)

Notice: not “if anyone tries hard enough,” but “if anyone is in Christ.” This is an identity already established, not a reward still to be won. In the original, “new creation” means a creation entirely new in kind — like the light in Genesis 1. The darkness did not try hard to grow brighter; God said, “Let there be light,” and there was light.
Jesus’ death broke the dominion of sin; Jesus’ resurrection gave us new life. So selflessness is not something we produce; it is something Jesus lives out within us.
Denying of self is that small choice we make every day
So what are we to do? The answer is just three words: deny your self.
“If anyone desires to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross daily, and follow me.” (Luke 9:23)
Notice the word “daily.” Daily — that one word turns the cross from a ceremony into an everyday thing.

The Greek word for “deny himself” means “to deny, to disown, to draw a clear line against” — and interestingly, it is the very same word as in Peter’s “you will deny me three times.” When Peter denied the Lord, he treated the Lord as a stranger; when the Lord asks us to deny ourselves, he is asking us to treat as a stranger the self that keeps wanting to sit on the throne.

The place where denying of self happens has never been a monastery deep in the mountains; it is your kitchen, your office and your group chats today. You can pin it down with four verbs: wanting to control, wanting to argue, wanting to prove, wanting to protect ourselves. These are the four faces of “self.”

A sister once said that the fiercest row she ever had with her husband started over whether the spoons should lie sideways or lengthways. Afterwards she said something very perceptive: “Actually, we weren’t fighting about the spoons. We were fighting about who gets the final say.”
Eight or nine out of ten conflicts in our lives aren’t about the spoons.
Sixty-six days, until it becomes like breathing
Someone will say, “I’ve tried. I can’t keep it up.”

Paul couldn’t keep it up either. He said, “What a wretched man I am! Who will deliver me out of the body of this death?” (Romans 7:24) But straight away he said, “I thank God through Jesus Christ, our Lord!” The way out is not suppressing ourselves; it is relying on grace.

One law can only be overcome by a higher law. Gravity makes a sheet of paper fall to the ground, but shape it into a wing and a higher law — aerodynamics — makes it fly. You no longer have to go head to head with “self”; you only need to walk by the Spirit.

In 2010 a research team at University College London found that it takes an average of sixty-six days for a new habit to become automatic. Deny yourself for only three days and it is a struggle; deny yourself for sixty-six days and it starts to become like breathing.
Set yourself three practices, and keep them for a full sixty-six days:
First, every day, as soon as you open your eyes and before your feet touch the floor, pray: “Lord, help me choose to deny myself today.”
Second, when opinions differ, first count to three silently and say in your heart, “Lord, you are King.”
Third, when facing a challenge, first ask: “Am I in charge here, or is Jesus?”
That grain of wheat

A grain of wheat lies in the palm of your hand — golden and plump. Grains unearthed from the pyramids have been preserved for thousands of years, their husks still intact. Yet however well it is kept, it remains just a single grain.
“Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains by itself alone. But if it dies, it bears much fruit.” (John 12:24)

When the wheat fell into the ground, there was no thunder in the sky, the earth did not shake, no one took a photo and no one applauded. Denying of self is often just like that — it happens in a retort left unspoken, in a door not slammed.
But God sees. And at harvest time, everyone sees.
Selflessness is not a faraway dream but a daily choice; denying of self is not a painful bondage but the starting point of freedom.
A question to leave with you
There is one thing today that you already know the Lord wants you to let go of. What is it?
Are you willing to let it go today, and let Jesus be King?
