Introduction: A Man Steps Out of the Line
Slide text:
Before the starvation bunker at Auschwitz
Father Kolbe said: I will take his place
The world says: as long as I’m happy
Jesus says: if anyone desires to come after me, let him deny himself
Key points:
1. History: at the end of July 1941 a prisoner escaped from Auschwitz and ten men were chosen for the starvation bunker; Gajowniczek cried out, “My wife, my children!”
2. Father Kolbe volunteered to take his place and died in the bunker on 14 August; Gajowniczek lived until 1995.
3. Contrast the world’s slogans, “As long as I’m happy” and “Be true to yourself” — that “me” can never be filled.
4. Augustine, Confessions, Book 1: “You have made us for yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in you.”
5. Lead into the call of Matthew 16:24.
Theme Verse and Background
Slide text:
1 Corinthians 8–10: the dispute over food sacrificed to idols
Those who have rights willingly lay them down
“Not seeking my own profit, but the profit of the many”
(1 Corinthians 10:33)
Key points:
1. Author: Paul, writing from Ephesus around AD 54–55 (1 Corinthians 16:8).
2. Corinth was the capital of Achaia, a two-port trading hub, full of idols and morally corrupt.
3. 1 Corinthians 8–10 deals with food sacrificed to idols; 8:1, “Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up.”
4. In 9:12 Paul says, “we didn’t use this right”; 11:1, “Be imitators of me, even as I also am of Christ.”
5. Conclusion: the theme verse is the conclusion of a dispute over rights.
The Rule for Living: For Jesus
Slide text:
The world’s centre is “me”
The Christian’s centre is Jesus
First ask: does this glorify the Lord?
In the original, “glory” means “heavy,” weighty
Key points:
1. Scripture: 1 Corinthians 10:31 — “eat, or drink” shows that glorifying God is a direction for daily living, not a religious activity.
2. Word meaning: Greek doxa, Hebrew kabod, whose root means “heavy.”
3. Illustration: an orchestra tuning up — every instrument tunes to A at 440 vibrations a second (adopted at an international conference in 1939).
4. 321: the Two Core Values — let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory; the first of the Three Foundations — Jesus is my role model.
The Rule for Living: For Others
Slide text:
“Let no one seek his own,”
“but each one his neighbor’s good” (1 Corinthians 10:24)
People matter more than tasks, relationships more than things
Life first, then relationships, then ministry
Key points:
1. Scripture: 1 Corinthians 10:24; Philippians 2:4, “each of you not just looking to his own things.”
2. Word meaning: “profit” is made up in the original of “together” and “bring” — true profit is never one person winning alone.
3. Research: Dunn, Aknin and Norton, Science, 2008 — people who spent money on others were happier that day.

The Rule for Living: Not for Self
Slide text:
“No longer live to themselves” (2 Corinthians 5:15)
The old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless
Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose
Humility inspires humility, and both sides win

2. Genesis 3:5, “you will be like God, knowing good and evil”; Isaiah 14:14, “I will make myself like the Most High!”

Change myself first, rather than demanding of others

2. The Two Core Values correspond to “for Jesus”; the Goal corresponds to “for others.”
3. Romans 8:14: deny yourself by the Holy Spirit and you bear fruit; deny yourself in your own strength and you only grow bitter.
4. 920 and 235: living it for you to see builds the 2, dying for you to see gives birth to the 3, and in the end we become the 5.
5. Rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; Proverbs 4:23.
Closing and Call
Slide text:
The broad road leads to emptiness; the narrow road to life
(Matthew 7:13–14)
Denying of self is not losing yourself
but letting Jesus be seen more clearly
Key points:
1. The lesson’s gentle reminder: the road of “for self” is broad, but it leads to emptiness.
2. The narrow gate only has room for one — not for you and your “self” together.
3. Illustration: the cleaner the window, the less you notice the glass and the more you see the light.
4. Philippians 1:21, “For to me to live is Christ.”
5. Call: let Jesus be King; let Jesus receive all the glory.
Prayer of Response and Blessing

Give me strength to show your love

Key points:
1. First lead brothers and sisters in declaring the lesson’s declaration of faith together.
2. Pray for the three places: home, church and work.
3. Pray for the “2” beside each person, asking the Lord to let them see Jesus.
4. Close with a blessing, pointing to letting Jesus be King and giving the glory to Jesus.

script: Brothers and sisters, peace be with you this morning. Today we come together to Lesson 68 of Morning Devotion 321 — “For Jesus, for Others, Not for Self.” Our theme verse says, “Whether therefore you eat, or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God.” (1 Corinthians 10:31) Today we are going to learn one principle and look at two practices: the principle is “for Jesus, for others, not for self,” and the practices are “living it for you to see” and “dying for you to see.”

Let me begin with a true story. At the end of July 1941, a prisoner escaped from Auschwitz concentration camp, and ten men were chosen for the starvation bunker in reprisal. One of the men whose name was called cried out, “My wife! My children!” At that very moment a thin priest, Maximilian Kolbe, stepped out of the line and said, “I am willing to take this man’s place.” He died in the bunker, and that man survived the war.

Brothers and sisters, what shakes us in this story isn’t the death; it’s a choice that was “not for self.” This world keeps telling us, “As long as I’m happy,” “Be true to yourself.” But that “me” can never be filled. Jesus, though, says, “If anyone desires to come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me.” (Matthew 16:24)

Our theme verse isn’t a maxim that floated down out of nowhere. Paul wrote 1 Corinthians around AD 55, and in chapters 8 to 10 he was dealing with a dispute: could you eat meat that had been sacrificed to idols? The knowledgeable said yes, and they weren’t wrong. But Paul said, “Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up.” (1 Corinthians 8:1) Then he laid himself open as an example: he had rights, yet he didn’t use them. Brothers and sisters, remember this: those who have rights willingly lay them down for the sake of others. That is the pattern of Jesus.

The first key point: the rule for living. The world lives with “me” at the centre, but Christians should live with “Jesus” at the centre. So in everything we do, first ask one question: “Does this glorify the Lord?”

The root of the Hebrew word for “glory” means “heavy,” “weighty.” To glorify God is to let God carry real weight in my life. It’s like an orchestra tuning up before it goes on stage — every instrument has to tune to the same reference pitch; if each tuned to its own, the result wouldn’t be freedom but noise. “For Jesus” is the tuning of our lives, and that is what 321 means by: let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive all the glory.

Second, for others. Scripture says, “Let no one seek his own, but each one his neighbor’s good.” (1 Corinthians 10:24) In the original, “profit” means “a benefit brought about together” — true profit is never one person winning alone.

In 2008 three researchers published a study in the journal Science: people who spent an unexpected sum of money on someone else were clearly happier that day. Harvard University has followed the same group of people for more than eighty years and found that what best predicts happiness in later life is not wealth but good relationships. This is exactly what 321 says: people matter more than tasks.

Third, not for self. Paul says, “He died for all, that those who live should no longer live to themselves.” (2 Corinthians 5:15) Brothers and sisters, this sentence is the heartbeat of today — no longer living for ourselves.

The old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. In the Garden of Eden the serpent said, “You will be like God, knowing good and evil.” (Genesis 3:5) Pride is leaving our originally intended position and grasping power, wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — letting man be man and letting God be God. That is why 321 says: pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility inspires humility, and both sides win.

The second key point: living it for you to see. Brothers and sisters, we often say, “It’s for your own good.” But in those few words, half is often tenderness and half is control. When the other person doesn’t comply, we get angry — and the real reason for our anger is that I wasn’t obeyed.

So truly being “for your good” doesn’t mean demanding that others change; it means starting by changing myself. 321 speaks of a fivefold change: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry — and the starting point is always me, not you. Peter says Christ left “you an example” (1 Peter 2:21); in the original, “example” is the copybook a schoolchild traces over. The Lord has written the letters out first, and we trace over them; and the people beside us are watching our exercise books.

“Living it for you to see” happens in three places: at home, not fighting for the last word; when serving at church, gladly taking a behind-the-scenes role and helping others flourish; at work, not fighting for your own advantage, but being willing to treat others fairly.

Look at Andrew — the first thing he did after meeting the Lord was to bring his brother Simon to Jesus. He never wrote a single letter, yet he brought Peter to the Lord. This is 321’s “920”: everyone we have a relationship with is our “2”; before them we live out the selfless “0,” and the ninefold fruit of the Spirit grows. Fruit is never for the tree to eat itself.

The third key point: dying for you to see. Let’s be clear first — this is not threatening people with death. Once denying of self becomes a weapon, it is no longer denying of self. “Dying for you to see” means: I am willing to pay the price for you, so that you may benefit.

The Lord said, “No one takes it away from me, but I lay it down by myself.” (John 10:18) In the original, “laid down his life” is an active “laying down.” This kind of death is mostly not a physical death; it is laying down our attachments, pride, face and rights: laying down who’s right for the sake of reconciliation in the family, laying down our own opinions for the sake of the church’s unity, laying down our convenience and comfort for the sake of someone else’s growth. The Lord said, “Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains by itself alone. But if it dies, it bears much fruit.” (John 12:24)

Brothers and sisters, there are three practices for today. First, before you do anything, ask: am I doing this for Jesus? For others? Or for myself? Second, with family or co-workers, say “It’s for your own good” less, and show love in action more. Third, write down one thing where you are willing to “die for others to see” — laying down your own ideas so that someone else can flourish.

Then walk it through the eight stages of changing our mindset: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication. Give yourself forty days — denying of self is a muscle, not a flash of inspiration.

The lesson ends with a gentle reminder: the road of “for self” is broad, but it leads to emptiness; the road of “for Jesus, for others” is narrow, but it leads to life. The Lord said, “Enter in by the narrow gate.” (Matthew 7:13) Why is the narrow gate narrow? Because there’s no room for you and your “self” to go through it together.

Brothers and sisters, denying of self is not losing yourself; it is letting Jesus be seen more clearly in you. The cleaner a window is, the less people notice the glass, and the more they see the light outside.

Let us declare together: Lord, today I choose to live “for you, for others, not for myself.” Give me the strength to show your love in every small thing, to live a life of denying self, and to be a blessing to others.

Dear Lord Jesus, let your Holy Spirit change our mindset and put off our old self. May we today, at home, at church and at work, live it for others to see — and be willing to die for others to see. May every choice we make let you be King; may every bit of glory go to you. In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.

Brothers and sisters, peace be with you this morning. Today we come together to Lesson 68 of Morning Devotion 321 — “For Jesus, for Others, Not for Self.” The theme verse of this lesson is: “Whether therefore you eat, or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God.” (1 Corinthians 10:31) And another: “By this we know love, because he laid down his life for us. And we ought to lay down our lives for the brothers.” (1 John 3:16) Today we are going to learn one principle and look at two practices: the principle is “for Jesus, for others, not for self,” and the practices are “living it for you to see” and “dying for you to see.”

Let me begin with a true story. At the end of July 1941, a prisoner escaped from Auschwitz concentration camp in Poland. Under the Nazi rules, ten men from the same block had to be locked in an underground starvation bunker and left to starve to death. When Franciszek Gajowniczek heard his number called, he cried out, “My wife! My children!”

At that very moment a thin figure stepped out of the line — Maximilian Kolbe, a forty-seven-year-old priest. Calmly he said, “I am willing to take this man’s place.” He died in the starvation bunker. And the man whose place he took survived the war and lived on until 1995, returning to Auschwitz year after year to bear witness.

Brothers and sisters, what shakes us in this story isn’t the death; it’s a choice that was “not for self.” Our world is exactly the opposite; two slogans float in the air: “As long as I’m happy” and “Be true to yourself.” But that “me” can never be filled; the more you feed it, the hungrier it gets. Augustine said, “You have made us for yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in you.”

So Jesus issues an invitation in the opposite direction: “If anyone desires to come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me.” (Matthew 16:24) Notice that denying of self is not repressing yourself; it is finding a higher direction for your life.

First let’s look at the background. Paul wrote 1 Corinthians in Ephesus around AD 54 to 55. Corinth was the capital of the province of Achaia, with a seaport on each side, east and west; wealth poured in, and idols stood everywhere.

Chapters 8 to 10 deal with food sacrificed to idols. The knowledgeable said there was no harm in eating, and theologically they weren’t wrong; but Paul reminded them, “Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up.” (1 Corinthians 8:1) Then he laid himself open as an example: “Nevertheless we didn’t use this right, but we bear all things, that we may cause no hindrance to the Good News of Christ.” (1 Corinthians 9:12) Brothers and sisters, remember this: those who have rights willingly lay them down for the sake of others. That is the pattern of Jesus.

The first key point: the rule for living. The world lives with “me” at the centre, but Christians should live with “Jesus” at the centre. Notice the example Paul gives — “eat, or drink.” God doesn’t only want those two hours of your Sunday; he wants your whole day.

In the original, the root of the word “glory” means “heavy,” “weighty.” To glorify God is to let God carry real weight in my life. It’s like an orchestra tuning up before it goes on stage: every instrument tunes to the same reference pitch — the A that vibrates 440 times a second. If each tuned to its own, the result wouldn’t be freedom but noise. “For Jesus” is the tuning of our lives.

Second, for others. Scripture says, “Let no one seek his own, but each one his neighbor’s good.” (1 Corinthians 10:24) In the original, “profit” is made up of “together” and “bring” — true profit is never one person winning alone.

Paul also says, “each of you not just looking to his own things, but each of you also to the things of others.” (Philippians 2:4) Brothers and sisters, listen carefully: it says “not just,” not “don’t.” Faith never denies people’s legitimate needs; it simply refuses to let “me” be the only audience.

Even social science bears witness to this principle. In 2008 three researchers — Dunn, Aknin and Norton — published a study in the journal Science: people who spent an unexpected sum of money on someone else were clearly happier that evening. Harvard University’s Study of Adult Development has followed the same group of people since 1938, for more than eighty years, and its director, Robert Waldinger, sums it up: what best predicts health and happiness in later life is not wealth, not fame, but good relationships.
Brothers and sisters, this is exactly what 321 says: people matter more than tasks, relationships matter more than things; life first, then relationships, then ministry.
Third, not for self. Paul says, “He died for all, that those who live should no longer live to themselves.” (2 Corinthians 5:15) This sentence is the heartbeat of today.

The old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. In the Garden of Eden the serpent said, “You will be like God, knowing good and evil.” (Genesis 3:5) At the heart of the temptation was not a piece of fruit but a position. Isaiah records the words of the fallen one: “I will make myself like the Most High!” (Isaiah 14:14) Pride is leaving our originally intended position and grasping power, wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — letting man be man and letting God be God.

In Mere Christianity, C. S. Lewis says that pride is essentially competitive: it gets no pleasure out of having something, only out of having more of it than the next person. When two proud people meet, it’s like two goats on a single-plank bridge — neither will back down, and in the end both fall into the water. 321 puts it vividly: pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility inspires humility, and both sides win.

Living like this looks like losing out, but change the frame of reference and the plus and minus signs are reversed. Because it was on the very road of “not for self” that Jesus accomplished salvation: “who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant.” (Philippians 2:6-7) In the original, “emptied himself” means “to pour out until empty.”

The second key point: living it for you to see. We often say, “It’s for your own good.” That sentence is often half tenderness and half control; when the other person doesn’t comply we get angry — and the real reason for our anger is that I wasn’t obeyed.

So truly being “for your good” doesn’t mean demanding that others change; it means starting by changing myself. 321 speaks of a fivefold change: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry — and the starting point is always me, not you. We often do it backwards: we set about correcting the other person first, and the result is that everyone is changing everyone else and nobody is changing themselves.

Peter says Christ left “you an example, that you should follow his steps” (1 Peter 2:21). In the original, “example” is the copybook a schoolchild placed underneath the page when learning to write. Jesus has already written out the lesson of “not for self”; we trace over it — and the people beside us are watching our exercise books.

In 1961 Albert Bandura of Stanford University conducted the Bobo doll experiment: after watching an adult hit a doll, children clearly imitated what they had seen. From this he developed social learning theory. Brothers and sisters, children don’t grow up according to what you say; they grow up according to how you live.

“Living it for you to see” happens in three places. The first is home: not fighting for the last word. In decades of marriage research, Gottman has shown that the strongest predictor of a marriage breaking down is not how often a couple argues but “contempt.” At home, living it for you to see usually isn’t doing something great; it’s saying one sentence less.

The second is church: gladly taking a behind-the-scenes role and helping others flourish. God gave the ministries “for the perfecting of the saints, to the work of serving, to the building up of the body of Christ” (Ephesians 4:12). The first thing Andrew did after meeting the Lord was to bring his brother Simon to Jesus; he never wrote a single letter, yet he brought Peter to the Lord.

The third is work: not fighting for your own advantage. Adam Grant of the Wharton School shows that givers often end up at the bottom of the performance rankings, yet the people who appear most often at the very top are givers too. We don’t refrain from fighting for ourselves in order to climb higher; we do it because our Boss is in heaven.

Brothers and sisters, a life of denying self is contagious. That isn’t because we are especially cultivated; it is the life of Jesus living within us: “It is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” (Galatians 2:20) Selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the infinite. A drop of water in the palm of your hand soon dries up; put it into the sea and it will never run dry.

On 9 March 1872, the twenty-seven-year-old George Leslie Mackay arrived in Tamsui. He pulled people’s teeth and preached Jesus at the same time, and extracted more than twenty thousand teeth in his lifetime. His motto is generally said to have been: “Rather burn out than rust out.” This is “920”: everyone we have a relationship with is our “2”; before them we live out the selfless “0” and bear the ninefold fruit of the Spirit. Fruit is never for the tree to eat itself.

The third key point: dying for you to see. Let’s be clear first — this is not threatening others with death. Some people use self-harm or threats of suicide to force the other person to give in; that isn’t denying of self, that’s blowing the “self” up to its very largest. Once denying of self becomes a weapon, it is no longer denying of self.

“Dying for you to see” expresses a love that holds nothing back: I am willing to pay the price for you, so that you may benefit. The Lord said, “No one takes it away from me, but I lay it down by myself.” (John 10:18) In 1 John, “laid down his life” is literally “laid down.” Denying of self isn’t having something snatched from us; it’s me laying it down myself.

This kind of death is mostly not a physical death, but laying down our attachments, pride, face and rights. Paul says, “I die daily.” (1 Corinthians 15:31) And the Lord says, “If anyone desires to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross daily, and follow me.” (Luke 9:23)

“Deny himself” is a very strong word in the original, meaning to disown utterly, to flatly refuse to acknowledge — the very same word used of Peter when he three times “denied the Lord.” Peter denied the Lord to save himself; what the Lord asks of us is to deny ourselves for the Lord’s sake. Brothers and sisters, whom will you deny today?

“Dying for you to see” also happens in three places. Laying down who’s right for the sake of reconciliation in the family — the hardest thing to let go of at home isn’t money; it’s “I’m right.” Paul asks, “Why not rather be wronged?” (1 Corinthians 6:7) Do you want to win the argument, or win the person?

Laying down your own opinion for the sake of the church’s unity — “being eager to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.” (Ephesians 4:3) Laying down convenience and comfort for the sake of someone else’s growth — in 1853 Hudson Taylor put on Chinese clothes and went into the interior; what he gave up was respectability, and what he gained was an open door.

The Lord said, “Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains by itself alone. But if it dies, it bears much fruit.” (John 12:24) The seed coat must split and the nutrients in the seed leaf must be used up before the new shoot can push up through the soil. In 2003 Brown and colleagues at the University of Michigan also found that older people who regularly gave others practical help had a lower risk of death. “It is more blessed to give than to receive.” (Acts 20:35)

Brothers and sisters, there are three practices for today. First, before you do anything each day, ask: am I doing this for Jesus? For others? Or for myself? Write it on a small card — and the smaller the matter, the more you should ask.

Second, with family or co-workers, say “It’s for your own good” less, and show love in action more. If you want to remind your child to go to bed early, first put your own phone down. Scripture says, “My little children, let’s not love in word only, or with the tongue only, but in deed and truth.” (1 John 3:18)
Third, write down one thing where you are willing to “die for others to see.” Is it that phone call you won’t make? The position you won’t hand over? Write it down, set a date, and then go and do it.

Let’s take it deeper through the eight stages of changing our mindset. Information — you have received it today. Revelation — ask the Holy Spirit to let you hear that “God is speaking to me.” Conviction — no longer saying, “But he was in the wrong first.” Implementation — do one thing today; understanding comes after obeying.

Evaluation — three minutes before bed looking in the mirror. Correction — if you’ve hurt someone, apologise. Repetition — give yourself forty days; denying of self is a muscle, not a flash of inspiration. Multiplication — take someone along and walk the forty days with them.

Brothers and sisters, this lesson is the heart of 321. The Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model — the ground of “for Jesus”; the Bible is my standard — the measure of “for others”; the Holy Spirit is my guide — the power for “not for self.” If you deny yourself in your own strength, you’ll end up exhausted and bitter; if you deny yourself by the Holy Spirit, you’ll end up bearing the ninefold fruit.

The Two Core Values: let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive all the glory. The Goal: establish God’s system. Living it for you to see builds the “2”; dying for you to see gives birth to the “3”; and in the end we become the “5.” And here’s a word for any brother or sister whose heart is weary today: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the heart and you rejoice, rely on the brain and you worry.

The lesson leaves us with a gentle reminder: the road of “for self” is broad, but it leads to emptiness; the road of “for Jesus, for others” is narrow, but it leads to life. The Lord said, “Enter in by the narrow gate; for wide is the gate and broad is the way that leads to destruction, and many are those who enter in by it. How narrow is the gate, and restricted is the way that leads to life! Few are those who find it.” (Matthew 7:13-14)

Why is the narrow gate narrow? Because there’s no room for you and your “self” to go through it together. Denying of self is not losing yourself; it is letting Jesus be seen more clearly in you. The cleaner a window is, the less people notice the glass, and the more they see the light outside.
So this morning I want to issue a call to you: let Jesus be King — hand the throne back to him; let Jesus receive all the glory — pass the applause on to him.

Let us declare together: Lord, today I choose to live “for you, for others, not for myself.” Give me the strength to show your love in every small thing, to live a life of denying self, and to be a blessing to others.

Dear Lord Jesus, though you existed in the form of God, for our sake you emptied yourself and walked a road that was wholly not for yourself, all the way to the cross. So often we speak of love with our lips while caring only for ourselves in our hearts; so often we say “It’s for your own good” when really we want others to listen to us. Please forgive us.

Let your Holy Spirit begin working today, and make us willing to live it for others to see — not fighting for the last word at home, gladly serving behind the scenes at church, treating others fairly at work; and willing to die for others to see — laying down who’s right for the sake of reconciliation, laying down our own opinions for the sake of unity, laying down our convenience and comfort for the sake of others’ growth. May every choice we make let you be King; may every bit of glory go to you. In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.

sections.heading: Introduction: An Order Hidden in the English Word for Joy
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning. This morning I’d like to begin by asking you to look at a very small yet very deep word — JOY.

JOY is, of course, simply the English word for joy. Someone took its three letters apart and found a spiritual order in them: J is for Jesus; O is for Others; Y is for Yourself. Jesus first, others second, yourself last. This is not a play on words; it is the arrangement of the kingdom of heaven. When a person’s life is set in this order, joy comes without being invited; when the order is turned upside down — yourself first, others second, Jesus last — that person may own the whole world and still be empty inside.

I often think of an elderly sister who served in her church for more than thirty years. She cooked, washed dishes, mopped floors, gave people lifts and visited the sick — all the kinds of work nobody applauds. One year she fell seriously ill and spent forty days in hospital. In those forty days the door of her ward was hardly ever still. People came to see her in wave after wave, bringing soup, bringing flowers, bringing prayers. In the end a nurse couldn’t help asking her, “Auntie, are you somebody important?” She smiled and said, “I’m not anybody important. I’m just someone who gave herself away.”

Brothers and sisters, that is today’s theme. In the last lesson we looked at the truth of living “for Jesus, for others, not for ourselves.” In this lesson we want to bring that truth down to earth, down into daily living. Because denying of self is not just a doctrine; it is a way of life.

Jesus never only “taught us.” He “lived it out before our eyes,” and he “died it out before our eyes.” His living was a service of love — every day, every hand stretched out, every time he turned towards someone. His dying was an offering of love — offered once, effective for ever. When we follow him and choose to live “for Jesus, for others, not for ourselves,” our lives are transformed, our relationships are healed and our surroundings are filled with joy.

Today’s message has three key points. First, Jesus lived it out before us — laying down his own rights for the needs of others. Second, Jesus died it out before us — willingly laying down his life so that others might have life. Third, denying of self brings joy — this is the spiritual principle of JOY.

In the 321 vision we often say that of the Three Foundations, the first is “Jesus is my role model.” A role model is not a portrait hanging on the wall; a role model is a set of footprints you can step into. Today, step by step, let’s walk in Jesus’ footprints.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: A Lord About to Depart, and the Last Testament He Left His Disciples
sections.html:
To understand today’s main passage, we first have to stand in that room.

John chapter 15 records words Jesus spoke after the Last Supper. John 13:1 puts it like this: “Now before the feast of the Passover, Jesus, knowing that his time had come that he would depart from this world to the Father, having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them to the end.” Chapters 13 to 17 are usually called the “Upper Room Discourse” or the “Farewell Discourse.” They are the last words Jesus spoke to the eleven disciples on the night he was betrayed, closing with the high-priestly prayer of chapter 17.

The book was written by the apostle John, the one who calls himself “the disciple whom Jesus loved.” According to the consistent testimony of church history — including Irenaeus in the second century — John lived in Ephesus in his old age and wrote this Gospel around the AD 80s to 90s. By then most of the first generation of apostles had been martyred, and the church faced persecution from the Jewish synagogue as well as the infiltration of early Gnostic ideas. John’s purpose in writing is very clear: “but these are written, that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that believing you may have life in his name.” (John 20:31)

Notice the setting. The one speaking is a Lord who, in a few hours, will be arrested, flogged and crucified. Those listening are a band of disciples who are about to scatter and run, one of whom will even deny his Lord three times. At a moment like that, Jesus talks not about his own fear but about his disciples’ joy. He says, “that my joy may remain in you, and that your joy may be made full.” (John 15:11)

Brothers and sisters, that alone is enough to make us bow our heads. Someone who, at the very moment of greatest pain, still cares about the joy of others — that is what “not for ourselves” means.

What comes before this in chapter 15 is the parable “I am the true vine” (verses 1–8): unless the branch remains in the vine, it cannot bear fruit by itself. Then verses 9–11 speak of “remain in my love,” and verses 12–13 take that love to its furthest point: “This is my commandment, that you love one another, even as I have loved you. Greater love has no one than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends.” (John 15:12–13)

So what comes before “joy” is “connection,” and what comes after “joy” is “laying down one’s life.” True joy sits between “union with the Lord” and “denying ourselves for others.” Apart from those two, everything people chase is mere emotion, not joy.

Today we’ll also look at two other passages. One is in Mark chapter 6, a slice of Jesus “living it out before us.” Mark is generally held to be the earliest Gospel, written around the AD 60s; its author, Mark (John Mark), recorded the testimony Peter preached and wrote it for the believers in Rome. Mark’s Jesus is a “servant” — always moving, always working, always serving — and the key verse of the whole book is Mark 10:45. The other passage is in John chapter 10, the Good Shepherd discourse, Jesus’ declaration that he would “die it out before us.”

A Lord who lived it out before us, a Lord who died it out before us, and who in the end left us “joy made full.” That is today’s road map.

sections.heading: Key Point 1: Jesus “Lived It Out Before Us” — Laying Down His Own Rights for the Needs of Others
1. The Text: A Weary Lord, a Compassionate Heart
sections.html:
Every day Jesus lived on earth, he was showing us the pattern of denying of self. Mark chapter 6 records a very real scene:

“The apostles gathered themselves together to Jesus, and they told him all things, whatever they had done, and whatever they had taught. He said to them, ‘You come apart into a deserted place, and rest awhile.’ For there were many coming and going, and they had no leisure so much as to eat. They went away in the boat to a deserted place by themselves. They saw them going, and many recognized him and ran there on foot from all the cities. They arrived before them and came together to him. Jesus came out, saw a great multitude, and he had compassion on them, because they were like sheep without a shepherd, and he began to teach them many things.” (Mark 6:30–34)

Brothers and sisters, look closely at these verses. The disciples had just come back from their mission, so worn out they didn’t even have time to eat. Jesus himself was wearier still — he had just heard the terrible news that John the Baptist had been beheaded. He proposed going to a deserted place to rest awhile; that was a perfectly reasonable right. He got into the boat, finally made it to the other shore, and what happened? The shore was already thick with people.

If it had been us, a sentence would most likely have bubbled up inside: “Can’t a person even get some rest?” But Scripture says that Jesus “saw a great multitude, and he had compassion on them.”

sections.heading: 2. The Original Language: A Love That Churns from the Depths
sections.html:
The word for “compassion” here is the Greek σπλαγχνίζομαι (splanchnizomai), whose root is σπλάγχνα, meaning “the inward parts, the bowels.” The Jews believed that the deepest emotions lived in a person’s inner organs. So this word is not polite sympathy, not standing at a distance and saying, “What a pity.” It means that a person’s whole insides are churned up and wrung. Chinese expressions such as “heart and bowels torn to pieces” or “moved with tender mercy” come closest to it.

In the New Testament this verb is used almost exclusively of Jesus, or of figures who stand for God in the parables Jesus told — like the prodigal son’s father, who “was moved with compassion” (Luke 15:20), or the good Samaritan, who “was moved with compassion” (Luke 10:33).

In other words, Jesus’ service didn’t come out of a schedule; it came out of his very insides. It came not from duty but from love; not because he “ought to” but because he “couldn’t bear not to.”

Duty can hold you up for a while; only love can hold you up for a lifetime. Much service dries up because it flows from “ought to” rather than from “can’t bear not to.” Service that comes from “ought to” turns into resentment over time; service that comes from “can’t bear not to” grows sweeter over time.

There’s another phrase worth savouring slowly: “they were like sheep without a shepherd.” This was not something new Jesus coined; it was a heavy lament from the Old Testament. As Moses was about to die, he asked God for a leader “that the congregation of Yahweh may not be as sheep which have no shepherd.” (Numbers 27:17) The prophet Micaiah saw a vision: “I saw all Israel scattered on the mountains, as sheep that have no shepherd.” (1 Kings 22:17) Ezekiel chapter 34 rebukes Israel’s shepherds even more severely: “You eat the fat. You clothe yourself with the wool. You kill the fatlings, but you don’t feed the sheep.” (Ezekiel 34:3)

So when Jesus says “like sheep without a shepherd,” he is announcing that the true Shepherd Ezekiel prophesied has come. Ezekiel 34:15 says, “I myself will be the shepherd of my sheep, and I will cause them to lie down,” says the Lord Yahweh. That day on the shore of Galilee, the prophecy was fulfilled — the true Shepherd stepped out of the boat, saw the flock, and walked towards them.

sections.heading: 3. Scripture Interpreting Scripture: Laying Down His Rights and Taking the Form of a Servant
sections.html:
What did Jesus lay down? His “rights.” He had the right to rest, the right to be served, the right to say, “No consultations today.” But he laid them down.

Paul puts this most clearly: “Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus, who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men. And being found in human form, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross.” (Philippians 2:5–8)

The Greek for “emptied himself” is κενόω (kenoō), meaning “to empty out.” Jesus did not lose his divine nature; rather, he laid down his right to use the privileges of that divinity. He could have called on more than twelve legions of angels, yet he chose to be crucified; he could have had quiet in the wilderness, yet he chose to teach.

Mark 10:45 is the key to the whole book: “For the Son of Man also came not to be served, but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.” He is the Lord, yet he carries the basin of water; he is the Teacher, yet he washes the disciples’ feet. John 13:14–15 says, “If I then, the Lord and the Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another’s feet. For I have given you an example, that you should also do as I have done to you.”

Brothers and sisters, please remember: true denying of self is not repressing yourself; it is an expression of love — compassion flowing from the heart of God. Repression locks your emotions away; love throws your life open. Repression builds up resentment; love bears fruit.

sections.heading: 4. Illustration: Giving Away Your Rights as a Gift
sections.html:
There’s a picture that captures this vividly. Someone once said that life is like holding a handful of sand. Open your hand, and the sand stays in your palm; clench your fist, and it runs out between your fingers. Our rights are the same: the tighter we grip them, the faster we lose them; the more willing we are to open our hands, the more we’re actually able to hold.

In daily living, this comes down to three very practical little things:

First, when you’re willing to listen instead of rushing to defend yourself, you’re living out the gentleness of Jesus. Most of us don’t lack the ability to talk; we lack the ability to stop talking. James 1:19 says, “So, then, my beloved brothers, let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger.”

Second, when you’re willing to help without seeking anything in return, you’re living out the servanthood of Jesus. Only help that expects nothing back can be called grace; the moment you start keeping accounts, it becomes a transaction.

Third, when you’re willing to give way rather than argue, you’re living out the peace of Jesus. Romans 12:18 says, “If it is possible, as much as it is up to you, be at peace with all men.”

“Living it out before others” isn’t about proving how good you are; it’s about letting people see how real Jesus is.

sections.heading: 5. Supporting Evidence from Science and Psychology: People Who Give Live Better
sections.html:
There is a frequently cited study in psychology. In 2003, Stephanie L. Brown of the University of Michigan and her colleagues published a paper in the journal Psychological Science titled “Providing Social Support May Be More Beneficial Than Receiving It.” The research team followed 423 older married couples in the Detroit area for five years. They found that, after controlling for health, age, finances and other variables, the people who regularly “gave help” had a significantly lower risk of dying, whereas simply “receiving help” had no such effect.

Brothers and sisters, this doesn’t mean we are saved by doing good; salvation is entirely God’s grace. But from another angle this research confirms the words of Scripture: human beings were made to live by “giving themselves away.” A heart that beats only for itself doesn’t actually live long.

Speaking of hearts, here’s a beautiful fact. The human heart beats about a hundred thousand times a day and never takes a day off in a whole lifetime, sending blood to every cell in the body. And the heart itself? It is supplied by just a few thin coronary arteries. It gives away the most and keeps the least for itself. God has written the truth of denying of self inside our very chests.

sections.heading: 6. Applying the 321 Vision: From the Self-Centred Life to Selflessness
sections.html:
In the 321 vision we say that the mark of the old self is the self-centred life, and the mark of the new self is selflessness. The self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall; pride is the root of every problem. Pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God.

What did Jesus do on the shore of Galilee? He laid down his “right to rest” and returned to his “position as Shepherd.” That is selflessness.

Selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the infinite and living out the infinite. Galatians 2:20 says, “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” What you lay down is your limited self; what you gain is the limitless Christ.

And remember the 321 order: life first, then relationships, then ministry. Jesus first had a life connected to the Father, then a relationship of compassion with the flock, and only last a ministry of teaching. Turn the order around, and ministry will crush life, and service will turn into a performance.

sections.heading: Key Point 2: Jesus “Died It Out Before Us” — Willingly Laying Down His Life So That Others Might Have Life
1. The Text: No One Takes My Life from Me
sections.html:
Jesus knew that to save the lost sheep of the world it would take not only teaching the truth but paying the price of his life. So in the Good Shepherd discourse he said:

“I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep.” (John 10:11)

“Therefore the Father loves me, because I lay down my life, that I may take it again. No one takes it away from me, but I lay it down by myself. I have power to lay it down, and I have power to take it again. I received this commandment from my Father.” (John 10:17–18)

Brothers and sisters, listen carefully to this sentence: “No one takes it away from me, but I lay it down by myself.” The cross was not an accident, not a slip, not a victory for Roman soldiers. The cross was the deliberate choice of the Son of God.

sections.heading: 2. The Original Language: Laying Down Life, and Authority
sections.html:
The Greek for “lay down his life” is τίθημι τὴν ψυχήν (tithēmi tēn psychēn), literally “to lay down one’s soul, one’s life.” The verb τίθημι means “to lay down, to set out, to place.” Jesus did not have his life snatched away by others; he laid it down himself, step by step.

The word translated “power” is the Greek ἐξουσία (exousia), meaning lawful authority and freedom. Jesus said, “I have power to lay it down, and I have power to take it again.” Only someone who truly has authority is in a position to lay it down; when someone without authority lets go, that is called helplessness. So denying of self is not the weak resigning themselves to fate; it is the choice of the one who has the power.

These words reveal what true denying of self is — not forced but voluntary; not grudging but born of love.

sections.heading: 3. Scripture Interpreting Scripture: The Logic of a Grain of Wheat
sections.html:
Jesus’ death was not a defeat but a glorious victory. His “death” bought our “life”; his denying of self accomplished our redemption.

He explained it himself with a picture any farmer understands: “Most certainly I tell you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains by itself alone. But if it dies, it bears much fruit.” (John 12:24)

A grain of wheat has two choices: stay in the barn and keep itself intact, or fall into the ground and lose itself. Stay in the barn, and it will be a single grain for ever; fall into the ground, and it becomes a whole field of wheat. The arithmetic of God’s kingdom is the exact opposite of the world’s: the world says “keeping is having”; God says “giving is gaining.”

The Old Testament foreshadowed this long ago. On the night of the Passover, the lamb was slain and its blood was smeared on the doorframe, and death passed over that household (Exodus chapter 12). The lamb had to die so that the firstborn would not. Isaiah chapter 53 paints this suffering Servant in the fullest colours: “Surely he has borne our sickness and carried our suffering … But he was pierced for our transgressions. He was crushed for our iniquities. The punishment that brought our peace was on him; and by his wounds we are healed.” (Isaiah 53:4–5) Notice the “we” and the “he” here — this is a complete exchange: he suffers, we receive; he dies, we live.

Paul says, “But God commends his own love toward us, in that while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” (Romans 5:8) John says, “By this we know love, because he laid down his life for us. And we ought to lay down our lives for the brothers.” (1 John 3:16) Peter says, “For you were called to this, because Christ also suffered for us, leaving you an example, that you should follow his steps.” (1 Peter 2:21)

So “dying it out before you” is not passive surrender but active self-offering — being willing to lay ourselves down for the good of others. When, in our relationships, we choose “I die so that you may live,” the love of Jesus is at work in us.

sections.heading: 4. Illustration: Marriage, Family, Co-Workers
sections.html:
The easiest place to test this truth is at home.

In marriage, when a husband is willing to “die it out before his wife” — to lay down his pride and apologise first — the marriage is healed. So many couples, when they quarrel, aren’t really fighting over right and wrong; they’re fighting over face. Whoever bows first looks like Jesus first.

When a wife is willing to “die it out before her husband” — to lay down her complaints and choose forgiveness — the family has joy. Complaining is taking yesterday’s bill out every day and settling it all over again; forgiveness is tearing up the bill and saying, “I’ve paid this one.”

When co-workers are willing to “die it out before one another” — not competing for name, not competing for credit — the church will be united. Philippians 2:3–4 says, “doing nothing through rivalry or through conceit, but in humility, each counting others better than himself; each of you not just looking to his own things, but each of you also to the things of others.”

sections.heading: 5. Supporting Evidence from Psychology: Findings from the Marriage Lab
sections.html:
From the 1970s onwards, the University of Washington psychologist John Gottman observed couples’ interactions in his famous “Love Lab.” In research he published with Robert Levenson in 1992, he showed that by observing a couple’s conflict conversation for a period of time, one could predict with considerable accuracy whether the marriage would head towards breakdown.

Gottman identified four of the most destructive patterns of interaction, which he called the “Four Horsemen of the Apocalypse”: criticism, contempt, defensiveness and stonewalling (the cold shoulder). The most damaging of them is “contempt.” He also found that healthy marriages are not marriages without conflict, but marriages in which the couple know how to make “repair attempts” in the middle of conflict — an apology, a joke, a reaching out. In his 1994 research Gottman also proposed that in stable marriages the ratio of positive to negative interactions is roughly five to one.

Brothers and sisters, have you noticed? What psychology calls a “repair attempt,” Scripture spoke of long ago: it’s called “first be reconciled.” Matthew 5:24 says, “leave your gift there before the altar, and go your way. First be reconciled to your brother, and then come and offer your gift.” Science can only tell us that it “works”; Scripture tells us “why” — because the cross is the repair attempt God reached out to make with us.

sections.heading: 6. Applying the 321 Vision: Humility Sparks Humility, and Everyone Wins
sections.html:
The 321 vision says: humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan. And it says: pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility sparks humility, and both sides win.

Why do quarrels at home keep escalating? Because pride is contagious. You raise your voice by one decibel, I raise mine by two; you drag up one old grievance, I drag up two. In the end both sides are hurt and there is no winner.

So how does it stop? Someone has to die first. Not the relationship dying — the “self” dying. When one person chooses “I die so that you may live,” that downward spiral is broken, and humility begins to spark humility.

What Satan fears most is not our gifts but our selflessness. His own downfall began with “I will” — Isaiah 14:13–14 records his five “I will”s: “I will ascend into heaven! I will exalt my throne above the stars of God! … I will make myself like the Most High!” But the Lord Jesus took the opposite road: he “emptied himself,” he “humbled himself,” he became “obedient.” That’s why James 4:6 says, “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.”

Brothers and sisters, if you want to overcome Satan, you don’t need to argue with him; you only need to go lower than he will. He will not bow his head, but you will; that is your victory.

sections.heading: Key Point 3: Denying of Self Brings Joy — the Spiritual Principle of JOY
1. The Text: That Your Joy May Be Made Full
sections.html:
When we take “for Jesus, for others, not for ourselves” as the conviction of our lives, we enter into the secret of joy. True joy lies not in what we gain but in what we are able to give away.

Jesus said, “Even as the Father has loved me, I also have loved you. Remain in my love. If you keep my commandments, you will remain in my love; even as I have kept my Father’s commandments, and remain in his love. I have spoken these things to you, that my joy may remain in you, and that your joy may be made full.” (John 15:9–11)

Notice three key phrases: remain, my joy, made full.

The Greek for “remain” is μένω (menō), meaning “to settle down, to stay, to continue on.” In the short space of the first eleven verses of John 15, this word appears ten times or more. It isn’t an occasional visit; it’s living there for good and never moving out. The branch doesn’t have to strain to bear fruit; the branch only has to stay on the vine. Jesus said, “apart from me you can do nothing.” (John 15:5)

Brothers and sisters, this sentence makes clear where the power for denying of self comes from. Denying of self doesn’t come from your willpower; it comes from connection. A branch that has been cut off, however hard it tries, cannot produce a single grape.

sections.heading: 2. The Original Language: Joy and Grace Share a Root
sections.html:
The Greek for “joy” is χαρά (chara), and “grace” is χάρις (charis); the two words share the same root. This tells us that joy is a product of grace, not a product of effort. You can’t “squeeze out” joy; you can only “receive” it.

The Greek for “made full” is πληρόω (plēroō), meaning “filled to overflowing.” Jesus uses it with the sense of completion — not filled for the moment, but continually full.

Notice too that Jesus says “my joy,” not “your joy.” What he wants to put inside us is his own share of joy. And what kind of joy is that? Hebrews 12:2 tells us: “who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising its shame, and has sat down at the right hand of the throne of God.”

So Jesus’ joy is a joy that passes through the cross. Joy, then, has nothing to do with comfort; joy has everything to do with denying of self.

sections.heading: 3. Scripture Interpreting Scripture: It Is More Blessed to Give Than to Receive
sections.html:
When Paul said farewell to the Ephesian elders at Miletus, he told them, “In all things I gave you an example, that so laboring you ought to help the weak, and to remember the words of the Lord Jesus, that he himself said, ‘It is more blessed to give than to receive.’” (Acts 20:35)

Interestingly, this saying, “It is more blessed to give than to receive,” is not found in any of the four Gospels, yet Paul solemnly marks it as “the words of the Lord Jesus.” This shows how much weight the saying carried among the Lord’s teachings passed down by word of mouth in the early church.

The Old Testament said the same long before. Nehemiah 8:10: “the joy of Yahweh is your strength.” Notice the order: it isn’t that we have joy once we have strength; it’s that joy brings strength. Psalm 16:11: “You will show me the path of life. In your presence is fullness of joy. In your right hand there are pleasures forever more.” Where is fullness of joy found? In God’s presence, not in our circumstances.

There is another person in the New Testament who lived this secret out: John the Baptist. When his disciples came running to complain that “all are coming to him,” John answered, “He who has the bride is the bridegroom; but the friend of the bridegroom, who stands and hears him, rejoices greatly because of the bridegroom’s voice. This, my joy, therefore is made full.” (John 3:29) And then came those famous words: “He must increase, but I must decrease.” (John 3:30)

Brothers and sisters, look closely: John’s joy was not made full when he was lifted up; it was made full when he stepped back. This completely overturns the world’s logic. The world says, “I’m happy when I’m seen.” John says, “When he is seen, I am satisfied.”

Paul wrote Philippians from prison, and the whole letter is about joy: “Rejoice in the Lord always! Again I will say, ‘Rejoice!’” (Philippians 4:4) A man in prison telling free people to rejoice proves that joy is not a thermometer of our circumstances but a spring deep within our life.

sections.heading: 4. Illustration: The Sea of Galilee and the Dead Sea
sections.html:
In Israel, one and the same river, the Jordan, feeds two lakes.

In the north is the Sea of Galilee. The river flows in, and it also flows out. So the lake has fish, its shores have grass, and villages surround it; most of Jesus’ ministry took place there.

In the south is the Dead Sea. The river flows in, but it cannot flow out. Water only comes in and never leaves; the blazing sun evaporates it and the salt grows more and more concentrated — the Dead Sea’s salinity reaches about 34 per cent, roughly ten times that of ordinary seawater. As a result, fish cannot live there and grass cannot grow, and so it is called the “Dead Sea.”

Brothers and sisters, the two lakes share the same source; the only difference between them is one thing — whether or not they have an “outlet.”

People are the same. Some people let grace come in and flow out again, and their lives have fish and grass. Others let grace come in and only keep collecting it inside, and their lives grow saltier and saltier, more and more bitter. Someone who refuses to give will sooner or later become a dead sea.

sections.heading: 5. Supporting Evidence from Science and Psychology: Spending Money on Others
sections.html:
In 2008, Michael I. Norton of Harvard University, together with Elizabeth W. Dunn and Lara B. Aknin, then at the University of British Columbia, published a study in the journal Science titled “Spending Money on Others Promotes Happiness.” They ran several experiments. In one of them, participants were each given a small sum of money (five or twenty dollars); half were told to spend it on themselves, and half were told to spend it on someone else or give it away. When their happiness was measured that evening, the group who had spent the money on others was clearly happier — and the amount of money made no difference.

In addition, Harvard’s Study of Adult Development, begun in 1938, has followed several hundred men for more than eighty years, making it one of the longest studies of human happiness ever undertaken. Its fourth director, Robert Waldinger, summed up the study by saying that what keeps people healthy and happy is not wealth, not fame, but good relationships.

Brothers and sisters, science has taken eighty years of detours to prove what Scripture said from the very beginning — human beings were made for love. But science can only measure “happiness”; it can’t measure “joy.” Happiness depends on circumstances; joy depends on Jesus.

sections.heading: 6. Testimonies from Well-Known Christians
sections.html:
The missionary Jim Elliot is generally held to have written this sentence in his journal on 28 October 1949: “He is no fool who gives what he cannot keep to gain what he cannot lose.” Six years later, in January 1956, he and four companions were martyred in Ecuador while trying to reach the Auca (Waorani) people with the gospel; the oldest of them was barely over thirty, and Jim himself was only twenty-eight. The world called it a waste, but later his wife, Elisabeth Elliot, went in among that tribe, the gospel took root there, and the very men who had killed them became disciples of the Lord.

At the opening of his Confessions, the Church Father Augustine wrote, “You have made us for yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in you.” That sentence goes straight to the heart of the matter: the restlessness of the human heart comes from getting the order wrong. Those who put themselves at the centre will never find rest; those who put Jesus at the centre can rest at any moment.

sections.heading: 7. The Order of JOY
sections.html:
When husband and wife deny themselves for each other, the home is filled with joy; when co-workers deny themselves for one another, the church overflows with joy; when brothers and sisters deny themselves for one another, the community is filled with love.

Denying of self looks like loss, but in fact it is entering into the true source of joy.

JOY — Jesus, Others, Yourself. Notice that this order doesn’t delete “yourself”; it simply puts “yourself” in third place. The Christian faith has never asked people to destroy themselves; it asks them to put themselves back in their proper place. When Jesus is first and others are second, you’ll find that “you” are actually the one best cared for — because a God who knows how to look after you far better than you do is looking after you on your behalf.

sections.heading: Integrating the 321 Vision: A Road Home
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let’s walk today’s message through the framework of 321.

The Three Foundations. Jesus is my role model — he lived it out before us and died it out before us. The Bible is my standard — we don’t define denying of self by our feelings, but by Scripture. The Holy Spirit is my guide — denying of self doesn’t come from gritting our teeth; it comes from the Holy Spirit. Galatians 5:22–23 says, “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control.” Notice that joy is a “fruit,” not a “product.” Fruit is grown; products are manufactured.

The Two Core Values. Let Jesus be King — move yourself off the throne and let him sit on it. Let Jesus receive all the glory — we don’t deny ourselves so that people will praise us for being loving, but so that people will see how real Jesus is. John the Baptist put it best: “He must increase, but I must decrease.” (John 3:30)

The Goal: establish God’s system — a system made up of selfless people, a system of “I die so that you may live,” a system of washing one another’s feet. This is exactly what the Lord’s Prayer asks for: “Let your Kingdom come. Let your will be done on earth as it is in heaven.” (Matthew 6:10)

The fivefold change: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry. In today’s lesson, the first thing to change is our mindset — from “denying of self is a loss” to “denying of self is a gain.” Change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living; change daily living and you change relationships; change relationships and you change ministry. The order can’t be skipped.

A shift in perspective: from man’s perspective to God’s perspective; from an earthly perspective to a heavenly one; from a temporary perspective to an eternal one; from a worldly perspective to a godly one. From man’s perspective, that grain of wheat died; from God’s perspective, that grain of wheat became a whole field.

The priority of relationships: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last of all with things. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than possessions. Many people find denying of self terribly hard because they’ve skipped the “first with God.” Those who haven’t drawn love from God have nothing to give but reluctance, not love.

The 920 practice: everyone connected with us is our “2.” Who is your “2” today? Your spouse at home, your child in a rebellious phase, a difficult colleague, that brother you’d rather avoid. Practise living a selfless (0) life, and on that person bear the fruit of the Spirit in all nine (9) of its expressions. You don’t need to feel it first; you only need to choose it first.

The 235 relationships: with a selfless person, become a “2” — spiritual companions who can speak the truth to each other; build a “3” — spiritual parents and spiritual children, passing life on; become a “5” — a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades, building up the body of the Lord together. Denying of self isn’t one person silently swallowing everything; denying of self is being seen, supported and passed on within relationships.

Then there is the Path of Serving: Spirit, Understanding, Life, Service, God. First let the Holy Spirit lead; then let Scripture open our understanding; then live out the life of Jesus; only then do we enter into service; and finally we give all the glory to God.

Brothers and sisters, 321 has never been a slogan. It is a road home.

sections.heading: Putting It into Practice: Walking the Truth into Daily Living Through the Eight Stages of Changing Our Mindset
sections.html:
The lesson gives us three practices. Let’s deepen them using the 321 “eight stages of changing our mindset” — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.

Practice One: A Prayer Every Morning

“Lord, today let me live for you, act for others, and not for myself.”

Information: you have heard today’s word — Jesus lived it out before us and died it out before us.

Revelation: ask the Holy Spirit to carry this sentence from your head into your heart, and to let you “see” it in one particular face.

Conviction: truly believe that “giving away is more blessed than holding on,” rather than merely thinking it sounds beautiful.

Implementation: make this prayer the very first thing you say when you open your eyes tomorrow morning. Don’t wait until you’re in a good mood to pray; prayer will bring the mood with it.

Evaluation: in the evening, ask yourself whether this prayer influenced any single decision you made today.

Correction: if it didn’t, move the prayer earlier — before you look at your phone.

Repetition: keep it up for forty days in a row. Forty is not a superstitious number; it’s a stretch of time long enough for a new habit to take root.

Multiplication: find a brother or sister and invite them to do these forty days of practice with you.

Practice Two: Take Practical Action — Give Someone Your Time or Care, Expecting Nothing in Return

Information: it is more blessed to give than to receive (Acts 20:35).

Revelation: let God name one particular person and lay them on your heart — not “everyone,” but “that one person.”

Conviction: believe that God remembers every bit of time you give. Matthew 10:42 says, “Whoever gives one of these little ones just a cup of cold water to drink in the name of a disciple, most certainly I tell you he will in no way lose his reward.”

Implementation: this week, do one concrete thing — a phone call, a meal, a lift, an hour of keeping someone company. Set a time and put it in your calendar.

Evaluation: while I was doing it, was I hoping for something in return? Was I hoping to be noticed?

Correction: if you find your motives are mixed, don’t condemn yourself; simply offer it up again. Even our motives for giving need to be cleansed — that is grace, not failure.

Repetition: at least once a week, for a whole season.

Multiplication: bring your small group or your family along to do it with you, so that this moves from an individual action to a shared culture.

Practice Three: An Evening Review — Did I Live Out the Order of JOY Today?

Jesus, Others, Yourself.

Information: the order of joy is Jesus first, others second, yourself third.

Revelation: let the Holy Spirit shine a light on what your real order was today. Much of the time our order is Y-O-J, and we still think we’re very spiritual.

Conviction: believe that once the order changes, everything changes.

Implementation: three minutes before bed, write three lines — What did I do for Jesus today? What did I do for others? Was I tied up by myself?

Evaluation: look back once a week and see your own patterns.

Correction: for the weakest link, add one small action tomorrow.

Repetition: let this review become a bedtime habit, as natural as brushing your teeth.

Multiplication: take the entry you’re most thankful for in your review notes and share it with your small group, so it becomes a blessing to others.

A Reminder

Living “for myself” brings only passing happiness; living “for Jesus and for others” is what brings eternal joy.

Happiness needs conditions; joy needs only Jesus. Happiness peaks at the moment you receive and slides downhill from there; joy begins at the moment you give and keeps increasing from there.

A Declaration of Faith

Let us declare together:

Lord, I want to learn from your example — to live for others and to die for others.

Help me choose every day to live “for you, for others, not for myself,”

so that my life is filled with your love and overflows with your joy.

sections.heading: Closing and Call: Let Jesus Be Seen
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, living “for Jesus, for others, not for ourselves” is a road of denying of self, but it is also a road full of glory and joy.

This road isn’t easy. It asks us not to defend ourselves when we’re misunderstood, to apologise first when we’re in the right, to keep reaching out when we ought to be resting. But please remember: every choice to deny yourself is a moment when Jesus is seen.

When you hand the credit to someone else at the office, someone sees Jesus.

When you’re the first at home to say “I’m sorry,” someone sees Jesus.

When you quietly stack the chairs and wash the cups at church, someone in heaven sees Jesus.

When we keep living like this, joy is no longer a feeling but the fruit of a life. Feelings change with the weather; fruit grows as life grows.

True joy will always belong to those who are willing to deny themselves for love.

So this morning I want to issue you a call: please move yourself off the throne and let Jesus be King. Not just King on Sundays, but King over your calendar, King over your wallet, King over your words, King over your grievances.

Paul says, “He died for all, that those who live should no longer live to themselves, but to him who for their sakes died and rose again.” (2 Corinthians 5:15)

Brothers and sisters, he has already died for you; today, will you live for him?

May all the glory go to the Lord Jesus Christ, who lived for us and died for us.

keyVerses: “If you keep my commandments, you will remain in my love; even as I have kept my Father’s commandments, and remain in his love. I have spoken these things to you, that my joy may remain in you, and that your joy may be made full.” (John 15:10–11)
declarations: Let us declare together:
Lord, I want to learn from your example — to live for others and to die for others.
Help me choose every day to live “for you, for others, not for myself,”
so that my life is filled with your love and overflows with your joy.
practices: A prayer every morning
Take practical action — give someone your time or care, expecting nothing in return
An evening review: did I live out the order of JOY today?
prayer: Dear Lord Jesus,
We thank you. You lived it out before us, so that we know what love looks like; you died it out before us, so that we know how far love can go.

Lord, forgive us. So often we put ourselves first, others second and you last. We serve in your name while in our hearts we are fighting for ourselves. Wash us in your precious blood, and nail the self-centred old self to the cross.

Give us a selfless heart. Let us be willing to bow first at home, to forgive first in our relationships, and to step back first in our service. Holy Spirit, work within us, so that denying of self is no longer a teeth-gritting effort but an outpouring of love.

Lord, put your joy in our hearts, so that our joy may be made full. Let our lives be like the Sea of Galilee — water flowing in and out, full of fish and grass; not like the Dead Sea, taking in and never giving out, growing ever more bitter.
Reign as King in our homes, reign as King in our fellowship, reign as King in every one of our twenty-four hours. May all glory, praise and honour be yours.
In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: Mark 6:31–34: Jesus had intended to “rest awhile,” but when he saw the flock he laid down his right to rest. Share: this week, what is one thing that “you have a right to enjoy but could lay down for someone”? What is the biggest obstacle to laying it down?

John 15:11: “I have spoken these things to you, that my joy may remain in you, and that your joy may be made full.” Share: in what experience of denying yourself have you tasted true joy? What did God show you at the time?

blog.title: Does Your Life Have an Outlet?

blocks.x: Seeing the true order of joy in one English word: JOY
One and the same river, the Jordan, feeds two lakes.

In the north is the Sea of Galilee. The water flows in, and it also flows out, so the lake has fish, its shores have grass, and villages surround it. In the south is the Dead Sea. The water flows in, but it cannot flow out; it only comes in and never leaves, and the salt grows more and more concentrated — its salinity reaches about 34 per cent, roughly ten times that of ordinary seawater. So fish cannot live there and grass cannot grow.
The two lakes have exactly the same source; the only difference between them is one thing: whether or not they have an outlet.
People are the same.
An order hidden in JOY
JOY is the English word for joy. Someone took its three letters apart and found a spiritual order in them: J is for Jesus; O is for Others; Y is for Yourself.
Jesus first, others second, yourself last.

This is not a play on words; it is the arrangement of the kingdom of heaven. When a person’s life is set in this order, joy comes without being invited; when the order is turned upside down — yourself first, others second, Jesus last — that person may own the whole world and still be empty inside.

Interestingly, this order doesn’t delete “yourself”; it simply puts “yourself” in third place. The Christian faith has never asked people to destroy themselves; it asks them to put themselves back in their proper place.
He lived it out before us, and he died it out before us
Jesus never only “taught us.” He “lived it out before our eyes.”

Mark chapter 6 records a very real day. The disciples had just come back from their mission, so worn out they didn’t even have time to eat, and Jesus proposed going to a deserted place to rest awhile. But the moment the boat reached the shore, the shore was already thick with people. Scripture says: “Jesus came out, saw a great multitude, and he had compassion on them, because they were like sheep without a shepherd, and he began to teach them many things.” (Mark 6:34)

The root of the Greek word for “compassion” here means “the inward parts.” It is not standing at a distance and saying, “What a pity”; it means a person’s whole insides are churned up. What he laid down was his “right to rest.”

He also “died it out before our eyes.” He said, “No one takes it away from me, but I lay it down by myself.” (John 10:18) The cross was not an accident, not a slip; it was the deliberate choice of the Son of God. True denying of self is not forced but voluntary; not grudging but born of love.
Denying of self is the doorway into joy
On the night he was betrayed, Jesus said to his disciples, “I have spoken these things to you, that my joy may remain in you, and that your joy may be made full.” (John 15:11)
Please notice that he says “my joy.” And what kind of joy is that? Hebrews tells us that for the joy that was set before him he endured the cross, despising its shame.
So Jesus’ joy is a joy that passes through the cross. Joy, then, has nothing to do with comfort; joy has everything to do with denying of self.

Psychology confirms this from the side-lines. In 2008, Dunn, Aknin and Norton published a study in the journal Science: participants were each given a small sum of money, and the group told to spend it on someone else was clearly happier that evening — and the amount of money made no difference. Harvard’s Study of Adult Development, begun in 1938 and running for more than eighty years, reached a similar conclusion: what keeps people healthy and happy is not wealth, not fame, but good relationships.
Science can measure “happiness,” but it can’t measure “joy.” Happiness depends on circumstances; joy depends on Jesus.
Three things you can start today
First, pray every morning: “Lord, today let me live for you, act for others, and not for myself.” Don’t wait until you’re in a good mood to pray; prayer will bring the mood with it.
Second, this week give someone your time or care, expecting nothing in return. A phone call, a meal, an hour of keeping someone company — set a time and put it in your calendar.
Third, review your day in the evening: was my order today Jesus, others, yourself?

In marriage, when a husband is willing to lay down his pride and apologise first, the marriage is healed; when a wife is willing to lay down her complaints and choose forgiveness, the family has joy; when co-workers don’t compete for name or for credit, the church will be united. Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility sparks humility, and both sides win.
Living “for myself” brings only passing happiness; living “for Jesus and for others” is what brings eternal joy.

Every choice to deny yourself is a moment when Jesus is seen. When we keep living like this, joy is no longer a feeling but the fruit of a life. Feelings change with the weather; fruit grows as life grows.
A question for reflection
This week, what is one thing you have every right to enjoy, yet could lay down for someone else?
Does your life have an outlet?
