brief12.title: For Jesus, for Others, Not for Self
notes: Morning Devotion 321 · Lesson 69
A Life of Denying of Self, the Secret of Joy
“That your joy may be made full”
John 15:11
Open with a warm greeting — “Brothers and sisters, good morning” — to set the tone of an early-morning devotion.
State the theme: last lesson covered the truth; this lesson brings it down into daily living — denying of self is not just a doctrine but a way of life.
Key verses: John 15:10–11; point out that the destination of the whole lesson is “joy made full.”
Preview the three key points: he lived it out before us, he died it out before us, denying of self brings joy.

brief12.title: An Order Hidden in JOY
notes: J = Jesus — first
O = Others — second
Y = Yourself — third
Get the order right, and joy comes
Open by taking the word apart: JOY is not a play on words but the arrangement of the kingdom of heaven.

Illustration: an elderly sister who served for over thirty years spent forty days in hospital with a constant stream of visitors; a nurse asked if she was somebody important, and she said, “I’m just someone who gave herself away.”
Contrast: someone whose order is upside down (Y-O-J) may own the whole world and still be empty inside.
321: the focus is Jesus — not ourselves, not others, not our circumstances.

brief12.title: Key Verse and Background
notes: Jesus’ farewell words on the night he was betrayed
“If you keep my commandments,
you will remain in my love”
John 15:10
Background: John 13–17 is the “Upper Room Discourse,” spoken on the night Jesus was betrayed.
Author and date: written by the apostle John in his old age in Ephesus, around the AD 80s to 90s.
The striking point: a Lord who, in a few hours, will go to the cross talks not about his own fear but about his disciples’ joy.
Context: before it comes the “connection” of the vine; after it comes the love of “laying down one’s life for one’s friends” (John 15:13).
Conclusion: joy sits between “union with the Lord” and “denying ourselves for others.”

brief12.title: 1. Jesus Lived It Out Before Us
notes: A weary Lord, about to rest awhile
“Saw a great multitude, and he had compassion on them,
because they were like sheep without a shepherd”
Mark 6:34
The scene: the disciples have just come back from their mission, with no leisure even to eat; Jesus has just heard that John the Baptist has been beheaded.
The turn: they set off by boat for a deserted place to rest, but the shore is thick with people when they land.
Original language: “compassion” is σπλαγχνίζομαι, whose root means the inward parts — a love that churns a person’s whole insides.
Old Testament background: “sheep without a shepherd” comes from Numbers 27:17 and Ezekiel 34; the true Shepherd has come.
Application: it came not from duty but from love; not because he “ought to” but because he “couldn’t bear not to.”

brief12.title: Laying Down His Rights, Taking the Form of a Servant
notes: Compassion: a love that churns the inward parts
“But emptied himself, taking the form of a servant”
Philippians 2:7
321: the old self is self-centred, the new self selfless
Scripture: Philippians 2:5–8; “emptied himself” is κενόω in Greek, meaning “to empty out.”
Scripture interpreting Scripture: Mark 10:45 — the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve.
Psychology: Brown and colleagues (2003, Psychological Science) followed 423 older married couples in Detroit for five years; those who regularly “gave help” had a significantly lower risk of dying.
Scientific fact: the heart beats about a hundred thousand times a day, gives away the most and is supplied only by the coronary arteries.
321: pride is leaving our originally intended position and grasping power; humility is laying down power and returning to our originally intended position.

brief12.title: 2. Jesus Died It Out Before Us
notes: “No one takes it away from me,
but I lay it down by myself”
John 10:18
Not forced, but willing
Scripture: John 10:11, 17–18 — the good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep.
Original language: “lay down his life” is τίθημι τὴν ψυχήν, literally “to lay down one’s own life”; “power” is ἐξουσία.
Key point: only when someone with authority lays it down is it denying of self; when someone without authority lets go, that is mere helplessness.
Old Testament foreshadowing: the Passover lamb (Exodus 12) and the suffering Servant of Isaiah 53:4–5.
Conclusion: the cross was not an accident but a deliberate choice.

brief12.title: I Die So That You May Live
notes: A grain of wheat dies and bears much fruit
John 12:24
Husbands apologise first, wives forgive first
Humility sparks humility, and both sides win
Picture: a grain of wheat kept in the barn stays a single grain for ever; fallen into the ground, it becomes a whole field of wheat.
Everyday examples: a husband lays down his pride and apologises first, a wife lays down her complaints and chooses forgiveness, co-workers compete for neither name nor credit.

Psychology: Gottman and Levenson’s 1992 research predicted marital outcomes with high accuracy; the “Four Horsemen of the Apocalypse” are criticism, contempt, defensiveness and stonewalling; healthy marriages know how to make “repair attempts.”
Scripture parallel: Matthew 5:24 — first be reconciled to your brother, then come and offer your gift.
321: pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility sparks humility, and both sides win.

brief12.title: 3. Denying of Self Brings Joy
notes: “That my joy may remain in you,
and that your joy may be made full”
John 15:11
Joy is a product of grace
Original language: joy (χαρά) and grace (χάρις) share the same root; “made full” (πληρόω) means filled to overflowing.
Key: what Jesus gives is “my joy” — Hebrews 12:2 shows it is a joy that passes through the cross.
Scripture interpreting Scripture: Acts 20:35, “It is more blessed to give than to receive”; Nehemiah 8:10, “the joy of Yahweh is your strength.”
Testimony: John the Baptist said, “He must increase, but I must decrease”; his joy was made full when he stepped back (John 3:29–30).
Reminder: joy has nothing to do with comfort; joy has everything to do with denying of self.

brief12.title: The Sea of Galilee and the Dead Sea
notes: One river Jordan, two outcomes
Flowing in and out: fish and grass
Only in, never out: about 34 per cent salt
Does your life have an outlet?
Geographical fact: the Jordan flows into both the Sea of Galilee and the Dead Sea; the Dead Sea has no outlet, and its salinity reaches about 34 per cent, roughly ten times that of seawater.
Spiritual contrast: the difference lies not in the source but in whether there is an outlet.
Psychology: Dunn, Aknin and Norton (2008, Science) found that people who spent money on others were clearly happier, regardless of the amount.
Harvard’s Study of Adult Development, running since 1938 for over eighty years; its director Waldinger concludes that good relationships are what keep people healthy and happy.
321: the 920 practice — everyone we relate to is our “2”; live out the selfless “0” and bear the ninefold fruit.

Practical action: care for someone, expecting nothing

Eight stages: implementation, repetition, multiplication

Practice Two: give someone your time or care, expecting nothing in return; set a time and put it in your calendar.

notes: Every act of denying self lets Jesus be seen
Joy is not a feeling but the fruit of a life
No longer living for ourselves, but for the Lord
2 Corinthians 5:15
The call: move yourself off the throne and let Jesus be King — King over your calendar, your wallet, your words and your grievances.
Three pictures: giving away the credit at the office, being first to say sorry at home, quietly stacking chairs at church.
Scripture: 2 Corinthians 5:15 — no longer living to ourselves, but to him who died and rose again for us.
Contrast: feelings change with the weather; fruit grows as life grows.
321: let Jesus be King; let Jesus receive all the glory.

Original language: “compassion” is σπλαγχνίζομαι; its root σπλάγχνα means the inward parts, the bowels.
This is not standing at a distance and saying “What a pity”; it is a person’s whole insides being churned up — “moved with tender mercy” comes closest.
The same word is used of the prodigal son’s father (Luke 15:20) and the good Samaritan (Luke 10:33).
Old Testament background: “sheep without a shepherd” — Numbers 27:17 and 1 Kings 22:17; Ezekiel 34:15 prophesies the coming of the true Shepherd.
Application: duty holds you up for a while; love holds you up for a lifetime — not because we “ought to” but because we “can’t bear not to.”

brief21.title: Laying Down Rights, Returning to Our Position
notes: “But emptied himself, taking the form of a servant”
Philippians 2:7
The Son of Man came to serve
Mark 10:45
Scripture: Philippians 2:5–8; “emptied himself” is κενόω in Greek, meaning “to empty out.”
Jesus did not lose his divine nature; he laid down his right to use the privileges of that divinity.
Scripture interpreting Scripture: Mark 10:45; John 13:14–15, the Lord washing the disciples’ feet.
Clarify: denying of self is not repressing yourself but an expression of love. Repression builds up resentment; love bears fruit.
321: pride is leaving our originally intended position and grasping power; humility is laying down power and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God.

brief21.title: Three Small Ways to Live It Out
notes: Listen, don’t defend: live out gentleness
Help, expect nothing back: live out service
Give way, don’t argue: live out peace
People who give live healthier lives
Picture: life is like holding a handful of sand — open your hand and the sand stays in your palm; clench your fist and it runs out between your fingers.
Scripture prompts: James 1:19, “swift to hear, slow to speak”; Romans 12:18, “be at peace with all men.”

Psychology: Stephanie L. Brown and colleagues (2003, Psychological Science) followed 423 older married couples in Detroit for five years; those who regularly “gave help” had a significantly lower risk of dying, while simply “receiving help” had no such effect.
Scientific fact: the heart beats about a hundred thousand times a day, sends out the most and is supplied by just a few coronary arteries.
Close: living it out before others isn’t about proving how good you are; it’s about letting people see how real Jesus is.

brief21.title: 2. Jesus Died It Out Before Us
notes: “I am the good shepherd.
The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep”
John 10:11
Saving lost sheep costs a life
Scripture: John 10:11, the Good Shepherd discourse.
Key point: saving the lost sheep takes not only teaching the truth but paying the price of a life.
Contrast: the hired hand sees the wolf coming and abandons the sheep, but the good shepherd lays down his life for them (John 10:12–13).
Old Testament foreshadowing: the Passover lamb (Exodus 12) — the lamb had to die so that the firstborn would not.
Isaiah 53:4–5: the punishment that brought our peace was on him, and by his wounds we are healed.

brief21.title: Not Forced, but Willing
notes: “No one takes it away from me,
but I lay it down by myself”
John 10:18
Only one with authority can truly lay it down
Scripture: John 10:17–18.
Original language: “lay down his life” is τίθημι τὴν ψυχήν, literally “to lay down one’s own life”; “power” is ἐξουσία, lawful authority and freedom.
Key: only when someone with authority lays it down is it denying of self; when someone without authority lets go, that is called helplessness.
Conclusion: the cross was not an accident, not a slip, not a victory for Roman soldiers, but the deliberate choice of the Son of God.
Definition: true denying of self is not forced but voluntary; not grudging but born of love.

brief21.title: The Logic of a Grain of Wheat
notes: “Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies,
it remains by itself alone. But if it dies,
it bears much fruit”
John 12:24
Scripture: John 12:24.
Picture: kept in the barn, it stays a single grain for ever; fallen into the ground, it becomes a whole field of wheat.
The arithmetic of God’s kingdom is the opposite of the world’s: the world says “keeping is having”; God says “giving is gaining.”
Related passages: Romans 5:8, 1 John 3:16, 1 Peter 2:21.

Quotation: generally held to come from the missionary Jim Elliot’s journal, 28 October 1949 — “He is no fool who gives what he cannot keep to gain what he cannot lose.” He was martyred in Ecuador in 1956.

brief21.title: I Die So That You May Live
notes: Husbands lay down pride and apologise first
Wives lay down complaints and forgive first
Co-workers compete for neither name nor credit
Humility sparks humility, and both sides win
Everyday examples: in marriage, whoever bows first looks like Jesus first; complaining is settling yesterday’s bill all over again every day, forgiveness is tearing up the bill.
Scripture: Philippians 2:3–4 — in humility, each counting others better than himself.

Psychology: John Gottman and Levenson’s 1992 research predicted marital outcomes from conflict conversations with considerable accuracy; the “Four Horsemen of the Apocalypse” are criticism, contempt, defensiveness and stonewalling; healthy marriages know how to make “repair attempts,” with a positive-to-negative ratio of about five to one.
Scripture parallel: Matthew 5:24 — first be reconciled to your brother, then come and offer your gift. The cross is the repair attempt God reached out to make with us.
321: pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility sparks humility, and both sides win. Satan’s downfall began with the five “I will”s of Isaiah 14:13–14.

brief21.title: 3. Denying of Self Brings Joy
notes: “That my joy may remain in you,
and that your joy may be made full”
John 15:11
What he gives is “my joy”
Scripture: John 15:9–11.
Three key phrases: remain, my joy, made full.
True joy lies not in what we gain but in what we are able to give away.
“My joy” — not ordinary happiness, but Jesus’ own share of joy.
321: shift from man’s, earthly, temporary perspective to God’s, heavenly, eternal perspective.

brief21.title: Remain: Joy Is the Fruit of Grace
notes: “Remain” in Greek means to settle down and stay
Joy and grace share the same root
“Who for the joy that was set before him
endured the cross, despising its shame” Hebrews 12:2
Original language: “remain” is μένω, meaning to settle down, to stay for good and never move out; it appears ten times or more in John 15.
Joy (χαρά) and grace (χάρις) share the same root — joy is received, not squeezed out; “made full” (πληρόω) means filled to overflowing.
Key: Jesus’ joy is a joy that passes through the cross (Hebrews 12:2). So joy has nothing to do with comfort and everything to do with denying of self.
Source of power: denying of self comes not from willpower but from connection. “Apart from me you can do nothing” (John 15:5).
Galatians 5:22–23: joy is the fruit of the Spirit — grown, not manufactured.

brief21.title: The Sea of Galilee and the Dead Sea
notes: One river Jordan, two outcomes
Flowing in and out: fish and grass
Only in, never out: about 34 per cent salt
Does your life have an outlet?
Geographical fact: the Jordan flows into both the Sea of Galilee and the Dead Sea; the Dead Sea has no outlet, and its salinity reaches about 34 per cent, roughly ten times that of ordinary seawater.
The Sea of Galilee has fish and grass and villages all around; most of Jesus’ ministry took place there.
Spiritual contrast: the difference lies not in the source but in whether there is an outlet.
Application: when grace comes in and flows out, life has fish and grass; when it only comes in, life grows saltier and more bitter.
321: the 920 practice — everyone we relate to is our “2”; practise living the selfless “0” and bear the ninefold (9) fruit of the Spirit.

brief21.title: It Is More Blessed to Give Than to Receive
notes: “It is more blessed to give than to receive”
Acts 20:35
Spending money on others makes us happier
He must increase, but I must decrease
Scripture: Acts 20:35, Paul quoting the words of the Lord Jesus as he bids farewell to the Ephesian elders.
Old Testament: Nehemiah 8:10, “the joy of Yahweh is your strength”; Psalm 16:11, “In your presence is fullness of joy.”
Psychology: Dunn, Aknin and Norton (2008, Science) found that participants told to spend money on others were clearly happier, regardless of the amount.

Harvard’s Study of Adult Development, running since 1938 for over eighty years; its director Robert Waldinger concludes that what keeps people healthy and happy is not wealth or fame but good relationships.
Testimony: John the Baptist’s joy was made full when he stepped back (John 3:29–30). Paul, in prison, still said, “Rejoice in the Lord always!” (Philippians 4:4).

brief21.title: Putting It into Practice (1)
notes: Morning prayer: live for you, act for others,
not for myself — forty days in a row
Practical action: give time and care
Expect nothing back; put it in your calendar
Practice One in full: “Lord, today let me live for you, act for others, and not for myself.”
Implementation: make this prayer the first thing you say when you open your eyes tomorrow; move it to before you look at your phone.
Repetition: forty days in a row, so the new habit takes root; Multiplication: invite a brother or sister to join you.
Practice Two: this week do one concrete thing — a phone call, a meal, a lift, an hour of keeping someone company.
Scripture: Matthew 10:42 — whoever gives one of these little ones a cup of cold water will in no way lose his reward.

brief21.title: Putting It into Practice (2)
notes: Evening review: is my JOY order right?
What did I do for Jesus today?
Eight stages: Information, Revelation, Conviction,
Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication
Practice Three: three minutes before bed, write three lines — What did I do for Jesus today? What did I do for others? Was I tied up by myself?
Be honest: much of the time our order is Y-O-J, and we still think we’re very spiritual.
The eight stages: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.
When correcting, don’t condemn yourself; even our motives for giving need to be cleansed — that is grace, not failure.
Reminder: living “for myself” brings passing happiness; living “for Jesus and for others” brings eternal joy.

brief21.title: The 3-2-1 Vision in Summary
notes: Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard
The Holy Spirit is my guide; let Jesus be King
The old self is self-centred, the new self selfless
Life first, then relationships, then ministry
The Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model (he lived it out and died it out before us); the Bible is my standard; the Holy Spirit is my guide.
The Two Core Values: let Jesus be King; let Jesus receive all the glory. The Goal: establish God’s system (Matthew 6:10).
The fivefold change: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry — the first thing to change today is turning “denying of self is a loss” into “denying of self is a gain.”
The order of relationships: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, last of all with things. Those who haven’t drawn love from God have only reluctance to give, not love.
The 235 relationships: become a “2” with a selfless person, build a “3” of spiritual parents and children, become a “5” — a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades.

brief21.title: Closing and Call
notes: Every act of denying self lets Jesus be seen
Joy is not a feeling but the fruit of a life
No longer living for ourselves, but for the Lord
2 Corinthians 5:15
Acknowledge the cost: not defending ourselves when misunderstood, apologising first when we’re in the right, still reaching out when we ought to be resting.
Three pictures: giving away the credit at the office, being first to say sorry at home, quietly stacking chairs at church.
Contrast: feelings change with the weather; fruit grows as life grows.
Scripture: 2 Corinthians 5:15 — he died for all, that those who live should no longer live to themselves.
The call: move yourself off the throne and let Jesus be King over your calendar, your wallet, your words and your grievances.

brief21.title: Prayer of Response and Blessing
notes: Lord, be the King of my life
Help me bow first and forgive first at home
May your joy fill my heart
May all the glory go to Jesus
Lead the brothers and sisters to pray aloud together, in a slow, warm voice.
Thanksgiving: you lived it out before us, so that we know what love looks like; you died it out before us, so that we know how far love can go.
Confession: forgive us for so often putting ourselves first and the Lord last.
Petition: ask the Holy Spirit to make denying of self no longer a teeth-gritting effort but an outpouring of love; ask the Lord to make us like the Sea of Galilee, flowing in and out.
Blessing and sending: may the joy of the Lord be our strength; go today and love the person next to you.

script: Brothers and sisters, good morning. Today we’re reading Lesson 69 of Morning Devotion 321 together, and the title is “For Jesus, for Others, Not for Self.” In the last lesson we talked about this truth; today we want to bring it down into daily living. Because denying of self is not just a doctrine; it’s a way of life. Jesus never only taught us; he lived it out before our eyes, and he died it out before our eyes. His living was a service of love; his dying was an offering of love.

Brothers and sisters, did you know? The English word JOY hides an order in its three letters. J is for Jesus — first; O is for Others — second; Y is for Yourself — third. Get the order right, and joy comes. Get it the wrong way round? You could own the whole world and still be empty inside. I know an elderly sister who served for more than thirty years — cooking, washing dishes, mopping floors, the kinds of work nobody applauds. One year she spent forty days in hospital, and the visitors never stopped coming. A nurse asked her, “Are you somebody important?” She smiled and said, “I’m not anybody important. I’m just someone who gave herself away.”

Today’s main passage is in John chapter 15. These are the farewell words Jesus spoke to his disciples after the Last Supper, on the night he was betrayed. Brothers and sisters, think about it: in a few hours he would be arrested, flogged and crucified. Yet that night he talked not about his own fear but about his disciples’ joy. That alone is enough to make us bow our heads. Someone who still cares about others at the moment of greatest pain — that is what “not for ourselves” means. Just before this comes the parable of the vine, which is about being connected to the Lord; just after it comes a weighty sentence: greater love has no one than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends. Brothers and sisters, have you noticed? Joy sits right in the middle — on one side union with the Lord, on the other side denying ourselves for others. Apart from those two, everything we chase is mere emotion, not joy.

First, Jesus lived it out before us. Mark chapter 6 records that the disciples had just come back from their mission, so worn out they didn’t even have time to eat. Jesus said, “You come apart into a deserted place, and rest awhile.” But the moment the boat reached the shore, the shore was already thick with people. Scripture says, “Jesus came out, saw a great multitude, and he had compassion on them, because they were like sheep without a shepherd.” The root of the original word for “compassion” means the inward parts. It isn’t standing at a distance saying, “What a pity”; it’s a person’s whole insides being churned up.

Brothers and sisters, what did Jesus lay down? His rights. He had the right to rest, and he laid it down. Paul says, “But emptied himself, taking the form of a servant.” To empty himself means to pour himself out. In 2003 the psychologist Brown published a study that followed more than four hundred older couples for five years and found that people who regularly gave help had a markedly lower risk of dying. You see, human beings were made to live by giving themselves away. Our hearts beat a hundred thousand times a day, giving away the most and keeping the least for themselves. God has written the truth of denying of self inside our very chests.

Second, Jesus died it out before us. He said, “No one takes it away from me, but I lay it down by myself.” Brothers and sisters, listen carefully to this sentence. The cross was not an accident, not a slip, not a victory for Roman soldiers. The cross was the deliberate choice of the Son of God. True denying of self is not forced but voluntary; not grudging but born of love.

Jesus explained it himself: unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains by itself alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit. Kept in the barn, it stays a single grain for ever; fallen into the ground, it becomes a whole field of wheat. Brothers and sisters, the easiest place to test this is at home. When a husband is willing to lay down his pride and apologise first, the marriage is healed; when a wife is willing to lay down her complaints and choose forgiveness, the home has joy; when co-workers don’t compete for name or credit, the church will be united. Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility sparks humility, and both sides win.

Third, denying of self brings joy. Jesus said, “I have spoken these things to you, that my joy may remain in you, and that your joy may be made full.” Notice that he says “my joy.” What kind of joy is that? Hebrews says that for the joy that was set before him he endured the cross, despising its shame. So Jesus’ joy is a joy that passes through the cross. Joy, then, has nothing to do with comfort; joy has everything to do with denying of self.

Brothers and sisters, in Israel one and the same river, the Jordan, feeds two lakes. In the north, the Sea of Galilee: water comes in and goes out, so there are fish and grass. In the south, the Dead Sea: water only comes in and never goes out, the salt grows more and more concentrated — about 34 per cent, ten times that of seawater — and that’s why it’s called the Dead Sea. The difference isn’t the source; it’s whether there’s an outlet. People are the same. When grace comes in and flows out again, life has fish and grass; when it only comes in and never goes out, life grows more and more bitter. Does your life have an outlet?

So today there are three practices. First, pray every morning: Lord, today let me live for you, act for others, and not for myself. Second, this week give someone your time or care, expecting nothing in return. Third, review your day in the evening: was my order today Jesus, others, yourself? Brothers and sisters, don’t do it just once. 321 says that changing our mindset goes through eight stages, and the most important are Implementation, Repetition and Multiplication. Do it for forty days, then bring someone else along to do it with you.

Brothers and sisters, living for Jesus, for others and not for ourselves is a road of denying of self, and it is also a road of joy. Every choice to deny yourself is a moment when Jesus is seen. When you hand the credit to someone else at the office, someone sees Jesus; when you’re the first at home to say sorry, someone sees Jesus. Paul says he died for all, that those who live should no longer live to themselves. He has already died for you; today, will you live for him?

Let’s pray together. Dear Lord Jesus, thank you for living it out before us and dying it out before us. Forgive us for so often putting ourselves first and you last. Give us a selfless heart, willing to bow first at home and to forgive first in our relationships. Put your joy in our hearts, so that our joy may be made full. Reign as King in our homes, and may all the glory be yours. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen. Brothers and sisters, go today and love the person next to you.

Brothers and sisters, good morning. May the peace of the Lord come upon you this morning. Today we’re reading Lesson 69 of Morning Devotion 321 together, and the title is “For Jesus, for Others, Not for Self.” In the last lesson we talked about this truth; today we want to bring it down into daily living. Our key verse is John 15:11: “I have spoken these things to you, that my joy may remain in you, and that your joy may be made full.” Brothers and sisters, the destination of this lesson is joy.

First, let’s look at a very small yet very deep word — JOY. J is for Jesus — first; O is for Others — second; Y is for Yourself — third. This is not a play on words; it is the arrangement of the kingdom of heaven. Get the order right, and joy comes without being invited; get it the wrong way round, and you could own the whole world and still be empty inside. I think of an elderly sister who served for more than thirty years — cooking, washing dishes, mopping floors, all the kinds of work nobody applauds. One year she spent forty days in hospital, and the visitors never stopped coming. A nurse asked her, “Are you somebody important?” She smiled and said, “I’m just someone who gave herself away.”

Brothers and sisters, that is today’s theme. Denying of self is not just a doctrine; it’s a way of life. Jesus never only taught us; he lived it out before our eyes, and he died it out before our eyes. His living was a service of love; his dying was an offering of love. When we choose to live for Jesus, for others and not for ourselves, our lives are transformed, our relationships are healed and our surroundings are filled with joy. 321 says: Jesus is my role model. A role model is not a portrait hanging on the wall; it’s a set of footprints you can step into. At the opening of his Confessions, the Church Father Augustine said, “You have made us for yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in you.” Brothers and sisters, the restlessness of the human heart really comes from getting the order wrong. Those who put themselves at the centre will never find rest.

To understand today’s passage, we first have to stand in that room. John chapters 13 to 17 are the farewell words Jesus spoke to his disciples on the night he was betrayed. The book was written by the apostle John, who lived in Ephesus in his old age, around the AD 80s to 90s. Brothers and sisters, think about it: in a few hours the one speaking would be crucified; the ones listening were about to scatter and run. Yet that night he talked not about his own fear but about his disciples’ joy. Just before this comes the parable of the vine, about being connected to the Lord; just after it comes a weighty sentence: greater love has no one than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends. Joy sits right in the middle.

The first key point: Jesus lived it out before us. Mark chapter 6 records a very real scene. The disciples had just come back from their mission, so worn out they didn’t even have time to eat. Jesus said, “You come apart into a deserted place, and rest awhile.” He himself was wearier still, because he had just heard the terrible news that John the Baptist had been beheaded. Going to rest awhile was a perfectly reasonable right. But the moment the boat reached the shore, the shore was already thick with people. If it had been us, a sentence would most likely have bubbled up inside: “Can’t a person even get some rest?”

But Scripture says, “Jesus came out, saw a great multitude, and he had compassion on them, because they were like sheep without a shepherd.” Brothers and sisters, the root of the Greek word for “compassion” here means the inward parts. It isn’t standing at a distance saying, “What a pity”; it’s a person’s whole insides being churned up. In the New Testament this word is used almost exclusively of Jesus — and of figures like the prodigal son’s father, who was moved with compassion, and the good Samaritan, who was moved with compassion. Jesus’ service didn’t come out of a schedule; it came out of his very insides. Duty can hold you up for a while; only love can hold you up for a lifetime.

So what did Jesus lay down? His rights. Paul says, “But emptied himself, taking the form of a servant.” In the original, “emptied himself” means to pour out. He did not lose his divine nature; he laid down his right to use the privileges of that divinity. Mark 10:45 says the Son of Man came not to be served, but to serve. He is the Lord, yet he carries the basin of water; he is the Teacher, yet he washes the disciples’ feet. Brothers and sisters, denying of self is not repressing yourself; it is an expression of love. 321 says: pride is leaving our originally intended position and grasping power; humility is laying down power and returning to our originally intended position.

How do we live it out before others in daily life? Three little things. When you listen instead of defending yourself, you live out the gentleness of Jesus; when you help without seeking anything in return, you live out the servanthood of Jesus; when you give way rather than argue, you live out the peace of Jesus. In 2003, Dr Brown of the University of Michigan published a study in the journal Psychological Science that followed 423 older married couples in Detroit for five years. She found that people who regularly gave help had a significantly lower risk of dying, whereas simply receiving help had no such effect. Brothers and sisters, human beings were made to live by giving themselves away. Look at the heart: it beats about a hundred thousand times a day, gives away the most, and is supplied by just a few coronary arteries. God has written the truth of denying of self inside our very chests.

The second key point: Jesus died it out before us. He knew that to save the lost sheep it would take not only teaching the truth but paying the price of his life. So he said, “I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep.” The Old Testament foreshadowed this long ago. On the night of the Passover, the lamb was slain, its blood was smeared on the doorframe, and death passed over that household. The lamb had to die so that the firstborn would not. Isaiah 53 says that by his wounds we are healed. This is a complete exchange — he dies, we live.

Jesus also said, “No one takes it away from me, but I lay it down by myself.” Brothers and sisters, listen carefully to this sentence. The cross was not an accident, not a slip, not a victory for Roman soldiers; it was the deliberate choice of the Son of God. In the original, “lay down his life” literally means to lay down one’s own life. And the word “power” means lawful authority and freedom. Only when someone with authority lays it down is it denying of self; when someone without authority lets go, that is called helplessness. True denying of self is not forced but voluntary; not grudging but born of love.

His death was not a defeat but a glorious victory. He used a picture any farmer understands: “Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains by itself alone. But if it dies, it bears much fruit.” Kept in the barn, it stays a single grain for ever; fallen into the ground, it becomes a whole field of wheat. The arithmetic of God’s kingdom is the exact opposite of the world’s: the world says keeping is having; God says giving is gaining. The missionary Jim Elliot has a saying generally held to come from his journal in 1949: “He is no fool who gives what he cannot keep to gain what he cannot lose.” Six years later he was martyred in Ecuador, yet the gospel took root in that tribe.

The easiest place to test this truth is at home. When a husband is willing to lay down his pride and apologise first, the marriage is healed. So many couples, when they quarrel, aren’t fighting over right and wrong but over face. Whoever bows first looks like Jesus first. When a wife is willing to lay down her complaints and choose forgiveness, the family has joy. Complaining is settling yesterday’s bill all over again every day; forgiveness is tearing up the bill. When co-workers don’t compete for name or credit, the church will be united. The psychologist Gottman identified the most destructive patterns in marriage, the Four Horsemen of the Apocalypse: criticism, contempt, defensiveness and stonewalling. He found that healthy marriages are not marriages without conflict, but marriages that know how to make repair attempts. The cross is the repair attempt God reached out to make with us. Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility sparks humility, and both sides win.

The third key point: denying of self brings joy. Jesus said, “I have spoken these things to you, that my joy may remain in you, and that your joy may be made full.” True joy lies not in what we gain but in what we are able to give away. Please notice that Jesus says “my joy,” not “your joy.” What he wants to put inside us is his own share of joy. Brothers and sisters, when husband and wife deny themselves for each other, the home is filled with joy; when co-workers deny themselves for one another, the church overflows with joy; when brothers and sisters deny themselves for one another, the whole community is filled with love. Denying of self looks like loss, but in fact it is entering into the true source of joy.

What kind of joy is that? Hebrews 12:2 says that for the joy that was set before him he endured the cross, despising its shame. So Jesus’ joy is a joy that passes through the cross. Joy, then, has nothing to do with comfort; joy has everything to do with denying of self. In the original, joy and grace share the same root — joy is received, not squeezed out. And “remain” means to settle down and never move out. The branch doesn’t have to strain to bear fruit; the branch only has to stay on the vine. Apart from the Lord we can do nothing.

Brothers and sisters, in Israel one and the same river, the Jordan, feeds two lakes. In the north, the Sea of Galilee: water comes in and goes out, so there are fish, grass and villages. In the south, the Dead Sea: water only comes in and never goes out, the salt grows more and more concentrated — its salinity is about 34 per cent, ten times that of seawater — so fish cannot live there and grass cannot grow. The two lakes share the same source; the only difference is whether they have an outlet. People are the same. A life that only takes in and never gives out grows more and more bitter. Let me ask you a question: does your life have an outlet?

When Paul said farewell to the Ephesian elders, he told them to remember the words of the Lord Jesus: it is more blessed to give than to receive. Nehemiah 8:10 also says, “the joy of Yahweh is your strength.” Notice the order — it isn’t that we have joy once we have strength; it’s that joy brings strength. In 2008, Dunn, Aknin and Norton published a study in the journal Science: participants were each given a small sum of money, and the group told to spend it on someone else was clearly happier that evening — and the amount made no difference. There is another person in the New Testament who lived this secret out: John the Baptist. He said, “He must increase, but I must decrease.” His joy was made full not when he was lifted up, but when he stepped back.

The lesson gives us three practices. First: pray every morning — Lord, today let me live for you, act for others, and not for myself. Brothers and sisters, don’t wait until you’re in a good mood to pray; prayer will bring the mood with it. Move it to before you look at your phone, do it for forty days, then invite a brother or sister to do it with you. Second: take practical action — give someone your time or care, expecting nothing in return. This week, do one concrete thing — a phone call, a meal, an hour of keeping someone company. Set a time and put it in your calendar.

The third practice: an evening review — did I live out the order of JOY today? Three minutes before bed, write three lines: What did I do for Jesus today? What did I do for others? Was I tied up by myself? To be honest, much of the time our order is yourself first and Jesus last, and we still think we’re very spiritual. 321 says that changing our mindset goes through eight stages: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication. Many people stop at Information — they hear it and that’s that. May the Lord lead us through all eight stages.

Let’s walk today’s message through the framework of 321. The Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide — denying of self doesn’t come from gritting our teeth; it comes from the Holy Spirit. The Two Core Values: let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory. The Goal: establish God’s system, a system of washing one another’s feet. The fivefold change: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry. The first thing to change today is our mindset — from “denying of self is a loss” to “denying of self is a gain.” Brothers and sisters, who is your “2” today? Practise selflessness towards that person, and on that person bear the ninefold fruit of the Spirit.

Brothers and sisters, living for Jesus, for others and not for ourselves is a road of denying of self, but it is also a road full of glory and joy. It asks us not to defend ourselves when we’re misunderstood, to apologise first when we’re in the right, to keep reaching out when we ought to be resting. But please remember: every choice to deny yourself is a moment when Jesus is seen. When you hand the credit to someone else at the office, someone sees Jesus; when you’re the first at home to say sorry, someone sees Jesus. Joy is then no longer a feeling but the fruit of a life. Feelings change with the weather; fruit grows as life grows. Paul says, “He died for all, that those who live should no longer live to themselves.” He has already died for you; today, will you live for him?

Let’s bow our heads and pray together. Dear Lord Jesus, we thank you. You lived it out before us, so that we know what love looks like; you died it out before us, so that we know how far love can go. Forgive us for so often putting ourselves first and you last. Nail the self-centred old self to the cross and give us a selfless heart, so that we are willing to bow first at home and to forgive first in our relationships. Put your joy in our hearts, so that our joy may be made full. Let our lives be like the Sea of Galilee, flowing in and flowing out. Reign as King in our homes, and may all the glory be yours. In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen. Brothers and sisters, go and love the person next to you.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction: What You Fear Losing Is Not God but Yourself
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning. This morning I want to begin with a very honest question: when you first heard the word “selflessness,” what was your real reaction inside?

I’ve met a good many brothers and sisters whose first reaction was almost identical: “Selflessness? Then won’t I have nothing left at all? Will I even be me any more?” One sister, very capable in her career, said to me, “Pastor, I can give my time, I can give my money, I can get up early to pray, I can go out and share the gospel. But when you tell me to lay down my ‘self,’ I start trembling inside. Because that’s the only thing I have left.”

Those words are very real, and they cut deep. What we fear is often not losing God but losing ourselves. We’re willing to give God everything except “me.” We’re willing to let Jesus be our Saviour, our friend, our helper, but not quite so willing to let him be King. Because letting him be King means that I am no longer king.

But brothers and sisters, this morning I want to tell you with great confidence: in spiritual truth, selflessness has never been loss but gain; not emptiness but abundance; not being weakened but being filled. Because when “self” is no longer in charge, Jesus can be King; when my limited life steps back, his limitless life comes in.

Let me use a picture. When someone goes diving, they carry an oxygen tank on their back. The air in the tank is limited; it usually lasts only forty to sixty minutes. You can breathe very sparingly, very carefully, very economically, but however hard you try, the air in the tank will eventually run out. That is the self-centred life — all your strength is confined to that one little tank.

But if there is a hose bringing air down from the surface in an endless supply, the situation is completely different. You no longer have to calculate how much is left, because the supply no longer comes from the tank on your back but from the boundless atmosphere above. That is the selfless life — you haven’t run out of air; you’ve been connected to the whole sky.

That is exactly Paul’s testimony: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” (Galatians 2:20) Notice that Paul doesn’t say “I have disappeared.” He says “it is no longer I who live.” He was still alive — still preaching, still writing letters, still sitting in prison, still being stoned — but the source of his life had been changed. The tank had been swapped for the hose; the limited had been swapped for the limitless.

This is the lesson we are entering together today: selflessness — entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus.

sections.heading: 2. Scripture Background: Three Passages, Three Scenes
sections.html:
To understand a verse, you first have to step into the scene where it was spoken. Today’s three main passages come from three very different scenes, which nonetheless confirm one another.

(1) Galatians 2:20: The Dispute at the Table in Antioch

Galatians is a letter of the apostle Paul. On the “South Galatian” view, it may well be Paul’s earliest letter, written around AD 48–49, close to the time of the Jerusalem Council (Acts chapter 15). It was addressed to the churches of Galatia that Paul had planted on his first missionary journey, including Pisidian Antioch, Iconium, Lystra and Derbe.

At that time a group of “Judaizers” had appeared in the church. They followed in Paul’s footsteps and told the Gentile believers: believing in Jesus isn’t enough on its own; you must also be circumcised and keep the law of Moses before you are truly saved. This was a battle over the very survival of the gospel.

Galatians 2:20 is not a devotional maxim Paul wrote in his study. It comes right after a very heated account. Paul has just described how he opposed Cephas (Peter) to his face in Antioch — because Peter had been eating with the Gentile believers, but as soon as men came from James, he drew back and separated himself from the Gentiles out of fear of the circumcision party (Galatians 2:11–14).

Why did Peter shrink back? Not because he couldn’t work out the theology, but because of “self.” Because he cared what others thought, because he was afraid of losing his standing among the Jewish believers. Paul says, “he drew back and separated himself, fearing those who were of the circumcision.” (Galatians 2:12)

So Paul goes straight on to speak of justification by faith (Galatians 2:15–21), and concludes with verse 20: the real issue is not whether the law is enough, but whether “I” am still there. If “I” am still sitting on the throne, then circumcision, the law, spiritual gifts — they are all just tools I use to shore myself up. Only when “I” have been crucified with Christ does the gospel truly become the gospel.

Brothers and sisters, remember this: Galatians 2:20 is a declaration of selflessness born out of a failure of the self-centred life.

(2) John 10:10: The Good Shepherd Discourse

The setting of John chapter 10 is Jesus’ Good Shepherd discourse in Jerusalem. From the context, these words follow straight on from chapter 9, the healing of the man born blind — the man who was healed and confessed Jesus, and as a result was thrown out of the synagogue by the Pharisees (John 9:34).

The Lord said, “The thief only comes to steal, kill, and destroy. I came that they may have life, and may have it abundantly.” (John 10:10)

The contrast here is very sharp. What the false shepherd does is “steal, kill, and destroy” — three verbs that build on one another: first he takes what is yours, then he takes your life, and finally he tears down the whole ecosystem. What the good shepherd does is to give the sheep “life, and … abundantly.”

The Greek word for “abundantly” is περισσόν (perisson), meaning “beyond what is needed, surplus, more than enough.” God’s abundance is never just enough; it overflows.

(3) Philippians 4:13: Contentment in Prison

Philippians is a letter Paul wrote from prison, generally thought to date from around AD 61–62, during his first imprisonment in Rome. The church in Philippi had sent Epaphroditus to bring Paul a gift, and Paul wrote to thank them, taking the opportunity to urge them to be of one mind.

Philippians 4:13 is not a motivational slogan to stick on the wall of a gym. Its context runs like this: “Not that I speak because of lack, for I have learned in whatever state I am, to be content in it. I know how to be humbled, and I also know how to abound. In everything and in all things I have learned the secret both to be filled and to be hungry, both to abound and to be in need. I can do all things through Christ, who strengthens me.” (Philippians 4:11–13)

The Greek for “learned the secret” is μεμύημαι (memyēmai), originally a technical term in the ancient mystery religions for “being initiated into the mysteries, receiving enlightenment.” Paul is saying that the lesson of how to abound and how to be humbled is something you are led into step by step, trained in by a master, not something that drops on you overnight.

And “strengthens me” is the Greek ἐνδυναμοῦντι (endynamounti), whose root is δύναμις (dynamis, power), with ἐν (in, within) placed in front. So the heart of the sentence is: the Lord who pours power into me from within. Not someone giving me a push from outside, but power welling up from inside.

Brothers and sisters, three scenes, three situations: one a conflict inside the church, one the loneliness of being thrown out of the synagogue, one the poverty of prison. And all three passages point to the same answer — not I, but he.

sections.heading: 3. The First Key Point: Selflessness Takes Us from the Limited into the Limitless
sections.html:
1. Every limitation we have comes from that “self”

Brothers and sisters, please think quietly for a moment: what is the greatest obstacle in your life? Is it your circumstances? Other people? The times we live in?

The lesson puts it very sharply: every limitation a person has comes from “self” — our own reasoning, our own feelings, our own experience, our own calculations.

Your vision is only as wide as your reasoning; your emotions are only as steady as your feelings; your courage is only as deep as your experience; your sense of security is only as great as your calculations are accurate. The trouble is that not one of these four is limitless. And so —

Where there is the self-centred life, there is fear, because I can’t see tomorrow;

Where there is the self-centred life, there is lack, because my pockets are only so deep;

Where there is the self-centred life, there is comparison, because I have to know where I rank;

Where there is the self-centred life, there is anxiety, because everything depends on me holding it up.

In his 2004 book The Curse of the Self, the Duke University psychologist Mark R. Leary points out that the uniquely human capacity for self-reflection, though it has given us civilisation and the ability to plan, has also become the source of much suffering — we grow anxious about things that haven’t happened yet, we are wounded by other people’s opinions, and we replay our own mistakes in our heads over and over. His observation simply confirms, from the angle of psychology, what Scripture said long ago: the root of the problem is not outside but inside; not in our circumstances but in “self.”

Another line of research is also worth noting. In 2004 the psychologists Jennifer Crocker and Lora E. Park published “The Costly Pursuit of Self-Esteem” in Psychological Bulletin. They showed that when people make their self-worth contingent on some condition (such as appearance, achievement or other people’s approval), the pursuit of self-esteem itself brings anxiety, damaged relationships and a drain on self-regulation. In other words, the harder we fight to protect the “self,” the more fragile the “self” becomes.

Brothers and sisters, this is exactly what the 321 vision says: the self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall; pride is the root of our problems. Pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God.

2. But when we are selfless, we are connected to the limitless

But thank the Lord, the story doesn’t end there. When we choose selflessness and let Jesus live in us, our lives are joined to the limitless God.

Jesus said, “I am the vine. You are the branches. He who remains in me and I in him bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing.” (John 15:5)

Notice the Lord’s words: not “apart from me you can do less,” but “apart from me you can do nothing.” The branch’s problem is never that it doesn’t try hard enough; it’s whether or not it is connected. Take a broken-off branch and tie fruit onto it, and in three days all you’ll have is rotten mush.

Jesus’ life is an “abundant” life. He said, “I came that they may have life, and may have it abundantly.” (John 10:10) That means he wants not only to keep us alive, but to make us live fulfilled, free and strong.

Paul’s prayer for the Ephesian church points the same way: “and to know Christ’s love which surpasses knowledge, that you may be filled with all the fullness of God. Now to him who is able to do exceedingly abundantly above all that we ask or think, according to the power that works in us.” (Ephesians 3:19–20)

“Above all that we ask or think” — brothers and sisters, hear this clearly: God’s plan is not capped by your imagination; your imagination is only the floor of God’s plan.

3. Four contrasts: from the self-centred life to selflessness

The lesson lists four very precious contrasts. Let’s confirm each one from Scripture:

First, the self-centred “we” are afraid, but the selfless “we” have peace. John says, “There is no fear in love; but perfect love casts out fear, because fear has punishment. He who fears is not made perfect in love.” (1 John 4:18) Fear isn’t driven out by willpower; it’s crowded out by love.

Second, the self-centred “we” are weak, but the selfless “we” are strong. The Lord said to Paul, “My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.” And so Paul said, “Most gladly therefore I will rather glory in my weaknesses, that the power of Christ may rest on me.” (2 Corinthians 12:9) What wonderful logic this is — weakness is no longer an ugly thing to hide, but the doorway to grace.

Third, the self-centred “we” are in want, but the selfless “we” are provided for. Paul says, “My God will supply every need of yours according to his riches in glory in Christ Jesus.” (Philippians 4:19) David says, “Yahweh is my shepherd: I shall lack nothing.” (Psalm 23:1) The Hebrew root behind “lack” is חָסֵר (chaser), meaning to be short of, to be insufficient. David means that as long as Yahweh is the shepherd, the books will always balance.

Fourth, the self-centred “we” fail, but the selfless “we” overcome through him. Paul says, “No, in all these things, we are more than conquerors through him who loved us.” (Romans 8:37) The Greek for “more than conquerors” is ὑπερνικῶμεν (hypernikōmen), which takes “to conquer” (νικάω) and adds “over and beyond” (ὑπέρ) — not a narrow win but a resounding one, a victory with something left over.

4. Stop relying on methods; start relying on the Holy Spirit

The lesson puts it well: true selflessness means ceasing to rely on our own methods and relying entirely on the guidance of the Holy Spirit.

There’s a saying in Chinese martial arts: “no set moves defeats set moves” — every set move has its opening; only having no set moves is true freedom. This fits the spiritual life remarkably well. When we cling to a fixed set of methods, we are limited by those methods; but when we are selfless, we no longer respond to our circumstances by our own logic. We are led by the Holy Spirit and live out wonderful breakthroughs.

What does Scripture say? “Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit,” says Yahweh of Armies (Zechariah 4:6). Zerubbabel was facing the ruins of a temple on which work had stopped for sixteen years. God didn’t give him more might and more ability; God gave him “my Spirit.”

Solomon also said, “Trust in Yahweh with all your heart, and don’t lean on your own understanding. In all your ways acknowledge him, and he will make your paths straight.” (Proverbs 3:5–6) The Hebrew for “trust” is בָּטַח (batach), whose basic meaning is “to lean your whole weight on something with ease,” like someone lying full length on a bed, no longer holding themselves up.

5. Applying 321: Jesus is the focal point; our perspective shifts from man’s to God’s

Brothers and sisters, of the Three Foundations in the 321 vision, the third is “the Holy Spirit is my guide.” This key point is exactly the practice of that foundation.

When we run into difficulty, if our first reaction is “What am I going to do?” that is the self-centred life; if it is “Lord, how do you see this?” that is selflessness.

When we weigh something up, if we use a human, earthly, temporary, worldly perspective, that is the self-centred life; if we shift to God’s perspective — heavenly, eternal, godly — that is selflessness.

321 says: Jesus is the focal point — not ourselves, not other people, not our circumstances. It also says: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the brain and you’ll be troubled, rely on the heart and you’ll be glad. Because “out of it is the wellspring of life” (Proverbs 4:23).

A limited tank connected to the limitless sky. That is the first key point.

sections.heading: 4. The Second Key Point: Selflessness Lets the Life of Jesus Replace Our Life
sections.html:
1. Selflessness is not becoming a blank; it is letting Jesus become everything

The lesson puts it very precisely: selflessness doesn’t turn us into a blank; it lets Jesus become our everything.

This has to be made clear, because many people misunderstand it. The selflessness the Christian faith speaks of is not the “emptiness and extinction” of Eastern philosophy; it is not dissolving the self into nothingness. The 321 vision puts it well: selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the infinite and living out the infinite; “I” no longer live, but Christ lives in me.

This is the mystery of selflessness: his life is the source of our life; his wisdom is the fountain of our wisdom; his power is the strength by which we overcome.

2. From “emptying himself” to “denying himself”: two key words in the original

To understand this “replacing,” we need to know two key words.

The first is “emptied himself.” Paul says, “Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus, who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men. And being found in human form, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross.” (Philippians 2:5–8)

The Greek for “emptied himself” is ἐκένωσεν (ekenōsen), from the verb κενόω (kenoō), meaning “to empty out.” Notice that what the Lord Jesus emptied out was not his divine nature — he existed in the form of God, and that never changed. What he emptied out was his right to use his authority, his entitlement to be served. This was the most thorough act of selflessness in the universe.

Brothers and sisters, the 321 vision says: pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position. In Isaiah 14:13–14 Satan says “I will” five times: “I will ascend into heaven! I will exalt my throne above the stars of God! I will sit on the mountain of assembly, in the far north! I will ascend above the heights of the clouds! I will make myself like the Most High!” But in the Garden of Gethsemane the Lord Jesus said only one thing: “Nevertheless, not my will, but yours, be done.” (Luke 22:42)

One says “I will” five times; the other says “not my will” once. The first fell from heaven; the second was lifted up from the earth. This is the great watershed of the whole Bible.

The second key word is “deny himself.” The Lord said, “If anyone desires to come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me.” (Matthew 16:24)

The Greek for “deny himself” is ἀπαρνέομαι (aparneomai), meaning “to deny, to disown, to cut off all connection.” Interestingly, this is the very same verb the Lord used when he foretold that Peter would “deny” him three times (Matthew 26:34).

In other words, Peter once said to people, “I don’t know this Jesus”; and what the Lord Jesus wants us to learn is that one day we will be able to say to the old self, “I don’t know you. You are no longer my master.” This is not self-abuse; it is a transfer of sovereignty.

3. The picture of the glove: no longer straining to be like him, but letting him live out himself

Let me use a simple picture. A glove lies on the table. It has five fingers, it’s perfectly shaped, and the material may even be expensive. But it can’t pick up a glass of water, can’t write a word, can’t hug anyone. Why? Because there is no hand inside it.

Now slip a hand inside. The same glove can suddenly play the piano, do a day’s work, lift up someone who has fallen. Nothing about the glove has changed; what has changed is that there’s a hand inside.

Brothers and sisters, this is what the lesson means: then we are no longer merely “trying hard to become people like Jesus,” but “letting Jesus live out himself within us.”

The difference between these two is far greater than we imagine. The first is “imitation”; the second is “indwelling.” In the first, I supply the effort; in the second, he does. The first is called religion; the second is called the gospel.

Paul speaks of “Christ in you, the hope of glory” (Colossians 1:27). And he says, “But by the grace of God I am what I am. His grace which was given to me was not futile, but I worked more than all of them; yet not I, but the grace of God which was with me.” (1 Corinthians 15:10)

Paul worked harder than all the apostles — he gave it everything; he was never passive. But he immediately adds, “yet not I.” That is the most beautiful posture of a selfless person: giving everything, yet claiming no credit.

4. His attributes made visible in us

The lesson lists three things. Let’s look at them one by one:

First, his love enables us to love the unlovable. The Lord said, “But love your enemies, and do good, and lend, expecting nothing back.” (Luke 6:35) In our own strength this is a mission impossible; but Paul says, “But God commends his own love toward us, in that while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” (Romans 5:8) We can love the unlovable because we ourselves were loved in just that way.

Second, his wisdom enables us to see a way out in hard places. James says, “But if any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask of God, who gives to all liberally and without reproach, and it will be given to him.” (James 1:5) Notice the phrase “without reproach” — God won’t scold you for being foolish just because you’ve come asking for wisdom.

Third, his faith enables us to keep believing in the face of the impossible. When Abraham was about a hundred years old, Scripture says that “looking to the promise of God, he didn’t waver through unbelief, but grew strong through faith, giving glory to God, and being fully assured that what he had promised, he was also able to perform” (Romans 4:20–21).

5. Supporting evidence from psychology and science

In his 2001 book Good to Great, the management writer Jim Collins described what he called “Level 5 Leadership”: the leaders who took their companies to sustained excellence had in common not dazzling charisma but “extreme personal humility” combined with “intense professional will.” He found that these leaders credited others and good fortune for success and took the blame themselves for failure. Collins’s research is management science, not theology; but it confirms from another angle that truly lasting fruitfulness comes from selflessness, not from self-exalting.

Here’s another scientific fact: an adult’s heart beats on average about a hundred thousand times a day. When you woke up this morning, you didn’t issue an order for your heart to start beating; when you fell asleep last night, your heart didn’t stop work either. The most vital operations of our life have never been kept going by our willpower.

6. Applying 321: the old self is self-centred, the new self is selfless; life first, then relationships, then ministry

The lesson concludes: a life like this no longer relies on the flesh but on the Holy Spirit.

The 321 vision describes this change as “the old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless.” Paul says, “Therefore if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old things have passed away. Behold, all things have become new.” (2 Corinthians 5:17)

And 321 is very clear about the order of this change: the fivefold change — mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry. First the mindset changes, then the life changes; once the life has changed, daily living changes; once daily living has changed, relationships will change; once relationships have changed, ministry bears real fruit.

That’s why we often say: life first, then relationships, then ministry. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than possessions. Many brothers and sisters throw themselves into ministry yet are dried up in their life, because the order has been reversed — trying to do selfless ministry with a self-centred life, and in the end everyone gets hurt.

Brothers and sisters, today don’t rush to do more things. First let Jesus live a little more within you.

sections.heading: 5. The Third Key Point: The Victory and Freedom That Selflessness Brings
sections.html:
1. The key is not “I can do all things” but “through him”

Brothers and sisters, Philippians 4:13 is probably one of the most quoted — and most misused — verses in the Bible.

Paul says, “I can do all things through Christ, who strengthens me.” (Philippians 4:13)

The lesson goes straight to the heart of it: the key to this sentence is “through him.”

Many people read this verse as “I can do all things.” Once the weight of the sentence shifts onto “I,” the verse turns from gospel into self-motivation, from comfort into a burden. Because someone who believes “I can do all things” has nothing left but self-blame when they fail.

If we rely on ourselves, we can do nothing; but if we rely on him, we can do all things. This sentence has two sides: it is both a limitation and a release. The limitation is that without him I am nothing; the release is that with him nothing is impossible.

Notice too that Paul wrote this sentence while he was in prison. The context makes it very clear: “I know how to be humbled, and I also know how to abound. In everything and in all things I have learned the secret both to be filled and to be hungry, both to abound and to be in need.” (Philippians 4:12)

Brothers and sisters, please hear one thing: Paul says he learned how “to abound” — which means that abounding is also a lesson that has to be learned, and perhaps an even harder one than being humbled. Because when we’re brought low, we know to cling to God; when we abound, we often think what we’re clinging to is ourselves.

2. Victory is not conquering our circumstances but overcoming the “I” that wants control

The lesson offers an extremely important definition: victory is not conquering our circumstances but overcoming the “self” — the “I” that wants to control, to prove itself, to take charge.

The world says victory is pushing the other person down and getting the result in your hands; Scripture says victory is the “I” on the throne giving way to Jesus.

The Lord Jesus himself is the best illustration. He said, “I have told you these things, that in me you may have peace. In the world you have trouble; but cheer up! I have overcome the world.” (John 16:33)

Brothers and sisters, notice when the Lord said this. It was the night of the Passover. In a few hours Judas would come to betray him, the disciples would scatter and run, Peter would deny him three times, and he would be nailed to the cross. Judging by the circumstances, everything was collapsing. But the Lord said, “I have overcome the world.”

The Lord’s victory came not from changing his circumstances but from never once leaving the Father’s will in the midst of them. That is the victory of selflessness.

I often use a picture: the thermometer and the thermostat. A thermometer can only reflect its surroundings — when the room is cold, it drops; when the room is hot, it rises. It is always passive. A thermostat is different. It has a set point inside it; it doesn’t swing with its surroundings but instead changes them.

Brothers and sisters, are you a thermometer today, or a thermostat? The self-centred person is a thermometer: one remark from someone else sets the temperature of their whole day. The selfless person is a thermostat, because the set point inside them is not their own emotions but Christ.

The Austrian psychiatrist Viktor Frankl survived the concentration camps, and in Man’s Search for Meaning, first published in 1946, he set down a profound observation: everything can be taken from a person but one thing — the freedom to choose one’s attitude in any given set of circumstances. That is the truth a psychiatrist saw in the most extreme conditions. And Scripture tells us something deeper still: the source of that freedom is not in the human will but in Christ.

3. From the bondage of anxiety into the freedom of faith

The lesson says: selflessness means we are no longer bound by weakness but enter into the freedom of faith; no longer anxious about outcomes, but enjoying the peace of walking with Jesus.

The Lord said, “If you remain in my word, then you are truly my disciples. You will know the truth, and the truth will make you free.” And he said, “If therefore the Son makes you free, you will be free indeed.” (John 8:31–32, 36)

The world thinks freedom is “doing whatever I want”; Scripture says freedom is “finally no longer being ruled by ‘me.’” Someone who must win, must be right, must be seen, is actually the least free person in the world — because their peace is locked inside other people’s reactions.

Paul gives us a very concrete path: “In nothing be anxious, but in everything, by prayer and petition with thanksgiving, let your requests be made known to God. And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your thoughts in Christ Jesus.” (Philippians 4:6–7)

Notice the order: prayer, petition, and then thanksgiving. The thanksgiving comes before the answer arrives. Research published in 2003 in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology by the psychologists Robert A. Emmons and Michael E. McCullough showed that participants assigned to write down things they were grateful for each week reported clearly higher well-being, and more optimism about the coming week, than control groups who wrote about everyday events or hassles.

Gratitude has power because it shifts the focus from “what I lack” to “what he has given.” That is selflessness in miniature.

4. Our circumstances may not have changed, but inside we have already overcome

The lesson has a sentence worth copying onto the flyleaf of your Bible: when we let Jesus reign, our circumstances may not have changed, but inside we have already overcome.

Brothers and sisters, what a great comfort this is. Perhaps you’ve been praying about that matter for three years and nothing has changed; perhaps you’ve shed many tears over that family member and they are still the same. But if, in the process, you are no longer the one who has to control how it ends, you have already overcome.

Paul begged the Lord three times about a thorn in his flesh. The Lord did not take it away, but said only, “My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.” (2 Corinthians 12:9) And Paul said, “Therefore I take pleasure in weaknesses, in injuries, in necessities, in persecutions, and in distresses, for Christ’s sake. For when I am weak, then am I strong.” (2 Corinthians 12:10)

The thorn was still there, but Paul had overcome.

Isaiah says, “but those who wait for Yahweh will renew their strength. They will mount up with wings like eagles. They will run, and not be weary. They will walk, and not faint.” (Isaiah 40:31) An eagle can circle high in the sky for hours without flapping its wings — not by the power of its own muscles but by rising thermals of warm air. All it does is spread its wings and stop struggling.

Brothers and sisters, this morning perhaps this is the very word the Lord wants to say to you: stop struggling, and spread your wings.

5. Applying 321: let Jesus be King, and become an overcomer

The Two Core Values of the 321 vision are: let Jesus be King; let Jesus receive all the glory.

The third key point is about exactly the first core value — let Jesus be King. And the other side of “let Jesus be King” is “I am no longer king.” A kingdom cannot have two kings. Every time we say, “Lord, you have the final say,” it is a coronation; every time we say, “No, I’m going to decide this one myself,” it is a coup.

The aim of 321 is to walk alongside every person until they become an overcomer. And the mark of an overcomer is not having no difficulties; it is still letting Jesus be King in the middle of them.

sections.heading: 6. Integrating the 321 Vision: From the Self-Centred Old Self to the Selfless New Self
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let’s set today’s three key points within the whole picture of 321.

1. The Three Foundations, the Two Core Values, the Goal

The Three Foundations are: Jesus is my role model; the Bible is my standard; the Holy Spirit is my guide.

All three foundations are present in today’s lesson. Jesus “emptying himself” in Philippians chapter 2 is our role model for selflessness; the truth Paul declares in Galatians 2:20 is our standard; and “ceasing to rely on our own methods and relying entirely on the guidance of the Holy Spirit” is the Holy Spirit being our guide.

The Two Core Values are: let Jesus be King; let Jesus receive all the glory. Selflessness is not the goal; letting Jesus be King is the goal. We lay ourselves down not to become empty of everything, but so that the One who is worthy may sit on the throne. Paul says, “Whether therefore you eat, or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God.” (1 Corinthians 10:31)

The Goal is: establish God’s system. When one person is selfless, he is an overcomer; when a group of people are selfless, they become God’s system. The Lord’s Prayer says, “Let your Kingdom come. Let your will be done on earth as it is in heaven.” (Matthew 6:10) God’s kingdom is not a place; it is the territory where he has the final say.

2. Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan

Scripture says, “Pride goes before destruction, and an arrogant spirit before a fall.” (Proverbs 16:18)

And it says, “But he gives more grace. Therefore it says, ‘God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.’ Be subject therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you.” (James 4:6–7)

Brothers and sisters, look carefully at the order in this passage: first “be subject to God,” and only then can you “resist the devil.” Submitting to God is selflessness; resisting the devil is overcoming. 321 puts it exactly: humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan.

Satan’s very nature is pride. He attacks us with pride, and he can only gain a foothold in us through pride. Satan can find no place to get a grip on a truly selfless person, because every bait he uses hangs on the hook of “self” — being seen, being affirmed, being proved right, being compensated. When the “self” is gone, so is the hook.

In Genesis 3:5 the serpent said to Eve, “for God knows that in the day you eat it, your eyes will be opened, and you will be like God, knowing good and evil.” He has only ever sold one product: you can be your own god. The Lord Jesus offers the opposite: “Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart; and you will find rest for your souls.” (Matthew 11:29)

321 also says: pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility sparks humility, and both sides win. It’s true in the family, it’s true in the workplace, and it’s true in the church. When a hard word meets a hard word, the fire flares up; when a soft word meets a hard word, the fire goes out.

3. The fivefold change and the priority of relationships

321 speaks of the fivefold change — mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry. Change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living.

Paul says, “Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what is the good, well-pleasing, and perfect will of God.” (Romans 12:2) “Transformed by the renewing of your mind” is a change of mindset, and the result of that transformation is being able to “prove” God’s will.

The priority of relationships is: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last of all with things. Today’s three key points fall precisely on the first two levels — our relationship with God (selflessness connects us to the limitless) and our relationship with ourselves (selflessness enables us to overcome the “I” that wants control). When these two levels are right, our relationships with people and with things will follow.

The shift in perspective is: from man’s to God’s, from earthly to heavenly, from temporary to eternal, from worldly to godly. Paul says, “Set your mind on the things that are above, not on the things that are on the earth.” (Colossians 3:2) And he says, “while we don’t look at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen. For the things which are seen are temporal, but the things which are not seen are eternal.” (2 Corinthians 4:18)

4. The 920 practice: living out the “0” before every “2”

The 920 practice in 321 means this: everyone connected with us is our “2”; before them we practise living a selfless (0) life and bearing the fruit of the Spirit in all nine (9) of its expressions.

Paul says, “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control. Against such things there is no law.” (Galatians 5:22–23)

Brothers and sisters, notice: what’s spoken of here is “fruit,” not a “product.” Products are manufactured; fruit is grown. You can’t squeeze out patience by effort; you can only stay joined to the vine and let patience grow.

And not one of these nine graces grows in a vacuum.
