blog.title: How Can One Finger Hide a Mountain?

blocks.x: Subtitle: When “I” Step Back, Jesus Steps In
Try it right now: hold up one index finger, about ten centimetres in front of your eye, and then look out of the window.
You’ll notice something strange — that one small finger blots out a whole row of trees, even a whole mountain.
The finger hasn’t grown, and the mountain hasn’t shrunk. The only thing that has changed is the distance: the finger is simply too close to your eye.
That is the truth about “self”. “Self” isn’t big, yet it can block out the whole of God. Because it sits so close to us — so close that we take it for the whole world.
1. The problem often isn’t our circumstances, but “self”

Jealousy is because “I” want what someone else has; strife is because “I” want to get what’s mine; irritation is because “my” feelings have been offended; worry is because “I” want to control the future; disappointment is because “my” expectations have fallen through.
Five emotions, five outlets, but only one source — “me”.

That’s why changing your job doesn’t help, and changing your church doesn’t help either. Change your surroundings, and the same frustration simply comes back with a different face — because you packed up “self” and took it with you.

That sounds harsh, but in fact it is the greatest grace. If the problem lay in our circumstances, we would be forever powerless; but if the problem lies in “self”, then in Christ there is a sure way out — because the Lord has already crucified our old self together with him on the cross.

“I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me.” (Galatians 2:20)
2. The way appears the moment we lay ourselves down
Jesus said, “I am the way, the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father, except through me.” (John 14:6)
Please notice that the Lord didn’t say he would “point out” a way; he said he “is” the way.

Sat-nav on your phone can only take you to your destination if it first knows where you are now. Once the location drifts, even the most detailed map will only take you to the wrong place. “Self” is that false location.

The Bible gives us three witnesses. At forty, Moses was mighty in his words and works, yet couldn’t save a single person; at eighty he was slow of speech and slow of tongue, yet God used him to lead out a whole nation. Joshua wanted to draw up tactics before Jericho, but the commander of Yahweh’s army said to him, “No”; the moment he fell down in worship, he received the victory of marching round the city for seven days. Peter toiled all night and caught nothing, yet with the words “but at your word I will let down the net”, the nets were close to breaking — and in front of the biggest catch of his life, he left everything and followed Jesus.
They have only one thing in common: each of them truly saw God’s way at the very moment he laid himself down.
So selflessness has never been passive waiting; it is active obedience: Moses really did walk into Pharaoh’s palace, and Peter really did put out into the deep.
3. Selflessness is not the self disappearing; it is letting Jesus reign completely

In 1972 three pathologists gave a name to a phenomenon: “apoptosis”. They found that a great many cells in the human body go to their death actively, following a set programme — this isn’t disease; it’s design. In the embryo our hands start out like a webbed paddle, and it is precisely because the cells between the fingers die off that five fingers separate. When this programme fails, and cells that should die refuse to die, that is cancer.
In the body God made, it is “what should die refusing to die” that is the disease.

The Lord said long ago, “Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains by itself alone. But if it dies, it bears much fruit.” (John 12:24) A grain of wheat that refuses to die can stay intact, beautiful and safe — but it will only ever be one grain. Its intactness is its poverty.

And dying together isn’t the end; it’s a passageway. Scripture says God made us alive together with Christ, raised us up with him, and made us sit with him in the heavenly places. Notice that last action — sit. To sit means to reign.
But there is only one throne. If “self” sits on it, the Lord can only stand outside the door and knock; if the Lord sits on it, we sit with him in the heavenly places.
So selflessness is not the self disappearing, and it doesn’t make you worthless; it moves your worth from a foundation that will collapse onto a rock that will never be shaken.
This week, practise three small acts of selflessness
1. When emotions surge up, first ask yourself: is this “me” reacting, or is Jesus reigning?
2. When facing a challenge, don’t rush into action; stop for thirty seconds and pray, “Lord, you are my way.”
3. Each day, practise one small act of selflessness: let go of one insistence, forgive one person, hand over one area of control.
When “I” step down, Jesus steps up. When Jesus is Lord, there will be a way through everything.
A question for reflection
This morning, what is the thing you find hardest to let go of? If you truly loosened your grip and handed it to the Lord, how do you believe he would make a way for you?

brief12.title: Selflessness: Entering Fullness and Victory
notes: When “I” step back, Jesus steps in
Morning Devotion 321 · Lesson 71
“It is no longer I who live”
(Galatians 2:20)
Key points:
Greet everyone and explain that this lesson is Part 2 of “Selflessness — Entering Jesus’ Fullness and Victory”.
Key verse: Galatians 2:20 — read the full verse once.
Supporting verse: John 10:10, “I came that they may have life, and may have it abundantly.”
The lesson’s main thread: only when “self” is crucified can life overflow.

brief12.title: Introduction: One Finger Hides a Mountain
notes: A finger isn’t big, yet it can hide a mountain
because it’s too close to the eye
“Self” isn’t big, yet it blocks out God
Where there is self there are problems; where there is selflessness, none
Key points:
Have the congregation do the experiment: hold an index finger ten centimetres from the eye and look out of the window.
The key isn’t the finger’s size but its closeness to the eye; “self” is the same.
State the lesson’s core proposition: where there is self, there are problems; where there is selflessness, there are none.
Reminder: if the problem lay in our circumstances, we would be powerless; if it lies in self, in Christ there is a way out.

brief12.title: Key Verse and Background
notes: “I have been crucified with Christ”
“It is no longer I who live”
(Galatians 2:20)
Paul writes to people tied down by legalism
Key points:
The author, Paul, was once Saul, a student of Gamaliel (Acts 22:3), whose “self” had been built up enormously high.
Galatians is Paul’s earliest and most fiery letter, written against the legalism of the Judaizers.
“Crucified with Christ” is in the perfect tense: already accomplished, its effect continuing to this day.
Legalism is “self” turned religious; the foundation is love — “who loved me, and gave himself up for me.”

brief12.title: Point 1: “Self” Is the Root of the Problem
notes: Jealousy: I want what others have
Strife: I want to get what’s mine
Worry: I want to control the future
Five rivers, one source: me
Key points:
The lesson’s five mirrors: jealousy, strife, irritation, worry, disappointment — all revolving around “me”.
James 4:1–2: wars and fightings come from the pleasures that war in your members — look for the root, not the symptoms.
Picture: “self” is like a background program quietly eating up all the memory.
Leon Festinger’s theory of social comparison (1954): our sense of worth gets tied to other people.

brief12.title: Deny Self, or Deny the Lord
notes: “Deny self” and “deny the Lord”: the same word
Deny self, or deny the Lord
“Let him deny himself, take up his cross”
(Luke 9:23)
Key points:
“Deny” is aparneomai in the original, meaning to disown completely, to cut off all connection.
The same word is used of Peter: “you will deny me three times” (Matthew 26:34).
Life has only two options: deny self, or deny the Lord.
Mor and Winquist (2002) meta-analysis: the stronger the self-focus, the more negative the mood.
The Lord Jesus said long ago: “don’t be anxious for tomorrow” (Matthew 6:34).

brief12.title: Point 2: Self Has No Way Through; Selflessness Has a Way
notes: “I am the way, the truth, and the life”
(John 14:6)
Go your own way, and you hit a dead end
Lay yourself down, and you see God’s way
Key points:
The Lord doesn’t point out a way; he himself is the way. Apart from him we aren’t walking slowly; we aren’t on the road at all.
Background: the Last Supper; Thomas asks for the way, and the Lord gives not a map but himself.
Proverbs 14:12: there is a way which seems right to a man, but in the end it leads to death.
Picture: if sat-nav has the wrong location, even the best map takes you to the wrong place.
Ellen Langer’s “illusion of control” study (1975): people only think they are in control.

brief12.title: Three Men Who Laid Themselves Down
notes: Moses laid down his eloquence, Joshua his strategy
Peter laid down his nets and left everything to follow
“I will even make a way in the wilderness”
(Isaiah 43:19)
Key points:
Moses: at forty he had ability yet couldn’t save one person; at eighty, slow of speech, he led out a whole nation (Exodus 4:10).
Joshua: the commander of Yahweh’s army said “No”, cutting short his strategy (Joshua 5:13–14).
Peter: “but at your word I will let down the net” — and at the biggest catch of his life he left everything (Luke 5:5, 11).
Selflessness isn’t passive waiting but active obedience: really entering the palace, really marching round the city, really putting out into the deep.
God makes a way in the wilderness and the desert, because there no one can take the glory for himself.

brief12.title: Point 3: Die, Live and Reign Together
notes: Dead to the law, to the world, to sin
When “self” dies, we are set free
“But if we died with Christ,
we believe that we will also live with him” (Romans 6:8)
Key points:
Three passages: Romans 7:4, Galatians 6:14, Romans 6:11.
Three deaths loosen three chains: relying on performance, relying on others’ opinions, “I can’t help it”.
John 8:32, 36: the truth will make you free.
Apoptosis (Kerr, Wyllie and Currie, 1972): it is what should die refusing to die that is the disease.
John 12:24: a grain of wheat’s intactness is its poverty.

brief12.title: Seated in the Heavenly Places, Reigning with the Lord
notes: Made alive, raised and seated together
(Ephesians 2:5–6)
To sit is to reign; there is only one throne
Let Jesus be King; serve from the Spirit
Key points:
In the original, three verbs begin with syn (“together”), like a three-stage rocket carrying someone to a seat in heaven.
Servants stand, masters sit; to sit on a throne means to reign (Revelation 3:21).
There is only one throne: if I don’t let the Lord reign within me, I can’t reign together with him.
John 5:19: the Lord said “the Son can do nothing of himself” — the perfect model of selflessness.
John 14:12–13: the greater works are for the Father’s glory, not for building a greater self.

brief12.title: Putting It into Practice
notes: Ask: is it me reacting, or the Lord reigning?
Pray: Lord, you are my way
Act: one small act of selflessness each day
Let go, forgive one person, hand over control
Key points:
Practice 1: emotions are the most honest dashboard; give yourself three seconds before an outburst.
Practice 2: when challenges come, stop for thirty seconds and pray, “Lord, you are my way” (Proverbs 3:5–6).
Practice 3: start with light weights — let go of one insistence, forgive one person, hand over one area of control.
Worthington and colleagues’ meta-analysis (2014): forgiveness reduces depression and anxiety.
Deepen through the eight stages: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.

brief12.title: Closing and Call
notes: When “I” step back, Jesus steps in
When Jesus is Lord, there will be a way
Selflessness is not the self disappearing
but letting Jesus reign completely within me
Key points:
Quickly draw the three points together: the source, the way, the throne.
Selflessness isn’t losing yourself; it moves your worth onto a rock that will never be shaken.
Call: what is the thing you find hardest to let go of today? Loosen your grip before the Lord.
Point to the Two Core Values of 321: let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory.

brief12.title: Prayer of Response and Blessing

Reign as King within me
It is no longer I who live, but you
May all the glory go to Jesus
Key points:
Lead the congregation in reading the declaration of faith together.
Short prayer of response: hand over the steering wheel, hand over control, hand over that name we won’t forgive.
Blessing: may the Lord help us bear the ninefold fruit of the Spirit with every “2”.
Mention the two small-group discussion questions and encourage everyone to practise this week.

Romans 6:4: so we also might walk in newness of life.
The world is afraid of death, so it clings to itself; Christians know there is a resurrection, so they dare to let go.
Emphasise the wording of Romans 6:8 — read the full verse: “But if we died with Christ, we believe that we will also live with him.”

script: Brothers and sisters, good morning. Today we come together to Part 2 of “Selflessness — Entering Jesus’ Fullness and Victory”. Our key verse is Galatians 2:20: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” And the Lord Jesus also said, “I came that they may have life, and may have it abundantly.” This lesson has just one main thread: only when “self” is crucified can life overflow.

Brothers and sisters, please hold up one index finger, about ten centimetres in front of your eye, and look out of the window. You’ll find that this one small finger blots out a whole mountain. The finger hasn’t grown, and the mountain hasn’t shrunk; it’s simply too close to your eye. That’s what “self” is like. “Self” isn’t big, yet it can block out the whole of God. Where there is self, there are problems; where there is selflessness, there are none. That sounds harsh, but in fact it is the greatest grace. Because we can’t change our circumstances, but “self” the Lord has already dealt with on the cross. Brothers and sisters, we often think the problem lies with that difficult person or that job that never goes right. But the problem often isn’t our circumstances; it’s ourselves.

Brothers and sisters, Paul, who wrote this verse, was once Saul. He was a student of Gamaliel — highly educated, highly zealous, highly moral. And yet it was this towering “self” that sent him out to arrest Christians — until the light on the Damascus road threw him from his horse. Galatians is his earliest and most fiery letter, because some people wanted believers to add the law on top of believing in Jesus. Brothers and sisters, legalism is “self” dressed in holy robes. That’s why Paul says: I have been crucified with Christ. In the original it’s the perfect tense — it is already done.

Brothers and sisters, let’s look first at Key Point 1: “self” is the root of the problem. Jealousy is because I want what someone else has; strife is because I want to get what’s mine; irritation is because my feelings have been offended; worry is because I want to control the future; disappointment is because my expectations have fallen through. Five rivers, one source — and that source is “me”. James says that wars and fightings come from the pleasures that war in your members. Changing your job, your church or your surroundings won’t help, because you take “self” along with you.

Brothers and sisters, the Lord said, “If anyone desires to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me.” In the original, the word “deny” here is the very same word as when Peter would “deny me three times”. Did you hear that? The same action, and only two choices: deny self, or deny the Lord. Before the rooster crowed, Peter chose the second; after Pentecost, he chose the first. Psychology confirms it too: the more people focus their attention on themselves, the worse they feel. The Lord said long ago: don’t be anxious for tomorrow.

Brothers and sisters, Key Point 2: the self-centred life has no way through; selflessness has a way. The Lord said, “I am the way, the truth, and the life.” Notice that the Lord didn’t say he would point out a way; he said he himself is the way. Proverbs says there is a way which seems right to a man, but in the end it leads to death. It’s like sat-nav on your phone: if the location is wrong, even the best map will take you to the wrong place. “Self” is that false location. Selflessness means honestly recalibrating and saying: Lord, I don’t know the way; you are the way. Psychological research has also found that people often overestimate their control — we only think we’re in control.

Brothers and sisters, the Bible gives us three witnesses. At forty, Moses had eloquence and ability, yet couldn’t save a single person; at eighty he was slow of speech and slow of tongue, yet God used him to lead out a whole nation. Joshua wanted to draw up tactics before Jericho, but the commander of Yahweh’s army said, “No”; the moment he fell down in worship, he received the victory of marching round the city for seven days. Peter toiled all night and caught nothing, but with the words “but at your word”, the nets were close to breaking — and he left everything and followed the Lord. God says: I will make a way in the wilderness, and rivers in the desert.

Brothers and sisters, Key Point 3: selflessness lets us die, live and reign with Christ. Dying to the law loosens “I have to perform to be worth anything”; dying to the world loosens “I can only stand if others approve of me”; dying to sin loosens “I can’t help it”. When “self” dies, we are set free. Paul says, “But if we died with Christ, we believe that we will also live with him.” Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains by itself alone. Its intactness is its poverty.

Brothers and sisters, more wonderful still, God has made us alive together with Christ, raised us up with him, and made us sit with him in the heavenly places. Notice that last action — sit. Servants stand; masters sit. To sit means to reign. But there is only one throne. If “self” sits on it, the Lord can only stand outside the door and knock. If the Lord sits on it, we sit with him in the heavenly places. The Lord himself said: the Son can do nothing of himself. That is the most perfect model of selflessness, and the standard for our service.

Brothers and sisters, this week please practise three things. First, when emotions surge up, ask yourself: is this “me” reacting, or is Jesus reigning? Give yourself three seconds. Second, when facing a challenge, don’t rush into action; stop for thirty seconds and pray: Lord, you are my way. Third, each day practise one small act of selflessness — let go of one insistence, forgive one person, hand over one area of control. Psychological research has found that the first person forgiveness heals is the one who forgives.

Brothers and sisters, today we have walked through three key points: first, “self” is the root of the problem; second, the self-centred life has no way through, while selflessness has a way; third, selflessness lets us die, live and reign with Christ. When “I” step down, Jesus steps up; when Jesus is Lord, there will be a way through everything. Selflessness is not the self disappearing; it is letting Jesus reign completely within us. The Lord doesn’t want to take anything from you; the Lord wants to sit in the place that has always belonged to him. Brothers and sisters, this morning, what is the thing you find hardest to let go of? May the Lord give us the courage to loosen our grip. Let Jesus be King; let Jesus receive all the glory.

Brothers and sisters, let’s pray together. Lord Jesus, you loved me and gave yourself up for me. Forgive me — so often I climb down from the cross by myself and lift myself back onto the throne. Lord, today I choose selflessness. I hand you the steering wheel, I hand you control, I hand you the person I have never been willing to forgive. Reign as King within me, and make me bear the fruit of the Spirit. May you receive all the glory. In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen. May the Lord bless you and give you peace today.
Brothers and sisters, good morning. Today we come together to Part 2 of “Selflessness — Entering Jesus’ Fullness and Victory”.

Our key verse is Galatians 2:20: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me.”
The Lord also said, “I came that they may have life, and may have it abundantly.” In the original, “abundantly” means overflowing, more than enough.
This lesson has just one main thread: only when “self” is crucified can life overflow.
Brothers and sisters, please hold up one index finger, about ten centimetres in front of your eye, and look out of the window.

You’ll find that this one small finger blots out a whole row of trees, even a whole mountain. The finger hasn’t grown, and the mountain hasn’t shrunk; the only thing that has changed is the distance — it’s simply too close to your eye.
That is the truth about “self”. “Self” isn’t big, yet it can block out the whole of God; because it sits so close to us — so close that we take it for the whole world.
Every morning when we wake, the first thing we think of is “me”; every night when we lie down, the last thing we can’t let go of is still “me”.

Many Christians long for victory and long for peace, yet keep going round in circles of worry and wearing themselves out in comparison. We assume the problem lies with that difficult person or that job that never goes right.
But please hear this clearly: where there is self, there are problems; where there is selflessness, there are none. Because “self” is the root of the problem.

That sounds harsh, but in fact it is the greatest grace. If the problem lay in our circumstances, we would be forever powerless; but if the problem lies in “self”, then in Christ there is a sure way out.
Brothers and sisters, Paul, who wrote this verse, was originally called Saul, a star pupil at the feet of Gamaliel. Concerning the righteousness which is in the law, he said he was found blameless.
Highly educated, highly zealous, highly moral — it was precisely this towering “self” that sent him to Damascus to arrest Christians, until that light threw him from his horse.

Galatians is Paul’s earliest and most fiery letter. Because some people wanted the Gentile believers, besides believing in Jesus, also to be circumcised and keep the law. Brothers and sisters, legalism is “self” dressed in holy robes.
That’s why Paul says: I have been crucified with Christ. In the original it’s the perfect tense — it has already been accomplished.
Key Point 1: “self” is the root of the problem.

The lesson gives us five mirrors. Jealousy is because “I” want what someone else has; strife is because “I” want to get what’s mine; irritation is because “my” feelings have been offended; worry is because “I” want to control the future; disappointment is because “my” expectations have fallen through.
Five emotions, five outlets, but only one source — “me”. Brothers and sisters, as long as “I” am still the centre, the problems will never end.

Brothers and sisters, change your job, and the same frustration will come back with a different face; change your church, and the same friction will be played out again by a different cast. Because you packed up “self” and took it with you.
James laid this bare long ago: “Where do wars and fightings among you come from? Don’t they come from your pleasures that war in your members?”
He doesn’t ask, “Who have you been quarrelling with?” He asks, “Where does this come from?” He doesn’t treat the symptoms; he looks for the root of the disease.
“Self” is like that program on your phone that keeps running in the background, quietly eating up most of the resources. No wonder we so often feel tired and fed up without being able to say why.
In 1954 Festinger put forward his theory of social comparison: comparing upwards makes us feel inferior, comparing downwards makes us proud, and our sense of worth is forever tied to other people.
The Lord said, “If anyone desires to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me.”
In the original, “deny” means to disown completely, to cut off all connection. Brothers and sisters, this same word is used when the Lord said to Peter, “You will deny me three times.”

Did you hear that? The same action, and only two choices: deny self, or deny the Lord. Before the rooster crowed, Peter chose the second; after Pentecost, he chose the first. Life offers no third option.
The cross isn’t an ornament worn on the chest; it’s an instrument of execution carried on the shoulder.
But when Jesus lives in us, four things happen naturally.
First, I no longer need to compare myself with others, because the focus is no longer on me. 321 says: the focus is Jesus — not ourselves, not other people, not our circumstances.
Second, I can forgive those who hurt me, because the Lord has already been wounded in my place.
Third, I no longer chase the satisfactions of the flesh, because the Lord is my complete satisfaction. Augustine says: our heart is restless until it rests in you.
Fourth, I no longer live in anxiety, because the Lord rules over everything. “Self” makes us see limits; selflessness makes us see Jesus.
Key Point 2: the self-centred life has no way through; selflessness has a way.
Jesus said, “I am the way, the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father, except through me.”
Please notice that the Lord didn’t say, “I will point out a way”; he said, “I am the way.” Apart from him, we aren’t simply walking more slowly — we aren’t on the road at all.

It was the Last Supper, and Thomas asked: we don’t know where you are going; how can we know the way? Brothers and sisters, Thomas wanted a route map; the Lord gave himself. Because “self” wants a map, so that “I” can stay in the driver’s seat; God wants companionship, so that he can lead the way.
Scripture says, “There is a way which seems right to a man, but in the end it leads to death.”

Notice the words “seems right to a man”. People who walk into a dead end felt perfectly reasonable at the start. “Self” never says, “I’m going to hurt you”; it always says gently, “You ought to think of yourself.”
Sat-nav can only take you to your destination if it first knows where you are. If the location drifts, even the best map will take you to the wrong place. “Self” is that false location.

In 1543 Copernicus did just one thing: he moved the earth out of the centre and put the sun back there. A problem that had tangled people for a millennium suddenly fell into place. Many people’s lives grow messier and messier — not because they haven’t tried hard enough, but because the centre is in the wrong place.
The Bible gives us three witnesses.

At forty, Moses was mighty in words and works in the royal palace. In his own hot-blooded strength he killed an Egyptian and fled to the wilderness for forty years. When God called him, he said, “I am slow of speech, and of a slow tongue.” Brothers and sisters, the eloquent Moses couldn’t save a single person; the slow-tongued Moses God used to lead out a whole nation.

Joshua stood before Jericho wanting to draw up tactics, but the man with the drawn sword said, “No; but I have come now as commander of Yahweh’s army.” God never joins our side; God calls us to join his. The moment Joshua fell down in worship, he received the victory of marching round the city for seven days.

Peter toiled all night and caught nothing, yet with the words “but at your word I will let down the net”, the nets were close to breaking. And in front of the biggest catch of his life, he left everything and followed Jesus.
Brothers and sisters, please don’t misunderstand: selflessness isn’t passive waiting; it is active obedience.

Moses laid down his eloquence, yet he really did walk into Pharaoh’s palace; Joshua laid down his strategy, yet he really did march round the city for seven days; Peter laid down his nets, yet he really did put out into the deep.
Selflessness doesn’t mean doing nothing; it means no longer doing what “self” wants to do, and giving everything to doing what the Lord wants me to do.

321 says: life first, then relationships, then ministry. God says, “I will even make a way in the wilderness, and rivers in the desert.” Notice the place — not the plain, but the wilderness; because there, no one can take the glory for himself.
Key Point 3: selflessness lets us die, live and reign with Christ.
Dying to the law — Romans 7:4; dying to the world — Galatians 6:14; dying to sin — Romans 6:11.

Three deaths loosen three chains. Dying to the law loosens “I have to perform to be worth anything”; dying to the world loosens “I can only stand if others approve of me”; dying to sin loosens “I can’t help it” — because a master has no authority to give orders to a dead man.

When “self” dies, we are set free: no longer bound by the world’s values, no longer enslaved by sin’s temptations, no longer held hostage by people’s opinions. The Lord said, “The truth will make you free.”
The Lord said, “Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains by itself alone. But if it dies, it bears much fruit.”
A grain of wheat that refuses to die can stay intact and safe, but it will only ever be one grain. Its intactness is its poverty.

In 1972 three pathologists gave a name to a phenomenon: “apoptosis”. A great many cells in the human body die actively, following a set programme. In the embryo our hands start out like a webbed paddle, and it is precisely because the cells between the fingers die off that five fingers separate. When this programme fails, and cells that should die refuse to die, that is cancer.
Brothers and sisters, it is what should die refusing to die that is the disease. A Christian whose old self refuses to die won’t have a fuller life — only a more swollen one.
Paul says, “But if we died with Christ, we believe that we will also live with him.”
Brothers and sisters, dying together isn’t the end; it’s a passageway. Behind the Christian’s cross there is always an empty tomb.
Bonhoeffer said: when Christ calls a man, he bids him come and die. That isn’t pessimism; it is the shortest road to resurrection.
The world is afraid of death, so it clings desperately to itself; Christians know there is a resurrection, so they dare to let go. Do you dare to let go today?

More wonderful still, God has made us alive together with Christ, raised us up with him, and made us sit with him in the heavenly places. The original uses three “togethers” in a row, like a three-stage rocket, carrying someone who was dead in trespasses all the way to a seat in heaven.
Notice that last action — sit. Servants stand; masters sit. To sit on a throne means to reign.
But there is only one throne. If “self” sits on it, the Lord can only stand outside the door and knock; if the Lord sits on it, we sit with him in the heavenly places.

The Lord himself said, “The Son can do nothing of himself, but what he sees the Father doing.” That is the most perfect model of selflessness. So service no longer comes from the flesh, but from the Holy Spirit.
Next come the three practices.

First, when emotions surge up, ask yourself: is this “me” reacting, or is Jesus reigning? Emotions are the most honest dashboard there is. People can pretend; emotions can’t. In that instant, give yourself three seconds.

Second, when facing a challenge, don’t rush into action; first pray, “Lord, you are my way.” The two words “self” loves most are “hurry up”. But the Bible says, “Trust in Yahweh with all your heart, and don’t lean on your own understanding.” Stop for thirty seconds first.
Third, each day practise one small act of selflessness.
Let go of one insistence — perhaps simply letting the other person choose the restaurant tonight, or choosing not to say, “I told you so.”

Forgive one person — not waiting until it feels right, but making the decision by an act of will. In 2014 a meta-analysis by Worthington’s team found that forgiveness significantly reduces depression and anxiety. It turns out that the first person forgiveness heals is the one who forgives.

Hand over one area of control — the Bible says, “casting all your worries on him, because he cares for you.” Deepen these through the eight stages: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.
Brothers and sisters, let’s draw the 321 vision together.

The Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide. The Two Core Values: let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory. The Goal: establish God’s system.

The serpent said to the woman, “You will be like God, knowing good and evil.” “Like God” — that is the prototype of “self”. Pride is leaving our originally intended position and wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down power and returning to our originally intended position — letting man be man and letting God be God. Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility sparks humility, and both sides win.
Selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the infinite. A drop of water in the palm of your hand soon dries up; placed in the ocean, it takes on the vastness of the ocean.
The 920 practice says: everyone around us is our “2”. The hardest person to get along with in your life today isn’t your problem; they are your training ground.

Brothers and sisters, today we have walked through three key points: “self” is the root of the problem; the self-centred life has no way through, while selflessness has a way; selflessness lets us die, live and reign with Christ.
So the lesson says: selflessness is not the self disappearing; it is letting Jesus reign completely within us.
Selflessness doesn’t make you worthless; it moves your worth from a foundation that will collapse onto a rock that will never be shaken.

This morning, the Lord may be knocking gently at one particular door of your heart: a relationship you’ve held on to for a long time, a name you refuse to forgive, a plan you’re clutching tightly. The Lord doesn’t want to take anything from you; the Lord wants to sit in the place that has always belonged to him.
Brothers and sisters, let’s pray together.
Dear Lord Jesus, you loved me and gave yourself up for me. Forgive me — so often I climb down from the cross by myself and lift myself back onto the throne.
Lord, may your Holy Spirit shine on me, and let me see that behind jealousy, strife, irritation, worry and disappointment, the real name is “me”.

Today I choose selflessness. I hand you the steering wheel, I hand you control, I hand you the person I have never been willing to forgive. Reign as King within me, so that I do what I see the Father doing. May you receive all the glory. In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
May the Lord bless you and keep you; may the Lord make his face shine on you and give you peace. Brothers and sisters, today, let Jesus step in.
